items.descriptionOriginal: Την Τετάρτη 25 Νοεμβρίου 2026, στις 12 το μεσημέρι , στο Αμφιθέατρο του Νοσοκομείου «Άγιος Δημήτριος» , ο Ελληνικός Ερυθρός Σταυρός και το νοσοκομείο διοργανώνουν ενημερωτική και εκπαιδευτική ημερίδα με κεντρικό μήνυμα «Δεν είναι Ατύχημα. Είναι Βία.», εστιάζοντας σε τρεις ιδιαίτερα κρίσιμες διαστάσεις του φαινομένου: Την έμφυλη βία, την εμπορία ανθρώπων και τη βία κατά των επαγγελματιών υγείας. Στόχος της ημερίδας είναι η ενίσχυση της γνώσης και της ετοιμότητας των επαγγελματιών υγείας, οι οποίοι βρίσκονται συχνά στην πρώτη γραμμή αναγνώρισης και υποστήριξης θυμάτων βίας, αλλά και η ανάδειξη της ανάγκης προστασίας των ίδιων από περιστατικά λεκτικής, ψυχολογικής και σωματικής βίας. Η πρώτη θεματική ενότητα, «Η Έμφυλη Βία μέσα από το Βλέμμα του Επαγγελματία Υγείας», θα εστιάσει στην ασφαλή λήψη ιστορικού, στις κλινικές και ψυχοκοινωνικές ενδείξεις κακοποίησης, στην αποφυγή της δευτερογενούς θυματοποίησης, καθώς και στην ορθή καταγραφή και τεκμηρίωση των ευρημάτων. Η δεύτερη ενότητα, «Εμπορία Ανθρώπων: Αναγνωρίζοντας το Αόρατο Θύμα», αναδεικνύει τον καθοριστικό ρόλο των υπηρεσιών υγείας στην αναγνώριση πιθανών θυμάτων trafficking, με αναφορά στις σύγχρονες μορφές εκμετάλλευσης, στις ευάλωτες ομάδες πληθυσμού και στα εθνικά και διεθνή πρωτόκολλα διαχείρισης. Η τρίτη θεματική ενότητα, «Βία κατά των Επαγγελματιών Υγείας: Μια Νέα Καθημερινότητα», επικεντρώνεται στις επιπτώσεις της βίας στην ασφάλεια και την ψυχική υγεία του προσωπικού, αλλά και σε πρακτικές διαχείρισης επιθετικών συμπεριφορών, τεχνικές αποκλιμάκωσης και μέτρα πρόληψης και προστασίας. Η ημερίδα φιλοδοξεί να συμβάλει ουσιαστικά στη μετάβαση από την αναγνώριση στην έγκαιρη παρέμβαση και την προστασία, ενισχύοντας τον ρόλο των επαγγελματιών υγείας απέναντι σε ένα σύνθετο κοινωνικό και υγειονομικό ζήτημα που απαιτεί γνώση, εγρήγορση και συντονισμένη δράση. Εισηγητές στην εκδήλωση είναι οι εξής: Ο αστυνομικός Υποδιευθυντής Αθανάσιος Θολούλης, προϊστάμενος του Γραφείου Καταπολέμησης Διακίνησης και Εμπορίας Ανθρώπων της Υποδιεύθυνσης Αντιμετώπισης Οργανωμένου Εγκλήματος Βορείου Ελλάδος θα μιλήσει για την «Αναγνώριση πιθανών θυμάτων εμπορίας ανθρώπων» Η δικηγόρος – διαμεσολαβήτρια, νομική σύμβουλος του Ελληνικού Ερυθρού Σταυρού Μαριάννα Αθανασάκη θα αναπτύξει το θέμα: «Όταν η ιατρική εξέταση αποκαλύπτει τη βία: Η υποχρέωση των επαγγελματιών υγείας για αναφορά στις αρχές μετά τον Ν. 5172/2025». Ο υπεύθυνος του Αυτοτελούς Τμήματος Ελέγχου Ποιότητας, Έρευνας και Συνεχιζόμενης Εκπαίδευσης του Γ.Ν.Θ. «Γ. Γεννηματάς – Ο Άγιος Δημήτριος», Οργανική Μονάδα «Ο Άγιος Δημήτριος», νοσηλευτής ΤΕ Ευάγγελος Μπέλτσος, θα παρουσιάσει απολογιστικά στοιχεία, καθώς και τις ενέργειες που έχουν πραγματοποιηθεί για τη διαχείριση των σχετικών περιστατικών. Κατά τη διάρκεια της εκδήλωσης η Κοινωνική Υπηρεσία του Περιφερειακού Τμήματος Θεσσαλονίκης του Ελληνικού Ερυθρού Σταυρού θα παρουσιάσει διαδραστικό δρώμενο με θέμα «Κάτι συμβαίνει εδώ! Πριν το δεις, τώρα που το ζεις, μετά πως το κλείνεις». www.ertnews.gr

items.titleOriginal: I CAN Earthshot Challenge | How TN Students Turned Old Newspapers Into Waste Bags and Won $2,000

items.descriptionOriginal: At a school in Ammaiyappan, Thiruvarur district, a discarded newspaper found a new purpose. Instead of being thrown away, it was folded into a waste bag, fitted with jute handles and coated with melted crayons to make it resistant to moisture. The idea was to offer households an alternative to polythene bags while addressing another problem: the difficulty of managing mixed waste. The students behind the initiative, called Decom POSSIBLE, have now won the 'Build a Waste-Free World' category at the inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge, earning a $2,000 grant to further develop their work. The project is developed by students of SSATN Panchayat Union Middle School in Ammaiyappan (West), Tamil Nadu. Turning discarded paper into an alternative The bags were made using materials that were readily available to the students. Old newspapers formed the main body, while jute was used for the handles. Discarded crayons were melted and applied as a coating to help the bags withstand moisture. The students took the idea beyond the school premises. Over a period of more than 30 days, they visited households, distributed the bags and spoke to residents about waste segregation. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Earthshot Prize (@earthshotprize) The initiative was designed to address mixed waste disposal as well as the challenges sanitation workers face when handling waste that has not been separated at source. But the students' work did not stop with the bags. A composting pit at school, and a community centre revived At the school, the team established a composting pit measuring 8 feet long, 2 feet wide and 3 feet deep. Organic waste, once separated from other household and school waste, was placed in the pit and converted into manure within a month. This gave the students a way to demonstrate what happens when biodegradable waste is kept separate instead of being mixed with plastic and other discarded mater The initiative also extended to an existing community facility. Within two weeks, the students helped revive a previously inactive community composting centre, creating another avenue for processing organic waste locally. The challenge invited children between nine and 17 years to identify environmental problems in their communities and develop solutions that could be put into practice. Photograph: (Earthshot Prize) The project reports that its activities have benefited 502 people. It also led to a response from the local panchayat: following the initiative, the panchayat announced that waste would have to be separately segregated before collection from 1 October 2026. This local policy change is an important part of the project. Household-level segregation depends not only on residents separating their waste, but also on collection systems that maintain that separation. When wet and dry waste are mixed again during collection, much of the effort made at home can be undone. From a school initiative to a national platform Decom POSSIBLE was among 15 finalist projects selected for the inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge. The finalists represented nine Indian states and Delhi, and their projects addressed five environmental priorities: protecting and restoring nature, reviving rivers, lakes and oceans, cleaning the air, building a waste-free world and fixing the climate. The challenge was organised by The Earthshot Prize in partnership with Alana and Design for Change. It invited children between nine and 17 years to identify environmental problems in their communities and develop solutions that could be put into practice. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Earthshot Prize (@earthshotprize) The other winning projects included a low-cost cooling crate developed by students in Punjab to keep vegetables fresh in hot conditions, biodegradable diyas designed to reduce pollution in the Godavari in Maharashtra , and a natural-material air filter developed by students in Bengaluru. For the students in Ammaiyappan, the next step is to keep the practices going beyond the award. According to the project details published by The Earthshot Prize, they plan to encourage more households to adopt composting and take the model to neighbouring schools and panchayats. Their next challenge will be to sustain these practices and encourage more households to adopt them. Sources: 'Discover the Winners of the Inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge' : Published on 22 October 2026 'The Earthshot Prize, Alana and Design for Change Announce Finalists of Nationwide I CAN Earthshot Challenge' : By NewsVoir, Published on 23 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Ιστορικό ρεκόρ πωλήσεων αναμένεται να καταγράψει το Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), το πολυαναμενόμενο βιντεοπαιχνίδι της Rockstar Games, που κυκλοφόρησε την Πέμπτη (19/11) προκαλώντας παγκόσμιο ενθουσιασμό. Σύμφωνα με τις πρώτες εκτιμήσεις, οι εισπράξεις του ενδέχεται να προσεγγίσουν τα 2 δισ. δολάρια μέσα σε μόλις 24 ώρες, υπερδιπλασιάζοντας τις πωλήσεις που είχε σημειώσει ο προκάτοχός του το 2013. Η επιστροφή των παικτών στη θρυλική Vice City, μέσα από τις περιπέτειες του εγκληματικού διδύμου Λουσία και Τζέισον , εξελίσσεται σε ένα από τα μεγαλύτερα εμπορικά γεγονότα στην ιστορία της βιομηχανίας ψυχαγωγίας. Η Take-Two Interactive , μητρική εταιρεία της Rockstar Games, βρίσκεται μπροστά στην προοπτική να καταγράψει πρωτοφανείς εισπράξεις, έπειτα από χρόνια ανάπτυξης και τεράστιες επενδύσεις στην παραγωγή και προώθηση του παιχνιδιού. Παρότι η Take-Two δεν είναι τόσο αναγνωρίσιμη στο ευρύ κοινό όσο οι τίτλοι που εκδίδει, διαθέτει μερικές από τις δημοφιλέστερες σειρές βιντεοπαιχνιδιών παγκοσμίως, όπως το Red Dead Redemption και το NBA 2K . 19,1 εκατομμύρια αντίτυπα και έσοδα 1,84 δισ. δολαρίων Σύμφωνα με την εταιρεία ανάλυσης δεδομένων Sensor Tower , μέχρι το πρωί της Πέμπτης είχαν πωληθεί περίπου 19,1 εκατομμύρια αντίτυπα του GTA VI. Οι πωλήσεις αυτές αντιστοιχούν σε εκτιμώμενα έσοδα 1,84 δισ. δολαρίων για την Take-Two, ποσό υπερδιπλάσιο από τα περίπου 800 εκατ. δολάρια που είχε συγκεντρώσει το GTA V την πρώτη ημέρα κυκλοφορίας του, το 2013. Το GTA V θεωρούνταν μέχρι σήμερα ένα από τα μεγαλύτερα εμπορικά επιτεύγματα στην ιστορία των βιντεοπαιχνιδιών, έχοντας σημειώσει εξαιρετικές πωλήσεις κατά το πρώτο 24ωρο. Η Take-Two, ωστόσο, παραμένει προσεκτική στις δημόσιες τοποθετήσεις της. Από τον Ιούνιο, όταν άρχισαν οι προπαραγγελίες, έχει περιοριστεί να χαρακτηρίζει τη ζήτηση «πρωτοφανή» και «πολύ μεγαλύτερη από τις προσδοκίες». « Ο τίτλος αναμένεται εδώ και πάρα πολύ καιρό, οι καταναλωτές φαίνονται εξαιρετικά ενθουσιασμένοι και η μέχρι στιγμής δημοσιότητα είναι καθολικά θετική. Ωστόσο, δεν είμαστε ακόμη έτοιμοι να ανακηρύξουμε τη νίκη », είχε δηλώσει νωρίτερα τον Νοέμβριο ο διευθύνων σύμβουλος της εταιρείας, Στράους Ζέλνικ. «Συνηθίζουμε να αποφεύγουμε να μιλάμε για επιτυχία πριν αυτή πραγματοποιηθεί», είχε προσθέσει. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP) Πάνω από 1 δισ. δολάρια το κόστος παραγωγής Το GTA 6 συγκαταλέγεται στα ακριβότερα εγχειρήματα στην ιστορία της βιομηχανίας ψυχαγωγίας. Σύμφωνα με εκτιμήσεις, η Take-Two έχει δαπανήσει τουλάχιστον 1 δισ. δολάρια για την παραγωγή του παιχνιδιού , επενδύοντας παράλληλα σε μια εκτεταμένη διεθνή διαφημιστική εκστρατεία. Η προώθηση του τίτλου περιλάμβανε μεγάλες συνεργασίες και εκδηλώσεις που ξεπέρασαν τα όρια της παραδοσιακής αγοράς βιντεοπαιχνιδιών. Η Sensor Tower εκτιμά ότι η προβολή του διαφημιστικού βίντεο «GTA VI: Extended Look» στο Netflix τον Αύγουστο συνέβαλε στον εξαπλασιασμό των προπαραγγελιών. Στο Μαϊάμι, την πόλη που αποτέλεσε την έμπνευση για τη φανταστική Vice City, η τοπική ομάδα του NBA γιόρτασε την κυκλοφορία με έναν αγώνα αφιερωμένο στο παιχνίδι. Παράλληλα, στη Σεούλ της Νότιας Κορέας, θαυμαστές συμμετείχαν σε μουσική εκδήλωση για την κυκλοφορία του «GTA VI: The Album» , ενώ στην Μπανγκόκ της Ταϊλάνδης καταγράφηκε έντονη κινητικότητα σε χώρους ηλεκτρονικών παιχνιδιών. Μουσικό φεστιβάλ με Cardi B, Travis Scott και Metro Boomin Οι εορτασμοί για την κυκλοφορία του GTA 6 συνεχίζονται και το Σαββατοκύριακο, με τη διοργάνωση του «GTA VI: The Festival» . Πρόκειται για μουσική εκδήλωση με τη συμμετοχή γνωστών καλλιτεχνών της διεθνούς χιπ χοπ σκηνής. Στο πρόγραμμα περιλαμβάνονται η βραβευμένη με Grammy Cardi B , ο μουσικός παραγωγός Metro Boomin και ο ράπερ Travis Scott . Η σύνδεση του παιχνιδιού με τη μουσική βιομηχανία, τον αθλητισμό και τη δημοφιλή κουλτούρα αναδεικνύει τη θέση που έχει αποκτήσει η σειρά Grand Theft Auto ως παγκόσμιο πολιτιστικό φαινόμενο. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP) Το επόμενο μεγάλο στοίχημα: GTA 6 για υπολογιστές και online παιχνίδι Παρά το εντυπωσιακό ξεκίνημα, το ενδιαφέρον των επενδυτών στρέφεται ήδη στα επόμενα βήματα της Take-Two. Η εταιρεία δεν έχει ακόμη ανακοινώσει συγκεκριμένο χρονοδιάγραμμα για την κυκλοφορία του GTA VI σε προσωπικούς υπολογιστές (PC) ή για τη διάθεση της διαδικτυακής έκδοσης πολλών παικτών. Ορισμένοι αναλυτές της βιομηχανίας εκτιμούν ότι και οι δύο εκδόσεις θα μπορούσαν να κυκλοφορήσουν μέσα στο 2027 . Η διαδικτυακή λειτουργία θεωρείται ιδιαίτερα σημαντική, καθώς μπορεί να εξασφαλίσει στην εταιρεία συνεχή έσοδα από αγορές και πρόσθετο περιεχόμενο για πολλά χρόνια μετά την αρχική κυκλοφορία. Η χρηματιστηριακή εταιρεία TD Cowen έχει συμπεριλάβει την Take-Two στις επενδυτικές επιλογές που ξεχωρίζει για το 2027. Ο αναλυτής της, Νταγκ Κρόιτς, εκτιμά ότι οι μακροπρόθεσμες δυνατότητες εσόδων από το GTA VI είναι εξαιρετικά μεγάλες. « Το δυνητικό ανώτατο όριο των μακροπρόθεσμων επαναλαμβανόμενων καταναλωτικών δαπανών για το GTA VI είναι πολύ υψηλό », ανέφερε. Όπως εξήγησε, το σημαντικότερο ερώτημα για τη χρηματιστηριακή πορεία της Take-Two δεν είναι τόσο ο αριθμός των αντιτύπων που θα πουληθούν, όσο το πότε θα κυκλοφορήσει το επόμενο GTA Online και πόσο μεγάλη επιτυχία θα σημειώσει . Στο χρηματιστήριο, η μετοχή της Take-Two υποχωρούσε περίπου 1% την Πέμπτη, μετά την άνοδο 6% που είχε καταγράψει στην προηγούμενη συνεδρίαση. Με τις πρώτες εκτιμήσεις να τοποθετούν ήδη τις πωλήσεις σε επίπεδα ρεκόρ, το GTA VI επιβεβαιώνει την τεράστια εμπορική δυναμική της σειράς. Η επόμενη πρόκληση για την Take-Two είναι να μετατρέψει τον αρχικό ενθουσιασμό σε μια μακροχρόνια πηγή εσόδων. Αποθεωτικές κριτικές για το GTA VI – Τι εντυπωσίασε και τι απογοήτευσε Η υποδοχή του GTA VI από τους κριτικούς είναι σχεδόν ομόφωνα ενθουσιώδης , με το πολυαναμενόμενο παιχνίδι της Rockstar Games να συγκεντρώνει βαθμολογία 99 στα 100 στο Metacritic , ισοφαρίζοντας το ιστορικό ρεκόρ του The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time του 1998. Οι πρώτες αξιολογήσεις κάνουν λόγο για ένα από τα πιο φιλόδοξα βιντεοπαιχνίδια που έχουν δημιουργηθεί, με ιδιαίτερους επαίνους για τον τεράστιο ανοιχτό κόσμο του, τον ρεαλισμό των περιβαλλόντων και την ελευθερία εξερεύνησης. Η νέα Vice City , εμπνευσμένη από το Μαϊάμι, παρουσιάζεται ως μια ζωντανή πόλη, με χαρακτήρες που αντιδρούν στις κινήσεις του παίκτη, παράλληλες δραστηριότητες και λεπτομέρειες που ενισχύουν την αίσθηση μιας πραγματικής κοινωνίας. Ιδιαίτερα θετικά σχόλια συγκεντρώνει και η σχέση των δύο πρωταγωνιστών, της Λουσία και του Τζέισον , με αρκετούς κριτικούς να εκτιμούν ότι η Rockstar επέλεξε αυτή τη φορά μια περισσότερο προσωπική και συναισθηματική αφήγηση. Ωστόσο, δεν λείπουν οι επιφυλάξεις. Ορισμένοι θεωρούν ότι, παρά την ελευθερία που προσφέρει ο ανοιχτός κόσμος, οι βασικές αποστολές παραμένουν υπερβολικά προκαθορισμένες, περιορίζοντας τις επιλογές των παικτών. Άλλοι επικρίνουν τον αργό ρυθμό των πρώτων κεφαλαίων, τις συχνές κινηματογραφικές σκηνές και ορισμένα τεχνικά προβλήματα απόδοσης. Παρά τις επιμέρους αδυναμίες, η γενική εικόνα των πρώτων κριτικών είναι ότι το GTA VI ανταποκρίθηκε στις τεράστιες προσδοκίες που είχαν δημιουργηθεί κατά τη 13ετή αναμονή από την κυκλοφορία του προηγούμενου τίτλου. Οι αντιδράσεις για το GTA V: Βία, σεξισμός και βασανιστήρια Η σειρά Grand Theft Auto, πάντως, δεν έχει συνδεθεί μόνο με εμπορικές επιτυχίες και διθυραμβικές κριτικές. Το προηγούμενο παιχνίδι, GTA V, που κυκλοφόρησε το 2013, είχε προκαλέσει έντονες αντιδράσεις για την απεικόνιση της βίας, των γυναικών και των κοινωνικών στερεοτύπων . Ένα από τα πιο αμφιλεγόμενα σημεία ήταν μια αποστολή στην οποία ο παίκτης, ελέγχοντας τον χαρακτήρα Τρέβορ, υποχρεωνόταν να βασανίσει έναν κρατούμενο χρησιμοποιώντας διαφορετικές μεθόδους. Η συγκεκριμένη σκηνή επικρίθηκε επειδή μετέτρεπε τα βασανιστήρια σε διαδραστική δραστηριότητα, ακόμη κι αν η πρόθεση των δημιουργών ήταν να σατιρίσουν τις πρακτικές ανάκρισης και την κατάχρηση εξουσίας από τις αμερικανικές υπηρεσίες ασφαλείας. Σημαντικές αντιδράσεις προκάλεσε επίσης η απεικόνιση των γυναικείων χαρακτήρων , οι οποίοι, σύμφωνα με επικριτές του παιχνιδιού, περιορίζονταν συχνά σε στερεοτυπικούς ρόλους, χωρίς την πολυπλοκότητα που είχαν οι άνδρες πρωταγωνιστές. Η κριτικός Κάρολιν Πετίτ του GameSpot είχε χαρακτηρίσει το GTA V πολιτικά αντιφατικό και βαθιά μισογυνικό, παρότι το είχε βαθμολογήσει με 9 στα 10, αναγνωρίζοντας τα εξαιρετικά τεχνικά και δημιουργικά χαρακτηριστικά του. Η διαμάχη απέκτησε και εμπορικές συνέπειες. Το 2014, η αλυσίδα Target στην Αυστραλία απέσυρε το GTA V από τα καταστήματά της , ύστερα από διαμαρτυρίες πελατών για την απεικόνιση της βίας κατά των γυναικών. Οι υποστηρικτές του παιχνιδιού αντέτειναν ότι η υπερβολή, η βία και η προκλητική σάτιρα αποτελούν διαχρονικά στοιχεία της ταυτότητας του Grand Theft Auto, το οποίο απευθύνεται σε ενήλικο κοινό. Η παρουσία της Λουσία ως μίας από τους δύο βασικούς πρωταγωνιστές του GTA VI αποτελεί σημαντική αλλαγή σε σχέση με το GTA V , όπου και οι τρεις βασικοί χαρακτήρες ήταν άνδρες. Ωστόσο, η αλλαγή αυτή δεν σημαίνει αυτομάτως ότι έχουν ξεπεραστεί όλες οι παλαιότερες ενστάσεις για τον τρόπο με τον οποίο η σειρά αντιμετωπίζει τη βία και τα κοινωνικά στερεότυπα. Hanford, ένα παροπλισμένο συγκρότημα πυρηνικής παραγωγής στον ποταμό Κολούμπια, s…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sandia National Laboratories engineers have built a pipe-crawling robot called SPIINE, designed to inspect pipes as small as 2 inches (5 centimeters) wide at the Energy Department’s Hanford Site in Washington state, according to Sandia and a paper in the journal Robotics. Hanford, a decommissioned nuclear production complex on the Columbia River, stores radioactive waste in underground tanks linked by a network of pipes, Sandia said. The decades-old pipes must be checked. Some run hundreds of feet (60-plus meters), are double-walled and measure as little as 2 inches. Digging them up isn’t realistic or cost-effective, the release said, and it can’t show whether they are corroding from the inside. Earlier tools fell short, Sandia said. Push cameras reached only about 10 feet (3 meters) at a time and couldn’t get around tight 90-degree bends. Conventional ultrasound probes, which test pipe walls with sound, were often too bulky for small pipes with sharp turns. A flexible body for tight bends A Sandia team led by mechanical engineer Steve Buerger built SPIINE, short for Self-Propelled Interior Inspector for Non-destructive-testing Examination. Non-destructive testing means checking a material for damage without cutting it open. According to the Sandia release , the robot measures 2 inches by 6 inches (5 by 15 centimeters) and carries a high-resolution camera with adjustable LED lighting. Operators steer it with a standard video game controller. Buerger said the team “wanted a flexible body to let the pipe sort of guide the robot.” In the Robotics paper , the researchers describe a six-wheeled design that crossed a 90-degree elbow with a radius as small as 3 inches (76 millimeters) at eight tested entry orientations. In straight steel pipe, it pulled more than eight times its own weight, which could let it tow sensors. The team verified power and video over tethers up to 361 feet (110 meters) and drove the robot through more than 197 feet (60 meters) of mixed horizontal and vertical pipe. Unproven at Hanford The robot hasn’t been tested at Hanford. Sandia said lab tests have been successful, but real pipes could reveal new challenges. The paper says its experiments were meant to show feasibility and first-order model accuracy, not full statistical performance. It lists wheel endurance testing under repeated high-load elbow traversal as future work, and the electronics still sit on a separate trolley that is to be built into the body later. The release names more open problems. Hanford’s pipes may hold liquid sludge and caked deposits, and the team wants a self-cleaning function for the camera lens, a fail-safe recovery system in case the robot gets stuck, and smaller ultrasonic sensors that fit through a 90-degree turn. Ultrasonic wall-thickness checks may depend on those sensors. Team member Daniel McArthur said the first goal is simply a camera view inside the pipe to look for corrosion, cracks or other damage. The next step is a field test at Hanford. The paper appeared Oct. 22 in Robotics .

items.descriptionOriginal: Note: The Vyasa Project does not publicly disclose the names of children who contribute to its platform. The child featured in this story has therefore been identified by their chosen nickname. For a Class 5 student (nickname Super_Goalie) at Royal Concorde International School in Bengaluru, narrating a story meant becoming six different people at once. One of the stories the young reader chose was Arjuna and the Bird's Eye from the Mahabharata. Having heard it from their parents several times, the child knew the story well. But recording it for other children offered a new experience: bringing each character to life with a different voice. "I particularly enjoyed this one because I could use different voices for the five Pandavas and their guru, Dronacharya. It felt like I could become six different people all at once," he shares. "I had heard this story from my parents many times, so I already knew it well. But this time, I got to tell it in my own way and add my own style." For the child, it was an opportunity to have fun with a familiar story. But with every page read aloud and every recording made, children are also practising their reading, exploring expression and becoming more comfortable with their own voices. A Class 5 student brings characters from the Mahabharata to life by narrating 'Arjuna and the Bird's Eye' in different voices for other children. This is the idea behind The Vyasa Project, a free, non-profit audio library where children narrate stories for other children. The initiative brings together two simple pleasures: reading a good story and listening to another child tell it. Its founders hope that this experience will encourage more children to pick up books, enjoy reading and discover the confidence that comes with expressing themselves. When children become storytellers The process begins with children exploring a curated collection of stories on the Vyasa Project platform. They can choose from Panchatantra tales, Aesop's fables, folktales, abridged classics and poems. The collection includes stories in English, Hindi, Telugu, Bangla and Kannada and Marathi, allowing children to explore narratives in languages they are comfortable with. From the Panchatantra to Aesop's fables, the platform offers children a growing collection of stories they can read, narrate or simply listen to. Once they have chosen a story, children practise reading it before recording their narration. They can listen to their recordings, re-record them if needed, and submit them for review. Every submission is manually checked before being added to the library. If a recording cannot be published because of quality issues, the child receives detailed feedback to help improve it. The platform also has demonstration videos to help children and parents understand its features and navigate the process. For Karan S Kumar, co-founder of The Vyasa Project, the idea comes from his own childhood relationship with books. "I was the kind of child who always had a book open. Those stories took me to worlds I could never have reached otherwise, and somewhere along the way they shaped how I think, how I speak and how I see other people," he says. He wanted to bring that same sense of wonder to more children. The idea of children narrating stories for their peers became a way to make reading feel less like a lesson and more like a shared experience. "When a child narrates a story, something changes. They find their voice and their confidence, and they discover that what they have to say matters. And when another child listens, it feels less like being taught and more like a friend sharing something special," he adds. A library that grows with every child's voice The stories are selected to be age-appropriate, engaging and enjoyable, with interesting characters, humour, unexpected twists and meaningful themes. Priyanka Tadipatri, co-founder of the project, says the English collection began with stories from different storytelling traditions, including the Panchatantra, Arabian Nights, Grimm's fairy tales, Aesop's fables and Zanzibar tales. It also includes abridged works by authors such as Charles Dickens, Mark Twain, L Frank Baum and Oscar Wilde. Karan S Kumar and Priyanka Tadipatri, co-founders of The Vyasa Project, hope to make reading a shared experience by encouraging children to tell stories to their peers. The collection has since expanded into regional languages, with the founders hoping to add more Indian and international languages over time. Importantly, children do not have to record stories to use the library. They can simply listen to narrations uploaded by other young readers and explore stories across genres and languages. The founders have also deliberately kept the platform free of likes, comments and peer-to-peer messaging. Their intention is to create an experience similar to visiting a library: children come to discover stories, enjoy them and return whenever they want to read or listen again. For Madurai Sridhar, a grandparent whose granddaughter regularly uses the platform, this interest has been particularly encouraging. "My granddaughter asks me to log in to The Vyasa Project regularly. What she loves most isn't the listening; it's reading stories aloud and recording them for other children. We're strict about screen time at home, and this is one of the few things on a screen I'm happy to say yes to," he says. He adds that seeing his granddaughter so absorbed in the activity has been reassuring, especially when children often move quickly from one activity to another. The early response has been encouraging. Within three months of starting the project, the team received close to 700 recordings across languages, with several children contributing more than 10 narrations each. Priyanka says they have also noticed children becoming more comfortable with narration after initially hesitating. Some begin tentatively but grow more confident within just a few paragraphs. A young reader records a story for The Vyasa Project, helping other children discover the joy of reading through listening. "We do not expect children to have perfect pronunciation or error-free submissions. For us, it is more important that they have fun, enjoy the journey and hopefully fall in love with stories and books," she says. Nischala Agnihotri, a working mother and children's author of Yellow Kabbadi , believes the value of reading extends beyond developing language and cognitive skills. "It's not just about cognitive skills. Reading as a habit works at a deeper level. It builds the unseen. It works on their character, personality, and how they develop their first response and thinking patterns," she says. She believes that folklore, poetry and storytelling traditions can play an important role in shaping how children understand the world. For her, The Vyasa Project is helping bring these experiences to more children. Making reading a shared experience To encourage more children to participate, The Vyasa Project is organising Readers' Quest 2026, a seven-day online storytelling challenge during National Library Week, from 14 to 20 November. Open to children in Grades 1 to 7, or those aged 6 to 12, the challenge invites participants to contribute at least seven narrations during the week. Up to 20 winners across junior and senior categories will receive prizes, certificates, and an opportunity to attend a Voice and Storytelling workshop led by RJ Jayashree Raj. But for the founders, the larger idea goes beyond a week-long challenge or the number of recordings in the library. With every story narrated, The Vyasa Project hopes to inspire another child to pick up a book and discover the joy of reading. As Karan puts it, "A child doesn't have to narrate a story to benefit from the platform. Listening is just as central to the experience." And perhaps that is what makes the idea special. One child discovers a story, another finds the courage to narrate it, and someone else listens and feels inspired to pick up a book. With every new voice added to the library, another child gets an invitation to discover a world between the pages. All images courtesy of Priyanka Tadipatri and The Blooming Dale School

items.descriptionOriginal: The shame belongs to stigma, not to the person asking for help. “Just eat less.” “Move more.” “You need more discipline.” Is weight mainly the result of personal choices? Not quite. Choices matter, but they operate within biology, genetics, appetite, environment, health conditions and access to support. Why does that distinction matter? Because blame can delay care. Obesity is recognised as a chronic, complex and relapsing disease. A better conversation doesn’t ask, “Why can’t you control your weight?” It asks how weight may be affecting health, and what realistic, evidence-led management support is available. So keep building habits that support you: balanced meals, regular movement, strength activity and good sleep. And speak to a qualified doctor about what support is appropriate for you. Asking for medical help is responsible care, not weakness, failure or cheating. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #WeightStigma #Obesity #WeightManagement #HealthNotJudgement [weight is not a character test, weight stigma, obesity is a chronic disease, willpower and weight, weight management support India]

items.descriptionOriginal: P arc des Madelinots, a humble wedge of green space in the Verdun borough of Montreal, is not in the most tranquil of settings. The 6,500-square-foot pocket park sits beside a busy junction and is flanked on two sides by roads often filled with cars. For years, locals in the historically working-class neighborhood had to deal with the noise of constant passing vehicle traffic while trying to relax, meet with friends, play with their kids or, indeed, do anything else in this outdoor community space. But today, Parc des Madelinots is bathed in a very different kind of sound: the lap of ocean waves, dulcet bird calls and the crunch of sand underfoot. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape It’s not because a beach has suddenly arrived in Verdun. The sounds are recordings being broadcast in an attempt to reshape urban noise, fighting sound with sound in a constructive way to reduce noise-induced disturbance, reinvigorate the use of the public space and even preserve cultural memory for displaced communities. “Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource,” says Catherine Guastavino, a professor at McGill University and principal investigator of Sounds in the City , a research team that is one of the collaborators on Les Madelinéennes , the sonic project in Parc des Madelinots. “We can use sounds to improve people’s experience of places.” A field recording session at the Parc des Madelinots. Credit: Paysages During the course of the 20th century, many inhabitants of the Magdalen Islands, a remote archipelago in eastern Canada, were forced to relocate to Montreal, largely in search of work. Many of them ended up in the Verdun district, which today has the largest community of madelinots outside of the islands. Yet this highly urbanized area has a problem: It’s noisy and a far cry from the islanders’ former home. So Guastavino’s team joined forces with France’s Ircam , the Institute for Research and Coordination in Acoustics/Music — one of the world’s largest public research centers dedicated to both musical expression and scientific research — and Paysages , a Montreal-based studio specializing in immersive installations, to create a more agreeable and “soothing” atmosphere in the Parc des Madelinots. This was done while at the same time paying homage to and evoking the cultural heritage of the Magdalen Islands’ diaspora. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The installation consists of four minimalist, mounted speakers, set up in 2023, that play field recordings taken on the Magdalen Islands by Canadian sound artist Charles Montambault. The idea is that playing these natural sounds in urban areas can make them more relaxing, particularly when the sounds are familiar to residents. This method — actively cultivating the balance of sounds that are heard in any given space — is known as soundscaping. “We wanted to investigate how these coastal sounds could change the mood of the park, which had been mostly used as a place of transit,” says Valérian Fraisse, a soundscape researcher who helped prototype the installation. Urban areas are often noisy due to road traffic, construction, large cultural events and other factors. The impact of chronic noise exposure on human health is well-documented , from sleep disruption to reduced concentration and even cardiovascular disease, and cities have belatedly begun to take action. The Montreal project is part of a new wave of experiments looking to harness the power of sound rather than simply blot it out. “Sound is typically underused, it’s often considered as noise pollution,” says Guastavino. “There are detrimental impacts of noise exposure and I’m not playing that down. But sound can enhance the quality of urban experience.” A speaker (center) in Parc des Madelinots as part of the Les Madelinéennes sonic project. Credit: Paysages While the field of urban soundscaping is still emerging, similar yet simpler methods have long been used in public and private spaces, such as positioning park benches far from roads or playing music in elevators. But a growing number of innovative projects are sprouting up across the world. In Antwerp, Belgium, for example, “noise-canceling” fountains have been deployed to replace unwanted background noise like traffic. In Warsaw’s main train station, a set of stairs has been turned into giant interactive piano keys , creating a playful public space. Dating back further, Japan’s metro stations have long played out Hassha-merodii chimes to induce calm and prevent rushing, among other functions. For soundscaping to be effective it must take into account the specific contexts of each site, according to André Fiebig, a researcher and head of the working group on Psychoacoustics and Noise Effects at the Technical University of Berlin. “The solution can’t be to play sounds everywhere,” he says. “It needs to be adequate, appropriate and fit to the place.” The impact of a soundscape depends a lot on what Fiebig calls “psychoacoustic” qualities, such as how people perceive the source of noise. “People will complain about sightseeing buses, but almost never public buses,” he says. Ocean waves are usually considered relaxing, elaborates Fiebig, but if they are played everywhere then their impact lessens. And there are plenty of varieties of sound, not only loud and quiet, but sharp and subtle, strange, exciting and surprising, he adds. Soundscaper Fraisse agrees: “I don’t think there’s a universal approach we can apply to every space.” In the case of Les Madelinéennes , collaboration with residents in the development phase was important, though those involved admit it could have been more integrated. The process involved plenty of trial and error, says Fraisse, and for the first few weeks many residents didn’t even realize the installation was there. Indeed, the project was notably challenging since the park is at the intersection of roads. “An interesting result was the potential confusion,” he says. “The sound of waves could be mixed up with traffic noise.” But Fraisse, who is currently developing a methodology for creating effective sound installations, including acoustic measurement and user feedback surveys , helped adapt the sound frequency ranges so that it wasn’t mistaken for traffic, and toned down the use of boat horns, which while authentic weren’t perceived as relaxing. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape with Horn Meanwhile, the seagull squawks weren’t quite as evocative of home as hoped — there’s plenty of them in Montreal already, and they can often be a nuisance. “That’s why it’s so important to get feedback, to design site-specific interventions with people from the place itself,” says Fraisse. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape with Seagulls Emilie Bourgey, a resident of Verdun who was not involved in the survey, says that in the past she would not regularly go to the Parc des Madelinots due to the noise of the vehicle traffic. At times, she might briefly sit on a bench and look at the trees. But she discovered the sound installation in the summer of 2025 when walking near the kids’ play area, and that transformed her experience of the space. “I love the installation, the sound of waves, the birds, it’s very rejuvenating,” says Bourgey. “I come here specifically for the boost it gives me afterwards.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime A growing body of research is echoing the benefits of soundscapes. A review of 22 academic studies, published in 2026, found that natural soundscapes in urban areas “were consistently associated with improved mental health outcomes.” In 2024, a study of 2,000 passengers by British train operator South Western Railway found that natural sounds such as birdsong, rivers and rainfall reduced passenger stress levels by 35 percent. The Montreal installation, initially a pilot, has since become permanent. And the team wants to take the collaborative aspect to the next level. Instead of simply asking residents to evaluate sounds, it plans to involve them in the creation and selection of sounds next year as part of a third iteration of the project. “We have to try to understand their logic, what they prefer, and then try to find solutions,” says Fiebig. “It shouldn’t be decided from the top, it should be about co-creation, close cooperation between the locals and those running the project.” The post Montreal Is Harnessing Soothing Ocean Sounds to Combat Traffic Noise appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Early each morning in the month of Margazhi , a statistics professor would set out on his motorbike to watch women at work on their doorsteps. Gift Siromoney admired the kolams , but he was chasing a different question. How did women, many of them nonliterate, loop a line around a grid of dots, close it without error and repeat the feat from memory the next day? Working with his wife and fellow academic Rani Siromoney at Madras Christian College in Tambaram during the early 1970s, he concluded that the drawing follows rules precise enough to be written down as a formal grammar that a computer can run. A tradition older than the textbooks Every morning, women across Tamil Nadu sweep their thresholds, sprinkle them with water and cow dung, and trickle powder between their fingers to build symmetrical patterns, as the mathematician Marcia Ascher described in American Scientist in 2002. A kolam begins with a grid of dots called pulli , and tradition holds that the rice flour feeds ants and insects, so the day opens with an act of kindness. In the early 1970s, mathematician Gift Siromoney observed these drawings, curious about the rules guiding their creation. Siromoney traced the earliest mentions of kolam in Tamil literature to the 16th-century Madurai Meenakshiammai Kuram , followed by the 17th-century Thiru Kutraala Kuravanji . He also noted that older Tamil word lists, ancient paintings and travellers' accounts say nothing about the art, so its documented literary history begins only in the 16th century. A red pen and seven sheets of carbon paper To see how a kolam grows, Siromoney devised a trick. He stacked seven sheets of paper, interleaved them with carbon paper, and asked practitioners to draw with a red ballpoint pen, removing the top sheet and its carbon at the end of each stage. Every sheet then showed earlier strokes in black and the newest stage in red, which gave him a frame-by-frame record of the drawing. Skilled practitioners always drew the pulli first and then built the pattern stage by stage in its natural segments, which suggested that they remembered kolams as chains of smaller units rather than as whole pictures. Practitioners and novices differed in how well they copied unfamiliar kolam patterns, so Siromoney treated kolam drawing as a learned skill. T Robinson of the college's mathematics department adds that the women drew almost like the turtle moves of a programming language, with instructions such as go forward, turn left, and make a loop. How a folk art became a picture language With the computer scientist Kamala Krithivasan, the Siromoneys published 'Picture languages with array rewriting rules' in 1973 and 'Array grammars and kolam ' in 1974. Using seven sheets of paper and carbon copies, Siromoney documented how women built kolams, one stroke at a time. Their idea treated each kolam as a sentence in a pictorial language , where rules rewrite a small array of symbols into a larger one, much as grammar rules grow a sentence. Computer programs could then generate kolam patterns of a given type mechanically. Later researchers use these models, which they call Siromoney array grammars. The team also asked whether a pattern is made of one strand or several. For interlaced sikku kolam , Siromoney introduced operations called cut and join, which turn a single-strand pattern into a multi-strand one and back. Rani Siromoney and colleagues later noted that the same operations appear in the theory of circular DNA splicing. Why the discovery still matters For computer scientists, kolams supplied ready-made examples of existing picture languages and inspired new types, so a doorstep craft helped shape how machines draw and recognise images. None of this required the women to know any grammar. R Narasimhan, who worked alongside Siromoney, observed that a large share of practitioners were nonliterate and unaware that their designs have grammatical properties. The couple's school of formal language theory at Madras Christian College, he wrote, became one of the best and most active in the field. The research continues. A 2018 paper by K G Subramanian, T Robinson and colleagues generated kolams using membrane computing, a model inspired by living cells, and showed that it can produce designs that earlier array grammars could not handle. Subramanian did that work in the college's Department of Mathematics, so the research still runs from Tambaram. Kolams were one strand of a restless career. Siromoney also used computing to date medieval Tamil inscriptions, applied cluster analysis to sculptures at Mamallapuram and built what South First describes as the first teleprinter keyboard for Tamil. He died on 21 March, 1988, aged 56. Yet every Margazhi morning, the women whose hands inspired his grammar keep drawing, and the rules he glimpsed keep running quietly beneath their fingers. Sources ' Gift Siromoney, polymath who used AI concepts in the 80s to solve historical mysteries ': by Poorani Balendra for South First, Published on 21 March, 2023 ' KOLAM ': by T. Robinson for Chennai Mathematical Institute (Gift Siromoney memorial pages) ' The Kolam Tradition ': by Marcia Ascher for American Scientist, Published in January-February 2002 (Volume 90, Number 1) ' Generation of Kolam-Designs Based on Contextual Array P Systems ': by Ibrahim Venkat, T. Robinson, K. G. Subramanian and Philippe de Wilde for Springer (Diagrams 2018), Published in 2018

items.descriptionOriginal: Καθώς πλησιάζει ο χειμώνας, η γρίπη των πτηνών επιστρέφει στο επίκεντρο της υγειονομικής επιτήρησης . Ο ιός δε γνωρίζει σύνορα: Τα μεταναστευτικά πτηνά μπορούν να τον μεταφέρουν σε μεγάλες αποστάσεις, ενώ η ικανότητά του να μολύνει και ορισμένα θηλαστικά προβληματίζει τους επιστήμονες. Ο Εθνικός Οργανισμός Δημόσιας Υγείας (ΕΟΔΥ) παρουσιάζει την επιδημιολογική εικόνα και ενημερώνει για ένα σημαντικό μέτρο πρόληψης: Το δωρεάν πρόγραμμα εμβολιασμού κατά της γρίπης των πτηνών για εργαζομένους με αυξημένη επαγγελματική έκθεση. Η κυκλοφορία του ιού στην Ευρώπη και την Ελλάδα Κατά την αντίστοιχη περίοδο του 2025, η Ευρώπη είχε καταγράψει έντονη δραστηριότητα της γρίπης των πτηνών, με κρούσματα σε εκατοντάδες πτηνοτροφικές μονάδες και χιλιάδες περιστατικά σε άγρια πτηνά. Η Ελλάδα έχει επίσης αντιμετωπίσει περιστατικά κατά τα έτη 2016, 2017, 2021, 2022 και 2025. Σύμφωνα με τον ΕΟΔΥ, το πιο πρόσφατο καταγεγραμμένο περιστατικό εντοπίστηκε σε κύκνο στην Καστοριά, τον Απρίλιο του 2026. Ιδιαίτερη σημασία έχει και η καταγραφή του ιού σε πτηνοτροφική εκτροφή στην Πελοπόννησο το 2017, σε περιοχή όπου δεν είχαν προηγουμένως εντοπιστεί κρούσματα. Το γεγονός δείχνει ότι η μετακίνηση των άγριων πτηνών μπορεί να οδηγήσει στην εμφάνιση του ιού σε διαφορετικές περιοχές της χώρας. Γιατί ανησυχεί η μετάδοση στα θηλαστικά Η γρίπη των πτηνών δεν περιορίζεται αποκλειστικά στα πτηνά. Έχει καταγραφεί μετάδοση και σε θηλαστικά, μεταξύ των οποίων τα μινκ εκτροφής. Αυτό δε σημαίνει ότι ο ιός μεταδίδεται εύκολα μεταξύ ανθρώπων. Ωστόσο, κάθε μετάδοση σε νέο ζωικό είδος δημιουργεί πρόσθετες ευκαιρίες για γενετικές μεταβολές του ιού. Γι’ αυτό η παρακολούθηση της κυκλοφορίας του και η προστασία όσων έρχονται συστηματικά σε επαφή με δυνητικά μολυσμένα ζώα αποτελούν βασικές προτεραιότητες δημόσιας υγείας. Ποιοι δικαιούνται δωρεάν εμβολιασμό Όπως ενημερώνει ο ΕΟΔΥ , στην Ελλάδα εφαρμόζεται πρόγραμμα δωρεάν εμβολιασμού με εμβόλιο εγκεκριμένο από τον Ευρωπαϊκό Οργανισμό Φαρμάκων (EMA). Το πρόγραμμα απευθύνεται σε συγκεκριμένες ομάδες εργαζομένων που ενδέχεται να εκτίθενται στον ιό λόγω του επαγγέλματός τους: Εργαζομένους σε πτηνοτροφικές μονάδες. Εργαζομένους σε εκτροφές μινκ. Κτηνιάτρους εκτροφής. Εργαζομένους σε οργανισμούς φροντίδας και διαχείρισης άγριων πτηνών. Ο εμβολιασμός αποτελεί πρόσθετο μέτρο προστασίας. Δεν αντικαθιστά τον ατομικό προστατευτικό εξοπλισμό, την τήρηση των κανόνων υγιεινής και τα μέτρα βιοασφάλειας, που παραμένουν απαραίτητα για την πρόληψη της έκθεσης. Υπάρχει κίνδυνος από τα αυγά και το κοτόπουλο; Για τους καταναλωτές, ο ΕΟΔΥ δίνει μια σαφή διευκρίνιση: Η γρίπη των πτηνών δεν μεταδίδεται μέσω της κατανάλωσης αυγών και κρέατος πουλερικών που διατίθενται νόμιμα στην αγορά. Τα προϊόντα αυτά υπόκεινται στους προβλεπόμενους κτηνιατρικούς ελέγχους. Παράλληλα, το καλό μαγείρεμα παραμένει βασικός κανόνας ασφάλεια ς τροφίμων. Επομένως, η ανάγκη αυξημένης επιτήρησης του ιού δεν συνεπάγεται ότι οι πολίτες πρέπει να αποφεύγουν τα νόμιμα διακινούμενα προϊόντα πουλερικών. Πού μπορούν να ενημερωθούν οι ενδιαφερόμενοι Για περισσότερες πληροφορίες σχετικά με τη γρίπη των πτηνών και το δωρεάν πρόγραμμα εμβολιασμού, οι εργαζόμενοι μπορούν να επικοινωνούν με τον ΕΟΔΥ. Η στενή σύνδεση της υγείας των ζώων με την ανθρώπινη υγεία καθιστά την πρόληψη ιδιαίτερα σημαντική. Ο εμβολιασμός των ομάδων αυξημένου κινδύνου, η συστηματική επιτήρηση και η τήρηση των μέτρων προστασίας αποτελούν βασικά εργαλεία απέναντι σε έναν ιό που συνεχίζει να εξελίσσεται. Διαβάστε επίσης Γρίπη, Covid, RSV: Οι νέες συστάσεις εμβολιασμού για τον χειμώνα – Ποιους αφορούν Πόσο κινδυνεύει η Ευρώπη από Έμπολα, γρίπη των πτηνών και ιό του Δυτικού Νείλου Γρίπη των πτηνών: Ξεκίνησαν δοκιμές για νέο εμβόλιο – Θα γίνεται σε άτομα υψηλού κινδύνου

items.titleOriginal: ‘I Turned My MRI Into a Lotus Painting’: How Art Helped a PhD Scholar Fight Cancer & Paralysis
items.description: Ακόμη και στο δωμάτιο έκτακτης ανάγκης, η Sapna Singh ζήτησε από μια νοσοκόμα στυλό και χαρτί. Ήθελε να ζωγραφίσει. Εν μέσω μιας τρομακτικής ιατρικής έκτακτης ανάγκης, η τέχνη πρόσφερε στον 44χρονο κάτι οικείο να κρατηθεί. Μέχρι τότε, έκανε διδακτορικό στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο, βασιζόμενη σε χρόνια δουλειάς ως καλλιτέχνης και δασκάλα. Τώρα, προσπαθούσε να βγάλει νόημα από α…
items.descriptionOriginal: Even in the emergency room, Sapna Singh asked a nurse for a pen and paper. She wanted to draw. In the middle of a frightening medical emergency , art offered the 44-year-old something familiar to hold on to. Until then, she had been pursuing a PhD in the UK, building on years of work as an artist and teacher. Now, she was trying to make sense of a diagnosis that would change almost every part of her life. In February 2025, she began experiencing weakness in her left hand and leg. An MRI revealed a cancerous brain tumour, and a seizure soon left the left side of her body paralysed. She had moved to the UK with her 13-year-old son, Kabir, only a few months earlier. Her research was underway, and she had cleared her PhD proposal. Her attention shifted from her research and future plans to treatment and the demands of everyday life. After returning to India in April, she underwent brain tumour surgery. She had to relearn everyday movements and depend on others for tasks she had once managed without a second thought. Walking became a goal in itself, and even the easiest routines required patience. Through the uncertainty, however, she kept returning to her art. "Cancer made me a patient, but art reminded me that I was still Sapna," she says. From failing an entrance exam twice to earning a PhD scholarship Her relationship with art began long before she imagined it would help her through an illness. Growing up in a joint family in Delhi, she spent much of her childhood drawing. By Class 9, she was making portraits, and when it came time to choose a subject in Class 11, she opted for painting. In September 2022, she enrolled in a master's in design at Leeds Arts University in the UK, specialising in world-building and creature design. Turning that interest into a career took determination. She failed the entrance examination for Delhi's College of Art twice, in 1999 and 2000. She tried again, secured admission in 2002, and went on to graduate in 2006, ranking second in her final year. She later completed a diploma in 3D animation and multimedia and began working in exhibition and stall design. Around 2008, she married Akshay Singh, an entrepreneur from Meerut. Over the following years, she continued to build her career while making room for family life. The family moved to Dubai in 2016, where she found new ways to work with art. She began teaching and taking private classes in 2017. Later, she joined Manipal Academy of Higher Education in Dubai, teaching animation, media, and communication. Teaching kept her connected to the creative world, but Sapna was not finished learning herself. In September 2022, she enrolled in a master's in design at Leeds Arts University in the UK, specialising in world-building and creature design. She completed the course in a year, opening the door to another ambition. In 2024, she received a vice-chancellor's scholarship to pursue a PhD at the University for the Creative Arts. Her proposed research focused on the impact of artificial intelligence on creative education and hiring in the industry. "Returning to education after so many years helped me rediscover my confidence and gave me a fresh motivation to keep learning," she says. "I wanted to show myself that it is never too late to learn something new or chase a dream. For me, it was about much more than earning another degree. It was about giving myself the chance to begin again." In October 2024, she moved to the UK with her son, while Akshay remained in Dubai for work and visited them frequently. She settled into her new life and began working towards her research. After years of studying, teaching, and finding her way into new areas of art, she was ready for the next chapter. A few months into her PhD, everything took an unexpected turn Around 10 February 2025, she noticed that her left hand and leg were becoming weak. Kabir was the first to pick up on the change. At the time, neither of them realised how serious it would turn out to be. "I thought it was something temporary and that she would soon be back to normal. I never imagined things would get this serious," he says. She visited her general practitioner after a few weeks and was referred to Frimley Park Hospital. An MRI scan revealed a cancerous brain tumour. She was alone when she received the news. Her blood pressure rose, and she later suffered a seizure that left the left side of her body completely paralysed. The change was devastating. A woman who had spent years studying, teaching, travelling and managing her own life now faced the possibility of losing much of that independence. An MRI scan revealed a cancerous brain tumour. Soon, the family had to return to India for her treatment. She underwent brain tumour surgery at Fortis Hospital in Noida in April 2025, followed by chemotherapy, radiation, physiotherapy, rehabilitation, and anti-angiogenesis therapy. As treatment progressed, she had to adjust to a very different daily routine. Moving from her bed to a wheelchair, bathing, dressing, and using the toilet all required help. She also experienced fatigue and vertigo, while problems with her vision made some activities more difficult. For a period, her right eyelid remained closed. Although it has gradually opened, medication can still leave her vision blurred . The physical challenges were difficult, but losing the freedom to manage her own life took an emotional toll, too. "The hardest part was losing my independence. I went from managing my own life to needing help with basic everyday tasks. That change affected not only my body, but also the way I saw myself," she tells The Better India . Akshay had to adjust, too. Before her illness, his wife was fiercely independent. She travelled on her own, pursued her studies, taught, and managed family responsibilities. Now, he was helping her through the most basic parts of the day while also caring for Kabir and keeping up with work. He cooked fresh meals to take to the hospital and spent as much time as he could with Sapna. Leaving her alone in the ward at night was especially hard. "There were moments when I would look at her and think, 'How did our life change so much, so quickly?'" he says. He wanted to make things easier for her, but he also understood that help could not replace what she had lost. For her, being able to do things for herself had always been important. "You want to help, but you also know that the thing she wants most is not help. She wants her independence back," he adds. Regaining that freedom has been a slow but consistent process. At first, she needed four people to help her walk. Over time, that number came down to three, then two, and eventually one. She has recently managed a few steps without support. She has also progressed from using a bedpan to a portable commode and later to using the toilet with assistance. These changes have taken time, and recovery has come with its share of complexities. Still, each improvement has given her something concrete to work towards. "I coped by focusing on very small improvements rather than thinking too far ahead," she explains. When an MRI scan became a painting of a lotus Even before she knew what her recovery would look like, Sapna had found a way to cope with the uncertainty. During the medical emergency, she continued sketching, keeping her materials close by. She represented the tumour as a lotus, a flower she associated with wisdom and awakening. "In the emergency room, I asked a nurse for a pen and paper to draw. It was just my coping mechanism to take my thoughts away from the uncertainty and chaos," she says. Her right hand, the one she used for painting and writing, remained functional. That gave her a way to return to a familiar part of herself, even as other parts of her life felt unfamiliar. Drawing also allowed her to express feelings that were difficult to put into words, from fear and frustration to loneliness, hope, and gratitude. One painting was based on her own brain MRI. She represented the tumour as a lotus, a flower she associated with wisdom and awakening. The scan that had delivered frightening news became the subject of a work she could interpret in her own way. Painting was not always easy . Her vision problems made it harder to work with fine details, which had been an important part of her practice. Rather than stop, she began adapting her approach, experimenting with patterns and finding different ways to create. Akshay has watched her work around these limitations. For him, seeing her paint is a reminder that her identity extends beyond her illness. "When she paints, I see her reconnecting with the person she has always been, not just the patient she has become," he says. He has seen how difficult it can be for her to work when her vision is affected, but also how determined she is to find another way. "For an artist, whose work depends so much on observation, detail, colour, and visual control, this could have easily become another reason to stop. But she did not stop. Instead, she adapted," he says. Art has not removed the challenges of recovery, but it has given Sapna a way to keep expressing herself while she works through them. She has continued painting and has also started writing about the turning points in her life, including the difficult moments she has experienced during treatment. Her son has seen how much effort this takes. Kabir, now in Class 8, notices the small changes in her recovery as well as her strength to keep working. "Nowadays, she can open her right eyelid and manages to eat by herself," he says. For her son, these changes are part of seeing his mother gradually regain some of the abilities she had lost. He has also watched her continue to work towards her goals, even when recovery has made everyday life harder. "Art has become a kind of therapy for my mother during her recovery. Even with all the challenges she faces, she continues to paint, write her autobiography, and plan exhibitions. She is determined to see her dreams through, and watching her keep going has been inspiring for all of us," he says. That aspiration has already taken her back to an exhibition. In March 2026, she participated in a four-day College Mate exhibition at a gallery near Parliament House in Delhi. After months of treatment and rehabilitation, it gave her the chance to share her work with an audience again. Art has not removed the challenges of recovery, but it has given Sapna a way to keep expressing herself. She is now planning a solo exhibition and hopes to publish an autobiographical book. Alongside these projects, she wants to return to her research and complete the PhD she began in the UK. Learning to measure progress differently Sapna's recovery is still underway. She continues to need help with everyday activities, and walking independently remains a goal. Fatigue and vision problems can also limit what she is able to do on some days. Her life is not the one she imagined when she moved to the UK in 2024. But she is finding ways to make space for the things that matter to her, even as she learns to live with the changes brought on by her illness. Her husband says her ambitions have not disappeared with the changes to her physical abilities. "Her body has gone through a huge change, but her dreams, inquisitiveness, and zeal are still very much alive," he says. "Her circumstances have changed, but she has not lost herself." For her, moving forward does not mean pretending that the past year has been easy or expecting herself to return to the person she was before her diagnosis. It means allowing recovery to take the time it takes, while continuing to work towards the things she still hopes to do. She wants to regain more independence, return to research, and keep creating. Some days are spent focusing on her health; on others, she paints or writes. The progress may be slower than she once expected, but she is learning to recognise it on its own terms. "This experience has taught me that starting over does not always mean beginning from zero. Sometimes it means continuing from a completely different place, with a different body, different circumstances, and a different understanding of life," she says. She knows that recovery cannot be rushed and that the plans she once made may take longer to realise. For now, she is learning to measure progress on her own terms. "Your timeline may change, but that does not mean you have to abandon your dreams. Give yourself permission to move slowly and redefine what progress looks like," she says. Sapna still has a long way to go in her recovery, and the PhD remains a goal she hopes to return to. There is no definite timeline for what comes next. Sapna still has a long way to go in her recovery, and the PhD remains a goal she hopes to return to . Right now, she is taking things one step at a time, making art when she can and putting her experiences into words. "I am still learning, creating, and hoping. For me, that itself is a form of moving forward," she says. All pictures courtesy Sapna Singh.

items.title: Η Google εμφανίζει κβαντική συμφραζόμενη στα 105 qubits καθώς το τσιπ Willow ξεπερνά τα κλασικά όρια

items.description: Η Google έχει επιδείξει κβαντική συμφραζόμενη στον κβαντικό επεξεργαστή Willow, δείχνοντας ότι η ασυνήθιστη ιδιότητα της κβαντικής μηχανικής μπορεί να παραμείνει σε μεγάλα συστήματα και να βοηθήσει στη συγκριτική αξιολόγηση του υλικού. items.descriptionOriginal: Google has demonstrated quantum contextuality on its Willow quantum processor, showing that the unusual property of quantum mechanics can persist across large systems and help benchmark hardware. The experiments tested whether quantum processors could outperform classical strategies in several tasks, including a game built around a mathematical paradox. The results could help researchers understand what gives quantum computers an advantage and develop better ways to measure their performance. In a paper published in Science , the Google Quantum AI team reported that its processor won the so-called magic square game 98.3 percent of the time, exceeding the maximum classical success rate of 88.89 percent. The researchers also demonstrated quantum-classical separation in tasks involving systems of up to 105 qubits. A quantum advantage Quantum contextuality describes how the outcome of a measurement can depend on which other compatible measurements are performed alongside it. In other words, a quantum system cannot always be described as having fixed properties waiting to be revealed by observation. The team illustrated the concept using a 3-by-3 grid in which every row must multiply to positive one and every column to negative one. No grid can satisfy both rules because the total number of negative entries would have to be both even and odd. In the magic square game, two players receive a row and a column and must provide matching values at their intersection without communicating. A prearranged classical strategy can win at most eight of nine rounds. Quantum correlations, however, allow the players to win every round in principle. Google tested all nine versions of the game 100,000 times each. Its Willow processor achieved a 98.3 percent win rate, with hardware noise accounting for the remaining losses. The researchers also measured contextuality using a Bell–Kochen–Specker inequality. The processor recorded a value of 5.590, comfortably above the classical limit of four and approaching the quantum limit of six. Testing larger systems The team then examined whether contextuality could survive as more qubits were added. In a separate Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) parity game, the processor remained above the best classical performance as the number of participating qubits increased to 71. Researchers also ran a hidden-linear-function problem using shallow quantum circuits across processor grids of up to 105 qubits. The system maintained success probabilities above the classical threshold, although performance declined as noise increased with system size. Beyond demonstrating quantum behavior, the experiments revealed a practical use for contextuality tests. The team said the tasks exposed subtle coherent errors that conventional random-circuit benchmarks can overlook. These tests could provide a more demanding measure of hardware quality by comparing a processor’s performance with fixed limits set by quantum mechanics. Such measurements may be useful for evaluating systems intended to run structured algorithms, including simulations relevant to chemistry and materials science. The findings also connect contextuality with magic states, which are important resources for running full algorithms on error-corrected quantum computers. Google said its results offer a way to investigate how this property contributes to quantum computing’s potential advantage.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) have identified a region of the human brain that helps generate spoken words before a person begins talking, challenging a 150-year-old understanding of how speech is processed. The discovery suggests that the brain’s systems for understanding and producing speech are more closely connected than previously thought. It could also help improve surgical procedures that map speech-related brain regions and open new possibilities for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) designed to restore communication. In a study published November 19 in Science , researchers led by Edward Chang identified a small region within Wernicke’s area that becomes active before a person speaks. The region generates a blueprint for the next intended word, rather than simply processing its meaning or monitoring the sound of speech. The finding addresses a longstanding puzzle in neuroscience. Damage to Wernicke’s area, traditionally associated with understanding language, can also affect a person’s ability to produce words. Revisiting a century-old theory In the 1870s, German neurologist Carl Wernicke observed that patients with damage to the posterior temporal lobe experienced difficulties understanding and producing speech. He proposed that the region contained an “auditory image of words” that helped translate intended words into the movements required for speaking. However, because the region sits within the auditory cortex, it came to be viewed primarily as a center for speech comprehension. Speech production was instead associated with other parts of the brain. The new research points to the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), a subregion within the same general area Wernicke identified. Researchers found that neurons there become active about a quarter-second before a person begins saying a word. This activity encodes properties of entire words, including their length, number of syllables, and frequency of use. Neurons in brain regions responsible for controlling the mouth then translate this information into the movements needed to speak. The researchers also found that neurons involved in hearing speech sit alongside, and sometimes overlap with, those that generate word blueprints. This proximity could help explain how humans learn to turn words they hear into words they can say. New possibilities for speech BCIs The findings could also change how surgeons identify speech-related regions of the brain before operations, potentially reducing the risk of disrupting a patient’s ability to communicate. The lpSTG may offer another target for BCIs that translate brain activity into speech. Current speech BCIs decode signals from motor regions that control the vocal tract. However, those areas can be damaged in some people who have lost the ability to speak. Because the lpSTG becomes active earlier in the speech-production process, it could provide an alternative source of signals for decoding intended words. In a proof-of-concept experiment, researchers used activity in this region to decode both intended words and heard speech in a person with severe paralysis who could no longer speak. The researchers believe the region’s involvement in both incoming and outgoing speech could eventually help BCIs support two-way communication, allowing people to participate more fully in conversations. The findings establish the lpSTG as an important part of the brain’s speech-generation process, rather than a region dedicated only to understanding language. They could provide a new foundation for technologies designed to restore communication in people with speech impairments .

items.descriptionOriginal: Many of us are fortunate to have a wildlife preserve right in our backyards, or just outside of our windows. City, rural, suburban—almost anyone can look outside and find a squirrel, a chipmunk, or even a strange insect we’ve never seen before. Perhaps the most common animal most humans see on an everyday basis is also the most fascinating: Your ordinary backyard birds . While not as intelligent and mysterious as the crow or raven, these birds are surprisingly adept at forming bonds with humans nonetheless. More than backyard birds than meets the eye Robins, house finches, and sparrows are wildly common in most parts of America. More regional, but still extremely common, are cardinals, blue jays, chickadees, and even magpies. Many of these songbirds are so commonplace, in fact, that we barely notice them. We’re more interested in rarer finds like the fox, deer, coyote, or hawk. But more rewarding than getting a passing glance at a fox might be making friends with the birds who visit, and live in, our yards every single day. These friendships can be wildly rewarding. Literally, some of these backyard songbirds will perch on you once you gain their trust. Some of them may even start to bring you gifts. Why birds give gifts to humans Again, crows get most of the good press when it comes to human-animal friendships. They’re incredibly smart and good at remembering faces. They’re also famous for giving presents to people they trust. For people who feed them, crows have been known to leave behind shiny things like tinsel, foil, or found jewelry. They might leave a pebble or a nice twig, or even a feather. Some people swear the crows have “made” them unique presents. The National Audubon Society writes of a person who, after feeding crows, found a “short pine sprig with a soda tab threaded through the end” several times in the same feeding spot. Not many people know that “regular” backyard birds can do this, as well. It’s particularly common in bird species that are related to crows like fellow corvids magpies and jays. Gift giving in birds is a deeply instinctual behavior. They use it in their courtship rituals, to reinforce social bird-to-bird bonds, and even sometimes just for fun. Chirp writes, “Play-based gifting is another way birds connect and collaborate with each other. Young birds pass pinecones, twigs, and other on-hand objects in playful exchanges, even engaging in tug-of-war and ‘keep away’ games. These activities help birds develop dexterity, explore their environment, and connect with other birds.” It’s hard to know exactly why birds seem to give gifts to humans who feed them. It could be a token of appreciation, or it could be because they accidentally dropped something and then food showed up—and they want to see if it will happen again. But we can all agree that, no matter what the intent, it’s still pretty flattering. Other benefits of befriending backyard birds Not everyone who feeds and makes friends with their local magpies, blue jays, sparrows, or robins will start receiving presents. It’s an unpredictable behavior, at best, and even more rare in the non-corvids (like sparrows and robins). But there are still tons of amazing benefits to interacting with the birds outside your window. Scientific studies have shown that watching, feeding, and interacting with birds has an incredible effect on overall well-being A study from Virginia Tech found that “People described feeling joy, gratitude, hope, and calm when they fed birds. Some said watching birds helped reduce stress or gave them something positive to focus on during difficult periods, such as illness or experiencing a death in the family.” Plus, responsibly feeding and caring for birds gives a major boost to your immediate ecosystem. Having more birds around helps control pests and even improves biodiversity when they spread seeds as they fly and eat. Everybody wins. 4 easy steps to make bird friends By now you’ve probably realized that the best way to make friend with birds is to feed them. But the real key is patience and consistency. 1. Experts advise putting out fresh food and water in feeders on a set schedule—the same time every day. Even wearing the same outfit and standing or sitting in the same spot can help the birds get used to your presence. 2. Use yummy, nutritious foods like bird seed and not processed human food. Never feed birds bread or crackers. 3. Over a period of time, you can start to gently move closer to the birds as they eat. Once they’re used to you and understand you mean no harm, they may allow you to come closer and closer. 4. Eventually, you can try putting some seed in your hand and leaving it extended. Once the birds like and trust you, they may perch and eat right from your hand. Finally, do yourself and the birds a favor and keep your cats inside. Domestic and feral cats kill over two billion birds a year , and they’re much less likely to become your friends if they’re terrified to set foot in your yard. It’s good for you and it’s good for the birds when you take the time to become friends. At the very least, it’s well worth your while to pause for a second the next time you look out the window and take these beautiful and fascinating creatures in. The post The common backyard birds that can remember your face, and sometimes bring you gifts appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Actress Audrey Hepburn was known for her classic beauty. From her full brows to her signature bangs, Hepburn’s stunning appearance always stood out on the silver screen. And Hepburn embraced aging gracefully . She famously rejected any plastic surgery or enhancements, and was proud of her wrinkles . Family members and others close to her have shared stories on her beauty philosophy over the years. And one story in particular is a stand out—with Hepburn refusing to have her wrinkles erased from one of her favorite photos of herself during her devoted work for UNICEF. Audrey Hepburn accepted her wrinkles Later in her life, Hepburn became a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador in 1988, and was devoted to helping people in need around the world. For her advocacy work, she earned the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1992. Hepburn’s granddaughter, Emma Ferrer, told PEOPLE in 2017 a story about her grandmother that “truly embodies her concept of beauty”, on how Hepburn refused to have her wrinkles removed from one of her most beloved UNICEF photos taken by John Isaacs, a photographer for the United Nations and National Geographic . American Photo magazine asked Hepburn to choose the photo she loved most, and it was one where her smile revealed wrinkles. “John called and asked her if she wanted him to do some Photoshop, because you could see her wrinkles. She told him, ‘Don’t you dare touch any one of those wrinkles, I earned every single one of them.'” Ferrer added, “She never once thought of getting plastic surgery. For her, wrinkles were symbols of age, experience and wisdom.” Audrey Hepburn’s thoughts on plastic surgery Pamela Keogh, author of Audrey Style , also told PEOPLE more about Hepburn’s beauty philosophy and her thoughts on plastic surgery. “Audrey never touched her face. In those days, there was no Botox. She would have had to have a facelift. Audrey never, ever did a thing,” she said. And Hepburn’s two sons, Sean Hepburn Ferrer and Luca Dotti, also shared more on their mother’s beauty philosophy with the publication. That said, she didn’t judge other women who chose plastic surgery, Dotti explained that while his mother didn’t opt for plastic surgery herself, she believed other women should have the choice and not be judged. “She wasn’t against plastic surgery,” he told PEOPLE. “She said, ‘If you really are unhappy about a feature about yourself that really depresses you… A woman should be free to indulge in whatever she pleases.’ She didn’t have a mantra that was for anybody else.” Ferrer added more on her thoughts of aging gracefully as an actress, sharing, “She always used to say, ‘I’m too old to be the love interest and too young to be the grandmother.’ She felt that in Hollywood. That’s ingrained in the 40s and 50s.” And in the book titled Intimate Audrey: An Authorized Biography , co-written by Ferrer and Wendy Holden, they also noted , “Any suggestion of plastic surgery was anathema to her, as she honored the history of every line on her face.” The post Audrey Hepburn gave a beautifully defiant response when a photographer offered to erase her wrinkles appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Before 86-year-old went viral for singing ‘Landslide,’ she had a job in Dallas that few karaoke singers can claim
items.description: Η Carole Wade τραγουδάει όλη της τη ζωή. Η βελούδινη φωνή της και η βαθιά σύνδεσή της με τους στίχους δεν χάνονται στους ακροατές.
