Μια εκδήλωση καραόκε πραγματοποιήθηκε μια ζεστή Κυριακή μετά…
items.descriptionOriginal: Carole Wade has been singing her whole life. Her velvety voice and deep connection to the lyrics she belts are not lost on listeners. At 86 , she continues to let that voice soar. She became known to Upworthy readers last year when I met her by chance at my mother’s senior living facility in Dallas. A karaoke event took place on a warm Sunday afternoon in July. Wade sang Fleetwood Mac’s “Landslide,” bringing the room to tears. We shared that clip, and millions of people heard and shared it too. View this post on Instagram But there’s even more to unveil about Wade’s fascinatingly brilliant life. Before she wowed audiences at senior karaoke and before she was in her local Dallas band, she sang backup for not one, not two, but three Elvis impersonators. I had a second chance to interview her and find out more. How it all began How did you land the job originally singing backup for Elvis impersonators? “I had a guy friend that I had known that was into music. And he knew the first (Elvis impersonator) that I worked with. His name was Steve West. I ended up knowing him over 20 years. So, we got together with him, and got to working, and did quite a bit of stuff. He thought he was Elvis, I think, really. And when he wasn’t performing, he was wearing clothes like Elvis, you know, the big sleeves and all that. But bless his heart. Now he died a couple of years ago. He had heart problems. His family is still good friends of mine. And so that’s how I got to start. He was the first one.” So he was doing these shows in Dallas and asked you to come sing backup? “Yes, and we did clubs and restaurants and, oh, anything he could, you know, on the holidays. We did the state fair. We did that. It was fun. It really was. He was easy to work with because I’d worked with him for so long.” Were you already an Elvis fan? “I was, but I wasn’t a maniac fan. You know. I didn’t go crazy. And I never did see one of his shows live, which I wish I had. Yeah, I liked Elvis. I really did. And I loved his songs. In fact, right now, in karaoke, I do ‘Burning Love.’” I love “Suspicious Minds.” “Oh, that’s my favorite. I didn’t think about that. I may do that one too, then. Oh, that’s nice. You reminded me about that one. Oh, that’d be a good one to do at karaoke.” When you were singing backup, did your appreciation for Elvis’s music grow? “Yeah, it did. It sure did. It definitely made me appreciate it more and note the songs and be familiar with them.” She couldn’t help falling in love Were there any songs that stood out as the toughest to sing, as far as range? “Well, yeah, um, oh, gosh, the last one of the night, he always sang, ‘Can’t Help Falling in Love.’ That had some highs in it. But we managed. It wasn’t bad at all. I don’t think I really ever had a problem harmonizing with that.” What about outfits, hair and makeup? Did you have to match his energy? “Yeah, well, this depended [on] where we were working. If we were doing something that required an evening gown or whatever like that, I would do that. And then the rest of the time, it was just normal. We tried to kind of duplicate what Elvis did, and what his backup singer did.” How many backup singers were there? “I worked with Steve longer than any of them, and some of them would come and go, and there usually would be about three of us. And sometimes four. But it just depended on who was working with us at the time.” You worked with other Elvis tribute artists as well, not just Steve. Was that before your band (Psychedelic Oatmeal) formed? “Yeah, it was. It was before my band all started.” Was Steve the best impersonator or was there another one that stood out? “Steve was really good. But we worked with a young guy that just popped up. And he was like, oh, my gosh, he must have been 18, 19 years old when he started. His name was Johnny Lovett. And, believe it or not, he has passed away too. He turned out to be really, really good. And, on top of that, he was real funny. He was kind of a comedian. And he would, you know, do things like that on the stage.” They were all fabulous Who else did you work with? “And then I worked also with George Campisi.” (The Campisi family had quite the legacy in Dallas, ultimately running one of the most popular Italian restaurants, Campisi’s, often frequented by Jack Ruby). “Now, we, we traveled a little bit with him. That was after Steve, I was kind of going back and forth with him. And, so when George would call, you know, we’d go do a job with him, because, you know, the music so well, you don’t have to rehearse that much. George was very good, and he looked Italian. He was a very, very nice guy. They all were. Every one of them I worked with. And I do miss working with them, it was fun.” How were the crowds? Did they draw in real big Elvis fans? Did they go crazy like it was actually Elvis? “Yeah, they sure did. They loved Elvis so much. And the majority were women.” That must have been interesting to be on stage from your point of view and to watch these women get so excited. “Yeah, it was! Johnny, now he was young when he passed away too. He was really good looking, good. Steve, of course, was an older guy. Not old, but older. And, when Johnny started singing, he sang with us. We kind of got him started on stuff. And then he went on his own and did real well.” ‘Don’t put it off’ Looking back at all your decades of singing and performing, if you had a piece of advice to give to another aspiring entertainer, what would it be? “I think what they should do is start when they’re young. And don’t put it off. And just push yourself as much as possible. You get to meet people, get to know them, and that’s how you get in with someone. And go to jam sessions and sing, and they see you there. That would be my advice on it.” The post Before 86-year-old went viral for singing ‘Landslide,’ she had a job in Dallas that few karaoke singers can claim appeared first on Upworthy .

Όταν κάτι δεν είναι ελαφρώς, όμως, το αισθάνονται πολύ πριν το πουν δυνατά. Ένας καλεσμένος που γ…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The best holiday parties tend to be the ones where nobody thinks about the hosting at all. Guests walk in, find a spot for their coat, settle in with a plate and a drink, and the evening carries them along. When something’s slightly off, though, they feel it long before they’d ever say it out loud. A guest who can’t hear the person next to them, or who’s stuck eating bread rolls all night because everything else has nuts in it, probably won’t complain. They’ll just leave a little earlier than they planned. The good news is that most of these little snags are easy to catch if you picture the evening from your guests’ side of the door. So let’s walk through it the way they will, from the moment they pull up to the moment they say goodbye. Before holiday guests arrive A clean home where it counts First impressions start at the entryway. Clutter underfoot or a sink full of dishes can make guests more focused on where to step than on catching up with each other. You don’t need a spotless house, though. Rooms that will stay closed can wait. Put your energy into the spaces people will use, like the bathroom, kitchen, and living room, plus the guest room if anyone’s staying over. Spreading the cleaning across a few days instead of saving it all for the night before keeps you from running on fumes when the doorbell rings. Parking, coats and the weather Even a beautifully decorated party can feel disorganized if guests circle the block looking for a parking spot or end up holding their coats for the first half hour. A short message a few days ahead covering where to park and what to expect when they arrive takes the guesswork out of it. If you live somewhere with snow or ice, it helps to have a backup plan ready in case the weather turns on the day. Food everyone can eat Nobody wants to be the guest pushing food around a plate because of an allergy the host didn’t know about. Before you settle on a menu, send a quick note asking whether anyone has dietary needs. Even if no one replies with anything, having a few dishes that happen to be gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free is an easy way to make sure no one goes hungry. Making holiday guests comfortable once the party starts Room to move around Every home has its own quirks, and the layout shapes how comfortable people feel once they’re inside. Before the party, take a slow lap through your space as if you’d never seen it. Where will people gather? Is the buffet in a spot that blocks the hallway? Is there somewhere to sit near the food? Shumaila Panhwar , a hosting professional, recommends exactly that kind of walkthrough. “When you walk through the space from the perspective of the guests and their experience, it makes it easier to determine placement of items and what makes sense best for flow,” she advises. Music that stays in the background A festive playlist does wonders for the mood, right up until people have to lean in and shout to hear each other. Keep the volume low enough that conversation comes first. Your neighbors will appreciate it too, and nothing ends a party faster than a noise complaint. Being a present host Let yourself enjoy it Here’s the one that catches even the most organized hosts. It’s easy to spend the whole evening refilling bowls and checking the oven, but your guests came to see you. Your presence matters most when people are meeting for the first time and could use an introduction to get a conversation going. Making a plan the night before and running through it once can help a lot. When you know everything is ready, it gets easier to set down the serving spoon, pour yourself a glass of something, and join the people you invited, which, when you think about it, is what made you want to host in the first place. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them) first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A cell therapy built to fight cancer is helping people with stiff person syndrome get back on their feet. In an early trial led by neurologists at Mayo Clinic, patients who had needed family members to help them walk and handle daily tasks regained enough function to return to work, exercise, and hobbies after a single round of CAR-T cell therapy. The results, published in JAMA Neurology , point to a treatment that targets the root of the disease instead of only easing its symptoms. A rare disease with no cure What stiff person syndrome does to the body Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system. The result can be severe rigidity throughout the body, painful muscle spasms, and frequent falls. Decades of research have produced treatments that can soften symptoms, but none that cure it. The condition drew global attention in December 2022, when singer Céline Dion revealed her diagnosis . In an Instagram video, she said it affected “every aspect of my daily life,” including her ability to sing. How CAR-T works against stiff person syndrome CAR-T therapy is already an established treatment for some blood cancers. Doctors extract a patient’s T cells, a type of immune cell, and engineer them in a lab to seek out and destroy specific targets. For this trial, the cells were redesigned to eliminate the immune cells that drive SPS, using a CD19-targeted therapy called mivocabtagene autoleucel. Each participant received a single treatment, and the study ran across three sites, Mayo Clinic among them. Dr. Anastasia Zekeridou , a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, said the scale of the response stood out. “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients,” she said. “With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function.” Patients back at work and on the treadmill Jonathan Walden: hunting and fishing again Before the trial, Jonathan Walden relied on his family for help with walking and basic daily tasks. He has since returned to his job. “I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.” Shari St. Germain: seven minutes on a treadmill Shari St. Germain’s illness progressed from severe leg cramps and trouble walking to rigid muscles and falls. After CAR-T, she said, each day has felt “better and better.” One morning she felt well enough to try the treadmill. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like: ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like: ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill,'” she said. Next questions for CAR-T in neurology Will the improvements last? The researchers are clear that this is early evidence from a small, nonrandomized trial, and that larger studies are needed. “These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time,” Zekeridou said. Beyond blood cancer Dr. Sean Pittock, who chairs the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, sees a wider opening. “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases,” he said, adding that the results offer hope for other immune-mediated neurologic conditions with few effective options. Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at the UK blood cancer charity Anthony Nolan, which was not involved in the trial, called the research “an exciting development” and more evidence that CAR-T could reach well beyond blood cancer. If the gains hold in larger trials, people with stiff person syndrome could have something they have never had before: a treatment aimed at giving them back the lives the disease took, not just making those lives easier to manage. items.descriptionOriginal: “Run the dishwasher twice” might sound like strange mental health advice, but a viral post is proving that it’s actually quite helpful. Danielle Wunker, a licensed professional counselor and supervisor, shared a story on her Facebook page that is resonating with people who struggle with mental health issues. It originally came from an answer from Kate Scott on Quora to the question “Has a therapist ever told you something completely unexpected?” It reads: When I was at one of my lowest (mental) points in life, I couldn’t get out of bed some days . I had no energy or motivation and was barely getting by. I had therapy once per week, and on this particular week I didn’t have much to ‘bring’ to the session. He asked how my week was and I really had nothing to say. “What are you struggling with?” he asked. I gestured around me and said, “I dunno man. Life.” Not satisfied with my answer, he said, “No, what exactly are you worried about right now? What feels overwhelming? When you go home after this session, what issue will be staring at you?” A woman is unhappy at a party. Photo credit: Canva She almost didn’t say it out loud I knew the answer, but it was so ridiculous that I didn’t want to say it. I wanted to have something more substantial. Something more profound. But I didn’t. So I told him, ‘Honestly? The dishes. It’s stupid, I know, but the more I look at them the more I CAN’T do them because I’ll have to scrub them before I put them in the dishwasher, because the dishwasher sucks, and I just can’t stand and scrub the dishes.’ I felt like an idiot even saying it. What kind of grown ass woman is undone by a stack of dishes? There are people out there with *actual* problems, and I’m whining to my therapist about dishes? But he nodded in understanding and then said: “Run the dishwasher twice.” A woman loading the dishwasher. Photo credit: Canva I began to tell him that you’re not supposed to, but he stopped me. “Why the hell aren’t you supposed to? If you don’t want to scrub the dishes and your dishwasher sucks, run it twice. Run it three times, who cares?! Rules do not exist.” There are no rules It blew my mind in a way that I don’t think I can properly express. That day, I went home and tossed my smelly dishes haphazardly into the dishwasher and ran it three times. I felt like I had conquered a dragon. The next day, I took a shower lying down. A few days later, I folded my laundry and put them wherever the f**k they fit. There were no longer arbitrary rules I had to follow, and it gave me the freedom to make accomplishments again. Now that I’m in a healthier place, I rinse off my dishes and put them in the dishwasher properly. I shower standing up. I sort my laundry. But at a time when living was a struggle instead of a blessing, I learned an incredibly important lesson: There are no rules. Run the dishwasher twice. The comments took it even further “For me it is not exactly that there are no rules, but I ask myself ‘Whose rules are these?’ ‘Do I want them to be mine or can I come up with better ones?’ No rules might work for some folks, but I like a little structure, the structure I supply and can alter if it is not working,” Sam wrote in the comments. “That is brilliant! Thank you for sharing that profound story. Isn’t it amazing how often we miss the faulty assumption that is stymying us? I’m glad to hear you are in a much better place now,” Charlie added. Motivation often follows behavior The therapist’s advice to the woman follows a psychological principle : motivation often follows behavior . So, when you don’t feel motivated to scrub the dishes, by simply doing part of the act, putting them in the dishwasher, you are prompting your brain’s reward system to build momentum. Simply taking one step can make it easier to keep going or help you rebuild a healthy routine. Anyone who has been in a mental or emotional place where even the most basic, mundane tasks feel overwhelming understands the wisdom of this lesson. Dishes might seem like such a minor detail of life, but those kinds of minor details can be the straw that breaks the camel’s back mentally. If you’ve never stared at a basket of laundry that would take three minutes to fold and thought, “Nope, can’t do it. Not now. Maybe not ever…” then you may not need this lesson, but there are millions of people who appreciate the express permission to let go of the rules in our heads about how things have to be done. Adjusting expectations and arbitrary ideas about how something works is incredibly freeing and can provide a temporary fix for a seemingly insurmountable problem. Oddly enough, that temporary fix can be the bridge that moves someone from being unable to cope with daily life to functioning on a somewhat normal level. Why this advice works, according to psychology Mental health is such a tricky thing to manage, and many of the tools for managing it run counter to what we might expect. That’s what therapists are for: they help us step outside the box of our own brains, adjust our thoughts and behaviors to create greater possibilities for ourselves, and give us permission to reject the negative voices in our heads that try to keep us locked in unhelpful or unhealthy patterns. Even when that unhelpful pattern is as simple as letting the dishes pile up instead of running the dishwasher twice. This article originally appeared five years ago. It has been updated. The post Woman shares her therapist’s life-changing mental health advice: ‘Run the dishwasher twice’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: There are a lot of personality tests out there, and we humans are endlessly fascinated by them. There are the ones popular in pop-psychology like Myers-Briggs and the Enneagram. There are highly clinical and academic models like the HEXACO and the MMPI. One of the most widely used and respected personality tests in academic and scientific circles is the Big Five, or OCEAN model. It scores people based on five traits: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. It doesn’t group people into concrete buckets with snappy names, like “The Innovator,” but your collective scores in the five areas it measures come together to tell a story about you. Personalities can be complex. Photo credit: Canva But some people’s results don’t fit neatly into a story. It’s rare, but fewer than 10% of people have unusual results that don’t fit within the usual personality maps. Scientific research uncovers personality mutants A 2018 study in Frontiers in Psychology , by Jüri Allik, Martina Hřebíčková, and Anu Realo of the University of Tartu, the University of Warwick, and the Czech Academy of Sciences, tested more than 4,000 participants from the Czech Republic and Estonia. Each person completed a personality inventory and was also scored based on someone who knew them well in order to get the most accurate and realistic data. What the researchers realized was that a handful of personality traits, while all scored individually, are typically related: “When people describe their own or somebody else’s personality, many of the descriptors typically go hand-in-hand with each other. For instance, people who are often angry also experience many other negative emotions. Similarly, individuals who have vivid imaginations are regularly more open to trying new food and entertaining new ideas and values. And those who are motivated to achieve are usually also self-disciplined and methodical.” Most people have personality profiles that make logical sense. People who are highly Extraverted are usually Open to trying new things. People who are highly Neurotic tend to be less Extraverted. But the researchers also discovered some fascinating outliers in their data. Fewer than one out of every 10 participants had a personality trait map that just… didn’t fit. For the purposes of their study, the researchers used the term “personality mutants.” The 3 types of personality outliers Not only did roughly 5% to 10% of the people studied not fit neatly into the usual pattern of personality traits, the data showed that there were three specific personality combos that accounted for most of the “mutants.” They had multiple traits that didn’t seem to go naturally together, or had only one of a pair of traits that are almost always found in the same person. The clusters, sadly, did not receive a cool, grabby nickname like “mutants.” The first cluster, called H1, saw people who scored high in “Straightforwardness” also score low in “Trust.” These are straight-shooters who are usually frank and sincere, but don’t trust that others are returning the favor. These traits don’t usually go together in this combination. Most people who are highly honest and frank project that worldview onto others and trust easily. But some are more skeptical, and use their acute understanding of what honesty sounds like to easily sniff out people who are being deceptive. The H2 cluster features people who are highly Conscientious, that is, disciplined, organized, and responsible, and who score high in Aesthetics, meaning they place a lot of value in their style and visual tastes. However, this cluster of people scores low in other areas of Openness. They are stubborn and extremely resistant to trying new things or changing their mind. Interestingly, this cluster also featured people who were highly Straightforward but distrustful, just like cluster H1. The third cluster, H3, is a fascinating one: These folks score low on Fantasy, Aesthetics, and Emotional Sensitivity. But they’re highly open to trying new things, exploring new ideas, and challenging conventional beliefs; even their own. They’re a cerebral bunch. Not big on imagination, art, or style. Deep thinkers who are more head than heart. It’s an unusual and rare combination. Even more fascinatingly, this group showed a different trust pattern than the other two: H3s were highly Trusting of others but lower in Modesty. The “mutant” personalities discovered in the research are not inherently good or bad. They simply exist as outliers, and the researchers cite about one in 3,000 people being born with an extra finger or toe as a parallel. It’s the normal elements, just configured a little differently. Human personality is hard to classify It goes to show that even the most scientifically validated personality tests can’t perfectly capture the full spectrum of human individuality. Any test that claims all people fit into one of a handful of rigid “types” is missing the forest for the trees. The researchers put it best, and beautifully: “Personality facets are more like Lego, which can be assembled into different configurations. In addition to the customary assembly of elements, several infrequent compositions of the same elements can emerge.” If you’ve ever felt like you weren’t quite like everyone else, like the personality tests could never quite peg you perfectly, well, you were probably right. This article originally appeared in June. It has been updated. The post 1 in 10 people have such unusual personality trait combinations that researchers call them ‘mutants’ appeared first on Upworthy .

Και δεν ήταν ιδιοκτήτης κατοικίδιου που τα έφερε μέσα, αλλά η ίδια η μαμά γάτα. Σύμφωνα με το Gulf Today, το προσωπικό είχε αφήσει προηγουμένως φαγητό και νερό για το αδέσποτο πορτοκαλί τιγρέ έξω από το νοσοκομείο στο Izmer, Τουρκία, β.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A family of kittens in western Turkey has won people’s hearts with an emergency visit to a hospital. Not an animal hospital, a human hospital. And it wasn’t a pet owner who brought them in, but the mama cat herself. According to Gulf Today , staff had previously left food and water for the stray orange tabby outside the hospital in Izmer, Turkey, but that morning she kept meowing outside. Finally, she fetched one of her kittens and carried it right into the hospital, clearly on a mission. She wasn’t scared or shy as hospital personnel cleared the path for her. With her baby in her mouth, she trotted through the hallways, seemingly looking for someone to help. Medical personnel examined the kitten along with its siblings and consulted with a veterinary clinic. As it turned out, the kittens had an eye infection. Mama kitty’s maternal instincts are really something else. Just look at this sweetness caught on video: According to the Daily Mail , one of the hospital workers told local media: “We were giving food and water to the mother cat living on the street with other people living in this area. However, we did not know that she gave birth to kittens. As we began to receive patients in the morning, she showed up with her kittens. She asked for help, meowing for a long time. We were shocked. Upon careful examination, we saw that the kittens were not able to open their eyes due to infection. We consulted with veterinarians and gave medicine as described. When the kittens opened their eyes a short time later, we were thrilled. Later, we sent the mother cat and kittens to Uzundere for further care. This is the first time something like this has happened to us. We were emotional and delighted to see that they recovered well.” It’s happened in Turkey before This isn’t the first time that a mama cat has made news for bringing her kittens into a hospital in Turkey, however. Last spring, a different cat brought her kitten into an emergency room at a hospital in Istanbul. Merve Özcan described the scene in Twitter posts that went viral at the time. “Today we were in the hospital emergency, a cat rushed to the emergency with her baby she was carrying in her mouth,” Özcan wrote. “Her baby is a little mischievous, her mother grabs it where she finds it.” Yavrusu biraz haylaz biri, annesi bulduğu yerde kapıp götürüyor pic.twitter.com/GYvBXt3UQz — Merve Özcan (@ozcanmerveee) April 27, 2020 Medics examined the kittens for apparent signs of illness, while the mama cat was given milk and food. Then they were sent to a vet. “The Turks have long been known for their love and care for stray animals,” Bored Panda reported , “with many leaving out food and water for them on the streets.” No wonder these cats felt so comfortable bringing their kittens into human hospitals for help. What this says about trust While we can’t know for certain what prompted these mama kitties to bring their babies to these medical professionals, it’s clear that their maternal instinct to protect and keep their kittens healthy is strong. And the fact that they seem to trust the hospital personnel to take care of their babies says a lot about how humans have treated them. Good for these Turkish medical workers for setting an inspiring example of kindness to animals. This article originally appeared five years ago. It has been updated. The post Mama cat rushed her kittens to a human hospital. Doctors treated them as patients. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: GTA6 , the latest in the wildly popular Grand Theft Auto video game franchise, launches this week and it’s not a stretch to say it may be one of the most anticipated video games of all time. The game has been in development for over eight years and its release date has been teased and pushed back multiple times, all the while promising fans one of the most ambitious open-world games ever. The game, though, is not without its controversy. GTA is one of the most popular and innovative games of all time, but it’s also one of the most violent. Players in the game world are encouraged to commit crimes, run from the police, and even harm innocent civilians just for kicks. The Guardian even calls it “ depraved ,” and there have even been incidents of real-world violence that some have linked to the game. But the newest iteration of the game does something that it has never done before: It rewards players for empathy, kindness, and non-violent actions. GTAVI players can choose a kinder path Throughout the Grand Theft Auto games over the years, attacking random civilians has always been a core element of the game. You can beat them up, or worse, and take their money and other items they might be carrying—even steal their car. You can still do all of that in GTAVI, but game developer Rockstar has implemented a redesigned “honor system,” that tracks player’s behavior throughout the course of the game. Repeatedly kinder, more empathetic decisions can unlock perks, rewards, and even entirely new storylines. Treating the NPCs with care can pay off Shooting up random pedestrians and stealing their cash? That’s old news. The world of GTAVI is populated with countless NPCS, or Non Player Characters, who are simply going about their business: commuting to work, running errands, enjoying a day in the park. In GTAVI, being kind to them may actually be the smarter route. Reviews note that you can stop to pet a stranger’s dog, pick up litter, and perform other acts of everyday kindness that can boost your in-game reputation as a do-gooder. But it goes even beyond that. Bloomberg reviewer Jason Schreier shares how he saved an NPC from a car wreck and, in exchange for the help, the civilian character rewarded him with thousands of dollars. This is incredible. Amazon is parodied as Sahara in GTA 6 lmfaooo. https://t.co/tyhM0MFZk5 pic.twitter.com/g6exyG7DgE — T𑀣ᑏI (@RexKwonDo92) November 18, 2026 Non-violent missions Most people know GTA as driving around the city and committing acts of chaos, but the game’s storyline also involves detailed and exciting “missions” for the character. In GTAVI, players may find that choosing non-violent approaches to completing missions is often the smarter play. Players can choose non-lethal weapons, stealth instead of confrontation, and preparation instead of coming in guns-a-blazing. Some reporting even indicates that building a non-violent reputation in the game can unlock new stories and side quests that won’t be available to the players who prefer to rampage. Domestic bliss is key Another new element in GTAVI is the introduction of dual protagonists Jason and Lucia. They’re a couple, and a key element of the game revolves around maintaining their relationship. It’s not all bank robberies and complex heists. Playing are encouraged to send messages between the pair, take walks on the beach, spend recreational time together, hold hands, and even show great teamwork during missions. Keeping the partners happy reportedly changes their in-game dialogue and even how the storyline plays out. It all adds up to a wildly different and surprisingly complex playing experience. Guardian reviewer Keza MacDonald wrote , “I was astonished to discover that the game offers you small incentives for acts of kindness, such as texting your partner a selfie, doing your neighbour a favour or throwing your rubbish in the bin rather than dropping it on the ground.” Not exactly the usual fare gamers have grown used to. Violence still a core element GTAVI has been in development for a long time. Many members of the franchise’s core audience have grown up and simply demand more complexity from their games than they did a decade ago. 40-year-olds who grew up playing early versions of GTA might enjoy a different flavor and challenge in the new game world instead of the usual shoot-em-up destruction. But even with the new empathy features, GTAVI is still a graphically violent game. Players won’t be punished for playing the “old way,” and the violence won’t be removed from the franchise any time soon. The American Psychological Association is clear that there is not a causal relationship between video games and real-life violence. But it’s understandable if anyone, a parent or otherwise, would be uncomfortable with certain aspects of Grand Theft Auto. For anyone curious about the groundbreaking aspects of the game and wanting to give it a try, just know that there is a much kinder way to play; and that might even be the smart strategy. The post GTA 6 surprisingly rewards players who choose kindness and empathy appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι ερευνητές ανακάλυψαν μια νέα θετική πτυχή της γήρανσης. Όσο μεγαλώνεις, τόσο λιγότερο σε νοιάζει η λύπη.
items.titleOriginal: Researchers found a new positive aspect of aging. The older you get, the less you care about regret.
items.description: Η γήρανση έχει πολλές θετικές πτυχές, και η μεγάλη είναι ότι μετά τη μέση ηλικία, οι άνθρωποι γίνονται συχνά πιο ευτυχισμένοι. Ιστορικά, οι ερευνητές έχουν διαπιστώσει ότι η ευτυχία ακολουθεί μια καμπύλη σχήματος U: οι άνθρωποι είναι πιο ευτυχισμένοι μέχρι τα 40 τους έως τα μέσα της δεκαετίας του πενήντα, όταν βιώνουν μια βουτιά και μετά επιστρέφουν στο προηγούμενο επίπεδο ευτυχίας στα 60 τους. Μια δημοσκόπηση του 2025 της Gallup βρήκε το…
items.descriptionOriginal: Aging has many positive aspects, and a big one is that after middle age, people often become happier. Historically, researchers have found that happiness follows a U-shaped curve : people are happier until their 40s to mid-fifties, when they experience a dip, then return to their previous level of happiness in their 60s. A 2025 Gallup poll found that, on a scale of 1 to 10, Americans ages 18 to 29 had an average flourishing score of 6.36, while those in their 60s average 7.68, meaning that older people report greater well-being, growth, and psychological and social functioning. Recently, a study published by the American Psychological Association found another reason people shouldn’t fear aging. Although younger people and older people report the same number of regrets , “older adults reported fewer and less emotionally intense recent regrets.” Study shows the pain of regret lessens as people age “Regrets are incredibly common. Almost all of us experience big regrets in our personal and professional lives—from marrying the wrong person to never finishing college,” lead author Julia Nolte, PhD, of Tilburg University in the Netherlands, said in a statement. “The good news is that for many of us, the experience of regret seems to become less negative with age.” One reason older people may not feel regrets as intensely is that, as we age, regrets become less beneficial. When most of your life is ahead of you, the sting of regret can help you avoid making the same mistakes again. After middle age, regret takes on a new emotional form. “It is assumed that regret helps us make better choices moving forward,” Nolte says. “But older adults may derive other benefits from regret, such as a chance to reflect or look for meaning.” A woman dealing with regrets. Credit: Canva Older people also tend to feel more regret over missed chances, when they failed to take action, rather than when they made a poor decision. This psychological phenomenon, known as the inaction effect , states that we feel less regret if we take an action that fails than if we do nothing and fail. We can learn from mistakes we’ve made, but we can’t recover a missed opportunity. The researchers measured the pain of regret across the age spectrum by surveying adults, aged 21 to 89, and asking them to list up to 5 regrets from the past year and another 5 long-term regrets. Participants were then asked how they cope with regret. Woman enjoying the sunshine. Credit: Canva Simply put: It hurts more to regret something you didn’t do than something you did The study is probably a relief for those who hope they’ll one day be free of painful self-reflection about the past. But it’s also a wake-up call to take advantage of opportunities in life, speak up when something needs to be said, and to be less afraid of taking risks. Because, as the study shows, the regrets we hang onto as we age aren’t the things we did, but the things we didn’t. The post Researchers found a new positive aspect of aging. The older you get, the less you care about regret. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο σκηνοθέτης του «Home Alone» Chris Columbus τελικά αποκαλύπτει γιατί απέλυσε το αρχικό Marv για τον Daniel Stern
items.titleOriginal: ‘Home Alone’ Director Chris Columbus finally reveals why he fired the original Marv for Daniel Stern
items.description: Είναι δύσκολο να φανταστείς το Home Alone χωρίς τον Joe Pesci ως Harry και τον Daniel Stern ως Marv. Η κωμική χημεία μεταξύ αυτών των δύο διαρρηκτών βοήθησε στη δημιουργία μερικών από τις πιο εμβληματικές σκηνές της ταινίας. Και κάπως έκανε τα ανελέητα σωματικά βασανιστήρια που έκανε ένα οκτάχρονο παιδί υγιεινό και διασκεδαστικό. Αλλά αυτό το δυναμικό δίδυμο ήταν σχεδόν ένα εντελώς διαφορετικό ζευγάρι.…
items.descriptionOriginal: It’s hard to imagine Home Alone without Joe Pesci as Harry and Daniel Stern as Marv. The comedic chemistry between these two bumbling burglars helped create some of the movie’s most iconic scenes. And somehow made merciless physical torture done by an eight-year-old wholesome and fun. But this dynamic duo was almost a completely different pairing. More than 35 years after the 1990 holiday classic hit theaters, director Chris Columbus revealed that another actor (and another Daniel, coincidentally) originally played Marv. Sort of. However, Daniel Roebuck, the original actor cast as Marv, is pushing back on Columbus’ version of why he was replaced. Daniel Roebuck was originally Marv Columbus recently appeared on the Wildmen podcast and explained that he had envisioned both Stern and Pesci in their respective roles. Stern’s asking price was too high for the studio, though, leaving Columbus to choose between the two actors. He went with Pesci. That left the production looking for another actor to play Marv. While Columbus didn’t name-check the actor set to replace him, multiple publications surmised that it was Daniel Roebuck, who has previously opened up about being fired from Home Alone . But that arrangement didn’t last long after a less-than-stellar screen test. According to Columbus, Roebuck and Pesci did a screen test together, and the chemistry simply wasn’t there. Columbus recalled that Pesci was great, while the other actor’s performance was, unfortunately, “just awful.” He said it was the only time he had ever fired an actor. The role eventually went to Stern, who clicked with Pesci and went on to become the Marv audiences know today. Still, Columbus didn’t want to burn a bridge with Roebuck, telling him, “We’ll work together at some point!'” Roebuck remembers the experience very differently. The River’s Edge actor has acknowledged for years that he was fired from Home Alone , but he disputes Columbus’ account of what led to it. After hearing Columbus’ recent comments, Roebuck told Entertainment Weekly that he found them “troubling.” Most significantly, he says there was never a screen test with Pesci. Back in 2023, Roebuck told the What a Character! podcast, “I was never gonna be Marv.” “Now that’s the one thing they never say. I was never ever ever going to film as Marv. I got the wettest handshake of my life with [writer and producer] John Hughes. It was the most disappointing handshake I ever received because I was a fan of the guy. And he clearly didn’t want me to be there. It was all so obvious.” That leaves two very different versions of the casting change, even though both Columbus and Roebuck agree on the basic outcome: Roebuck was out, and Stern was in. Daniel Stern reveals how asking for a pay raise nearly cost him his ‘Home Alone’ role As reported by US Weekly, Stern writes in his memoir, Home and Alone , that he initially agreed to a $300,000 salary for six weeks of work on the original film. Then the studio changed that schedule from six weeks to eight weeks, without offering additional pay. Stern pushed back, asking whether his salary would increase along with the additional time. When the answer was no, producers then attempted to hire another actor. Fortunately for Stern, that arrangement didn’t work out. He was brought back, and the studio honored his original six-week contract. But that experience apparently stayed with him when Home Alone 2: Lost in New York came around. By then, the first movie had become a massive hit, and Stern knew the sequel would be a much bigger payday. Stern was originally offered $800,000 after some negotiating from his reps. However, when he learned that Pesci was reportedly making somewhere between $2 million and $3 million plus a percentage of the profits, Stern fired his agent and negotiated for himself, asking for $1.5 million plus 2% of the gross. The final deal gave him the $1.5 million salary and 1% of the gross instead. “I knew they couldn’t do the movie without me, but I was also insecure, since I almost blew it the first time,” he wrote. “I didn’t want to be too greedy when I loved the movie and the part so much.” Home Alone 2 ultimately made about $359 million worldwide. One percent of that total works out to roughly $3.59 million, although that calculation shouldn’t be treated as a confirmed amount Stern personally received because the exact contractual terms aren’t public. Regardless, it’s a pretty remarkable turn of events for an actor who almost didn’t get to play Marv at all. Feel free to share this new bit of trivia during your holiday rewatches. The post ‘Home Alone’ Director Chris Columbus finally reveals why he fired the original Marv for Daniel Stern appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Call out “Linda” on a 1950s playground, and you’d better be specific about which one you meant. Odds were good that more than one girl would look up. For a generation of American women now in their 70s, sharing a first name with half the neighborhood was simply part of growing up. Linda was the most popular name for baby girls in the United States from 1947 through 1952, according to the Social Security Administration . In 1947 alone, 99,692 newborn girls were given the name. That works out to about 1 in every 18 girls born that year. Today, the top spot belongs to Olivia, which has led the girls’ list for seven straight years. In 2025, 13,544 baby girls were named Olivia . That sounds like a crowd, but it comes to roughly 1 in 130 girls. At its peak, Linda was about seven times as common as America’s most popular girls’ name is today. Roll call looked very different A typical classroom of 30 kids has about 15 girls. Based on the odds in 1947, that works out to nearly one Linda per classroom. A grade school with 250 girls born during Linda’s run at No. 1 could expect roughly a dozen Lindas. The same school today would have about two Olivias. Parents also choose from a much wider variety of names today. In 1950, the 10 most popular girls’ names accounted for more than 1 in 5 baby girls. By 2025, the entire top 10 combined accounted for only about 6% of girls. In 1947, Linda nearly matched that all by herself. Meanwhile, the name that once filled classrooms has nearly vanished from nurseries. Only 294 baby girls were named Linda in 2025 , putting it at No. 902. That’s roughly 1 in 6,000 girls. A hit song gave the name a lift Linda bumped Mary from the top spot in 1947. Mary had led the girls’ list every year since Social Security’s baby-name records began in 1880, so this was no small upset. It didn’t hurt that Linda means “pretty” in Spanish and Portuguese. Linda had been climbing since the 1930s, but 1947 was something else entirely. The number of baby Lindas jumped by nearly 47,000 in a single year—the largest one-year increase for any girls’ name on record, according to an analysis of Social Security data by Nancy’s Baby Names. A popular song gave the name a boost. Songwriter Jack Lawrence wrote “Linda” for the young daughter of his attorney, Lee Eastman. A recording by Ray Noble’s orchestra, featuring Buddy Clark on vocals, reached No. 1 in 1947—the same year Linda topped the baby name charts. The little girl behind the song grew up to become photographer Linda McCartney, who married Paul McCartney in 1969. In a 1998 interview with NPR , Lawrence recalled writing the song to settle a debt he owed Eastman. Names that rise fast tend to fall fast Linda’s slide started almost as soon as it peaked. By 1956, the yearly count had dropped by more than half , to 48,192. By 1964, that number had fallen to 23,725. That arc fits a pattern researchers have documented. In a 2009 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , Wharton marketing professor Jonah Berger and Universitat Pompeu Fabra economist Gaël Le Mens analyzed more than 100 years of first-name data from the U.S. and France. Names that caught on quickly also faded quickly, while those that gained popularity more gradually stuck around longer. The same researchers surveyed expectant parents and found that they shied away from names that had recently surged in popularity, worried those names would turn out to be short-lived fads. That caution helps make the fear come true. Harvard University sociologist Stanley Lieberson explored the same puzzle in his 2000 book A Matter of Taste , which describes “internal taste mechanisms” that keep preferences evolving even when society itself isn’t changing much. Every generation had its own Linda Ask anyone which name was everywhere when they were in school, and they can usually answer in a second. It’s the name that filled every attendance sheet and followed a whole crop of kids from kindergarten straight through graduation. For Baby Boomers, that name was Linda. For their children, it was Jennifer. And for anyone who grew up in the 1990s, chances are they knew more than one Jessica or Ashley. Jennifer ruled the baby-name charts from 1970 to 1984 , peaking in 1972 when 63,600 baby girls were given the name. By then, Linda had already passed the torch to a new generation of girls growing up with a name that seemed to be everywhere. Then came the ’80s and ’90s. Jessica took over in 1985, with Ashley close behind. Anyone who remembers those school years might recall hallways full of Jessicas and Ashleys, or the familiar scramble to figure out which one the teacher was calling. Jessica topped the charts for most of the years between 1985 and 1995 , while Ashley claimed the No. 1 spot in 1991 and 1992. By 2005, Emily had taken over, with 23,950 baby girls given the name that year. Those names have followed Linda’s path downward. In 2025, only 501 baby girls were named Jennifer , putting it at No. 586. Jessica fell to No. 665, with 424 births. Ashley has held on better at No. 164, but that’s a long way from 1987, when 54,856 baby girls were given the name. Plenty of vintage names have since found new life. Evelyn, a favorite in the early 1900s, ranked No. 8 among girls’ names in 2025 . Linda hasn’t had its comeback yet, but there are still plenty of Lindas out there. Social Security records show that nearly 1.46 million girls have been given the name since 1880, with the biggest wave born between 1947 and 1952. Somewhere right now, a retirement party is being planned for a Linda, and there’s a good chance another Linda is on the guest list. If the name ever makes a comeback, the next little Linda may finally get to answer roll call alone. items.descriptionOriginal: ndia burns millions of tonnes of paddy straw every year. But what if this agricultural waste could grow mushrooms instead? At ICAR-National Rice Research Institute in Cuttack, scientists are helping farmers explore mushroom cultivation using paddy straw. Fungi break down tough plant fibres, allowing farmers to turn straw into growing beds for paddy straw mushrooms. According to a 2022 ICAR study, cultivating 4,000 mushroom beds annually could generate ₹3 lakh in net income, with leftover material potentially adding another ₹1.36 lakh through vermicomposting. But this isn’t a magic fix for stubble burning. These mushrooms need temperatures of 30–35°C, while poor-quality spawn, contamination, limited markets and food-safety risks remain serious challenges. Scientists estimate this method could handle only 8–12% of a region’s straw burden. Mushroom farming won’t end stubble burning on its own. But it shows how agricultural waste can become food, income and new livelihood opportunities when science meets the right conditions. #StubbleBurning #PaddyStraw #MushroomFarming #AgriculturalInnovation #FarmersIncome #SustainableAgriculture #ICAR #Vermicomposting #AgriTech #CropResidueManagement #IndianFarmers #WasteToWealth #ClimateSolutions #TheBetterIndia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have long used chemogenetics to study brains in the lab. A pilot trial for seizures is its first leap into medicine. Flashing lights. Buzzing noises. A sudden wave of fear. For some people with epilepsy, these sensations herald an oncoming seizure. Drugs can keep some seizures at bay, but over 30 percent of patients don’t respond to them, a statistic that hasn’t budged in decades. Frequent, uncontrolled seizures rob people of a normal life. They can’t drive or swim alone. Some struggle to stay in school, hold down jobs, or maintain relationships. And despite growing public awareness, stigma lingers. For people with severe drug-resistant epilepsy, surgery is an option. If the seizures are associated with a local brain region, doctors can remove the tissue. It’s a drastic operation, but it isn’t rare. In 2024, over 2,000 patients elected to undergo the procedure. Depending on the brain region removed, surgery can control seizures in nearly 70 percent of patients, but they risk losing memory, language, and other cognitive abilities. A new gene therapy could offer an alternative. In a clinical trial , three men who had lived with epilepsy for at least a decade saw monthly seizures drop over 90 percent. One remained seizure-free for a year. In the trial, the team shuttled a gene into a small patch of the hippocampus, the source of their seizures. The gene produces a kind of protein “dimmer switch” in neurons. Normally silent, the protein springs into action when activated by an FDA-approved drug, allowing scientists to dial down the region’s electrical activity rather than shutting it off completely—something that’s not possible with current treatments. The technology, called chemogenetics, has been a staple of animal research in neuroscience. The findings, though early, suggest it could finally make the leap into human medicine. “It certainly has caused a lot of excitement in the field,” said Dimitri Kullmann at University College London to Chemical & Engineering News , who was not involved in the study. Chemical Romance Intricate webs of neurons underlie every brain function. Our ability to feel, move, remember, and reason all stem from electrical and chemical signals that wire brain cells into circuits. It’s a delicate balance. Some neurons release chemicals that fire up their neighbors; others dampen them. In epilepsy, this goes awry. The causes are plenty. Genetic mutations can disrupt how neurons develop or function. Brain injuries, tumors, stroke, and infections can also fuel the condition. In some frustrating cases, the culprit remains unknown. Rebalancing these circuits could tame runaway seizures. Most antiseizure drugs prevent neurons from firing too rapidly or boosting inhibitory chemical signals. But medication is a Band-Aid, not a cure. Because the drugs flood the whole brain, they can trigger fatigue, dizziness, mood swings, and sometimes more serious side effects , including liver or heart problems. Dampening electrical activity at the source could be a better bet. Around two decades ago, an emerging technology called chemogenetics first amazed neuroscientists with its precise control of single neurons. The technology relies on two parts: gene therapy and a drug. First, an engineered virus delivers a gene encoding a designer receptor into targeted neurons. The receptor is silent until a specific drug activates it. By adjusting the drug’s dose, scientists can fine tune the activity of modified neurons. Rather than simply flicking neurons on or off, the approach is flexible and targeted. Chemogenetics soon caught the attention of epilepsy researchers. In 2019, a team at Ghent University in Belgium tested the method in mice with seizures originating in the hippocampus. They delivered a designer receptor called hMADi to the region. A single dose of clozapine, an FDA-approved antipsychotic, controlled seizures for at least 15 hours. With repeated treatment, seizures nearly vanished. A subsequent study in monkeys also dramatically slashed seizures. Given these encouraging findings, some researchers were ready to take the next step. “I think scientists like me felt like, ‘Why haven’t we tried it in humans yet?’” said study author Minmin Luo at the Chinese Institute for Brain Research. Restoring Balance The trial enrolled three men under 40 diagnosed with epilepsy for 10 to 25 years. All had tried at least two antiseizure medications without success. Brain scans traced their seizures to a scarred hippocampus on one side of the brain. The same structure on the other side remained healthy. Despite their long history of epilepsy, none showed notable signs of cognitive troubles. Similar to previous work, the team delivered a gene encoding the hMADi receptor into the damaged region of each patient’s hippocampus in a series of three shots. A dye mixed with the therapy confirmed it reached nearly the entire region in two patients and spread slightly beyond it in the third. The infusion took roughly two hours. Two weeks later, the men began taking clozapine pills every eight hours. After five months, their average monthly seizure count had dropped from roughly four to nearly zero. Brain recordings also showed far fewer epilepsy-related electrical spikes, and their damaged hippocampuses increased metabolism, though levels remained below those in the region’s healthy counterpart. The benefits lasted. In check-ups throughout the following year, two patients remained seizure-free. The third experienced two “breakthrough” seizures after an unexpected interruption in medication, but the seizures stopped once he restarted the drug regime. All three participants also reported improved quality of life. The study’s main goal, however, was to gauge safety. The viral carrier has a relatively established safety record, but high doses have been linked to severe immune reactions and even deaths . Delivering the therapy directly into brain tissue requires far smaller doses than when injected into the bloodstream and perhaps, counterintuitively, could be safer overall. Blood tests, brain scans, and other assessments find no major side effects. One patient experienced a temporary rise in liver enzymes, a sign of liver stress, but levels returned to normal without intervention. The team plans to expand the trial, but there are plenty of unsolved questions. All three men continued taking their existing antiseizure medications throughout the trial, making it difficult to isolate the treatment’s effects. For example, could clozapine have somehow synergized with those medications to reduce seizure counts? The study was also open-label, without a placebo control. And clozapine, when taken at high doses, carries risks of heart and other problems , though the doses given here were much lower than those used in psychiatric disorders. Whether chemogenetics can deliver lasting seizure relief in larger groups remains to be seen. But its debut in human medicine is a hopeful glimpse of what’s possible, not just for epilepsy, but potentially for addiction, mood disorders, and other neurological conditions involving unbalanced brain circuits too. “These findings offer initial proof of concept,” the team wrote. The post Novel Gene Therapy Nearly Erases ‘Drug Resistant’ Seizures appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Vithabai Narayangaonkar was nine months pregnant and in the middle of a Tamasha performance when her labour began. She slipped backstage, delivered her baby and cut the umbilical cord with a stone. Maharashtra's folk theatre world has told the story ever since, and it stands for a woman who gave her life to the stage and spent decades keeping the Tamasha tradition alive. The stage was her first classroom Vithabai grew up in Solapur district in a family that lived by the stage. Her father, Bhau Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar, ran a Tamasha troupe founded by her grandfather, Narayan Khude, and she grew up on Lavani, Gavlan and Bhedik, the songs and forms of Tamasha, Maharashtra's travelling folk theatre. Nine months pregnant, Vithabai slipped backstage, delivered her baby and returned to a life devoted to Tamasha. Photograph: ( Lokmat ) She followed the family trade from village to village, performing and refining her art . When the Marathi playwright Mama Varerkar saw her on stage, he was so mesmerised that he invited her to join his troupe, where she mastered techniques such as Angik, Vachik, Satvik and Abhinaya without formal drama training. Her daughter, the Tamasha artist Mangala Bansode, later recalled that Vithabai had danced since the age of 7, and that she pulled her own daughter out of school in class two to put her on the stage at 9, because the troupe needed more women. In families like theirs, song and dance were the first lessons, drilled in by parents through long hours of rehearsal, and the stage was the classroom. Such artists traditionally came from nomadic, lower-caste and Dalit communities. She won hearts, but couldn't make ends meet Fame did not guarantee food. The family had name and recognition but little money to buy a meal, and Vithabai's songs said as much . In a Lavani she sang in the 1960s, she asked the men in the audience to keep their own sense of shame, because she was dancing for her daily living and cared for nobody else's opinion. From village performances to national honours, Vithabai made Maharashtra's travelling folk theatre her lifelong stage. Photograph: ( Mid Day ) Fans began calling her Tamasha Samradni, or Tamasha Empress, and when the India-China war began she performed a special Tamasha at the North-East Frontier Agency border. The President of India honoured her twice, in 1957 and 1990. Even then, her work depended on contractors, who decided when a Tamasha opened or closed, and on audiences who set the terms of what artists performed. Mangala recalled dancing at a tamasha held under a tree, with no stage and the crowd pressing in, where she had to walk up to men to collect money and some pulled at her sari. Holding on to art even on the hardest days After the birth, the contractor stopped the Tamasha and the family was moved back into a dharmashala. Mangala remembered visiting her mother in hospital, where there was no food and no clothes for the newborn. When she asked the contractor for help, he told her nothing could be done until the Tamasha started again. Someone suggested pawning the harmonium for cash, but Mangala refused, calling the harmonium and ankle bells the family's wealth. She instead asked another troupe for ₹1,000 and agreed to dance for it every evening. With that money she bought food for everyone, mutton biryani for her mother and clothes for the baby. The hardship never fully lifted. Despite the honours, Vithabai and her family were never financially stable, and she died in 2002. 3 generations & a shared love for Tamasha In 2006, the Government of Maharashtra instituted the Vithabai Narayangaonkar Lifetime Achievement Award for artists working in Tamasha, the art she had dedicated much of her life to. The state has given grants to traditional folk arts, including Tamasha, Dashavatar and Shahiri, since 2008. When money ran short, her daughter protected the harmonium and ankle bells that kept their family's art alive. Photograph: ( News24 ) Mangala carried the stage forward, calling her mother her guru and saying she was famous because of her. By 2004, she was 55 and still dancing, a Tamasgir, or troupe leader, with around 150 people depending on her for their daily survival. She called Tamasha a public service rather than a business, and said she would keep performing as long as the public wanted her. Three generations of her family had performed in Tamasha, and her son took the stage at 7. Yet Mangala said audiences were thinning as remixes and orchestras drew crowds away, and she wanted the state to do more for its traditional artists. She had the fame a stage can give and little of the security it cannot. She left behind a harmonium her daughter refused to pawn, ankle bells that kept sounding through a daughter and a grandson, and an award in her name for those who keep Tamasha alive. items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, thousands of mothers and newborns in India are lost during labour and the 24 hours that follow, even though 9 in 10 births now happen in health facilities. What if early warning signs never went unnoticed? A Mumbai-based startup born at IIT Bombay is putting AI-powered fetal and labour monitoring into the hands of frontline health workers and hospitals. Strapped on the mother, the devices send real-time data to a smartphone, flag risks like fetal distress and PPH early, and cut documentation time for nurses by up to 50%, so they can focus on care. Innovation like this proves that quality maternal care shouldn’t depend on where a woman lives. If you have a working, tech-led solution, share your innovation with us. items.descriptionOriginal: "Uruvaai arivil olirvaai Kanna! Uyirin amudhaai pozhivaai Kanna!" Shine within my consciousness, O Kanna; pour forth as the nectar of my life. In Subramania Bharati's poetry, the imagery of devotion and love often reaches beyond the immediate moment. More than a century after his words were written, one of his compositions has found a new musical life — this time, on a global stage. But when the Grammy nominations were being announced on 16 November, the man behind that contemporary interpretation was nowhere near a television screen. Back from a project in Sri Lanka, Devan Ekambaram could not bring himself to watch the nominations unfold. He went instead to a temple. "I was too nervous to watch," he recalls. At 6.47 pm IST, his phone lit up. A friend in Los Angeles sent him a message: "Congratulations!" His phone soon filled with 80 or 90 similar messages. "I realised what had happened and immediately broke down crying," he says. Released independently in August 2026, Varuvaaiy became the first Tamil song nominated for a Grammy. The song that had brought him to this moment was Varuvaaiy , an independent Tamil recording he composed and produced with vocalist Subhiksha Rangarajan, known as Susha. It had been nominated for Best Global Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards, becoming the first Tamil song to receive a Grammy nomination. For Ekambaram, the moment carried a childhood dream: watching Michael Jackson win a Grammy for Thriller and hearing presenter Whoopi Goldberg urge young viewers to hold on to their dreams. It was also a milestone reached without a family music legacy. "I come from a family of doctors and engineers. Nobody is in the art field, and I had to embark on this journey all alone," he says. A childhood tuned to music Growing up in New Jersey, often one of the few Indian children in his neighbourhood, Ekambaram found it difficult to fit in. Music became a source of confidence . His mother introduced him to different genres, while programmes such as American Bandstand and Solid Gold showed him performers building careers around music. He began playing guitar between the seventh and tenth grades, then joined the school choir and marching band. He learnt to listen for harmonies and how musical parts fitted together, and began recording at home. "I knew my weakness, but I found my strength," he says. He developed his musical identity through choir, harmony and arranging. Growing up in New Jersey, Devan Ekambaram found his first musical inspiration through school choirs, guitars and American television. The Grammys entered his imagination around this time. "I remember watching Michael Jackson win for Thriller , and hearing presenter Whoopi Goldberg urge young viewers to hold on to their dreams, come what may. And that became my dream," he says. At 19 or 20, while studying electrical engineering at the University of Illinois, he explored music opportunities during a college break in India. He eventually left engineering and moved to Chennai at 21. "I just quit my engineering degree in the US and came here with no support and no direction. It was the scariest thing because I never saw anyone do this growing up," he says. Building a life in music — and finding the right voice Ekambaram's move to Chennai gradually opened doors. His 1998 album Kamban Oru Kannile , made with S P Charan, caught A R Rahman's attention and led to work on Kadhalar Dhinam . He made his playback debut with "Oh Maria" in 1999 and went on to sing on more than 500 film soundtracks, while also working as a composer, voice artist, and vocal arranger. He had contributed to Grammy-winning projects such as Winds of Samsara (2015) and Divine Tides (2022). But this time, he wanted to create something that was unmistakably his own: an independent album reimagining the poetry of Subramania Bharati through contemporary arrangements. For the first single, he had a particular voice in mind. Ekambaram had met Subhiksha Rangarajan, known as Susha, back in 2007, when they appeared on the television programme Coffee with Anu . He had wanted to collaborate with her ever since, but the opportunity never quite came together. When he began working on the Bharati project, he reached out to her again. Years after meeting vocalist Susha in 2007, Ekambaram brought her into his independent project celebrating Subramania Bharati's poetry. Photograph: ( Instagram/@sushasings ) In June 2026, Susha arrived at his home studio with her mother, Lakshmi Rangarajan. The composition they were about to record was one Lakshmi had taught her, set to a tune by L Krishnan that was already around 40 to 50 years old. What followed was an unusually quick coming together of ideas . Ekambaram asked Susha to sing, and the recording took shape over the next two to three hours. For him, her voice brought together the musical sensibilities the song needed. Trained in Carnatic music and having studied jazz at the University of Toronto, Susha could move between the classical foundation of the composition and the contemporary sound he wanted to create. She had also been building her own independent music career, including through NEXA Music, an initiative by A R Rahman and Clinton Cerejo that selected her among 24 artistes in 2019. "Without her singing, nobody would have listened to the song," Ekambaram says. Giving an old poem a new sound He wanted to rebuild the traditional arrangement while retaining the melody's character. "I just gave it a makeover," he says. "I looked at it thinking, how I would want to hear this?" He wanted to make the form inviting to a new generation of listeners unfamiliar with Carnatic music without flattening its identity. Set in raga Desh, the arrangement brings Carnatic phrasing together with piano, slide guitar, acoustic guitar, bass and tabla. Ekambaram played keyboards and produced the track. It features pianist Anil Srinivasan, slide guitarist Prakash Sontakke, guitarist Naveen Samson, bassist Joseph John and tabla player Sarvajit Krishna Mohan. Roshan Sebastian mixed and mastered it. The collaboration was largely remote: Susha recorded at Ekambaram's home studio, while the instrumentalists sent their parts from elsewhere. "I coordinated the musicians and worked with Sebastian on the final mix. The result was a three-minute-and-26-second recording released independently on 12 August 2026," he says. Susha's Carnatic training and jazz influences shaped Varuvaaiy, a contemporary interpretation of a century-old Tamil composition. Susha's contribution was central to the sound he had imagined. "Without her singing, nobody would have listened to the song," Ekambaram says. Her Carnatic training, jazz studies at the University of Toronto and contemporary sensibility shaped the recording. In 2019, she was among 24 artistes selected for NEXA Music, an initiative by A R Rahman and Clinton Cerejo. Her debut album, Love Language , arrived in August 2026. Written more than a century ago, the poem's exact date is unknown, though it is believed to date from Bharati's years in Pondicherry. Its imagery calls for a force to enter human thought and dispel darkness, and has been read as a metaphor for resisting oppression and colonial rule. That purpose appealed to Ekambaram. Rather than create a new song with contemporary lyrics, he wanted to bring a poet whose words shaped Tamil public life to younger listeners. "I thought this had a purpose," he says. He hoped a fresh musical arrangement would allow his children's generation to encounter Bharati's language without feeling distanced by it. A release against the clock Getting the single out in time required a difficult decision. Ekambaram says labels he approached were hesitant because the underlying work was in the public domain, and the permissions process threatened to delay the release. "With the Grammy submission deadline approaching, I chose to release the track independently and complete the distribution myself. But I never imagined how well it would work," he recalls. Rooted in raga Desh, the recording blends Carnatic nuances with jazz influences, guitars, piano and tabla. He had submitted work before and contributed to Grammy-winning projects, but this time concentrated on Varuvaaiy , preparing its streaming links for the Best Global Music Performance category. The category had 526 submissions, he says, and seeing the names on the ballot made a nomination feel far from certain. On nomination morning, the song had around 300 YouTube views, according to Ekambaram. As the news spread, the count rose to about 35,000. Messages of appreciation came from musicians including Scott Hoying of Pentatonix and Chandrika Tandon. What comes after the nomination The recognition arrived as Ekambaram questioned what came next. He had considered continuing in Chennai or returning to the United States if work did not move forward. He wanted to build a body of work listeners could associate with him, not a film or star. He worried that short-lived online trends left less room for songs that stay with people. The February 2027 Grammy ceremony will see Varuvaaiy compete alongside recordings by internationally acclaimed musicians. "The nomination has renewed my resolve to make independent music, compose and experiment rather than rely only on past successes. To think that I almost gave up and left for L. A., but we never know when opportunities will come. Today, I'm glad I continued on the path," he says. Ekambaram credits mentors including Madhav Das at Magnus Sound, choir director Ruth Lane McIntyre and the high-school teacher who encouraged him to sing. He wishes they could have witnessed the announcement. The larger Bharati album is now the next step. Ekambaram says it will contain 10 to 12 contemporary interpretations, with the tracks already taking shape and around two months of work remaining at the time of the interview. He is also waiting for a bilingual Tamil-Telugu film for which he composed the music to reach audiences. The ceremony is scheduled for February 2027 in Los Angeles, where Varuvaaiy will compete alongside recordings by Ang lique Kidjo, Rosal a, Shakira and Burna Boy. Winning would be wonderful, he says, but the nomination has already given him something deeply valuable. For Ekambaram, the nomination is already a milestone: bringing Tamil poetry and music to a global audience. "I don't care whether I win the category or not," he says. "I've been a catalyst in placing Tamil music on the global map. That is my win." More than a century after Bharati wrote the poem, its words have travelled into a new musical language: first through a melody passed down across generations, then through a contemporary arrangement shaped by musicians working across genres and distances. Now, listeners far beyond Tamil-speaking communities are being invited to hear it, too, today. That, perhaps, is the lasting possibility of Varuvaaiy . A poem written in another time has not been left behind in it. It has been given another voice, another audience and another chance to be understood. And somewhere, a listener encountering Bharati for the first time may follow the song back to the words that began it all.
