items.descriptionOriginal: A car brakes suddenly as a two-wheeler slips into the gap ahead. An auto-rickshaw swerves to avoid a bus, while another vehicle edges into the next lane. On Indian roads, where cars, buses, three-wheelers and two-wheelers often share limited space, traffic can change its rhythm in seconds. For urban planners and traffic engineers, understanding this movement is no easy task. Many conventional traffic models assume that vehicles follow lanes and maintain relatively predictable speeds. But Indian roads rarely offer such orderly conditions. Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Guwahati are working to bridge this gap. By combining drone footage, automated vehicle tracking and machine learning, they have developed mathematical models that better account for the unpredictable ways vehicles move on Indian roads. Tracking nearly nine million vehicle positions Led by Professor Akhilesh Kumar Maurya from the Department of Civil Engineering, the research team studied traffic on an eight-lane divided highway on the outskirts of Delhi. Using drones equipped with high-resolution cameras, they recorded around five hours of daytime traffic footage in 4K resolution. The videos were then processed using DataFromSky, an automated software that extracts vehicle movements from aerial footage. Led by Professor Akhilesh Kumar Maurya, the IIT Guwahati research could help improve traffic simulations, highway planning and congestion management in India. Photograph: (IIT Guwahati) The result was a dataset of 36,818 vehicles and 8,938,920 vehicle-position data points, captured at 10 frames per second. Researchers categorised the vehicles into six groups: two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses, heavy commercial vehicles and light commercial vehicles. This gave them a detailed picture of how different vehicles moved, how closely they followed one another and how their speeds changed as traffic became denser. Explaining why India-specific data is necessary, Prof Maurya says, "Traffic conditions in India are different from those in many countries where existing traffic models have been developed. We need traffic data that represents the diversity and characteristics of Indian roads." Drone-based data collection provides an opportunity to observe a large number of vehicles and their movements over a road section at high spatial and temporal resolution. Teaching traffic models to account for unpredictability One interesting finding was that the distance vehicles maintained from one another changed with traffic density. On relatively empty roads, vehicles kept larger gaps. As traffic increased, these gaps became smaller. However, when congestion became severe, the spacing patterns changed again. This variability is important because two vehicles travelling under seemingly similar traffic conditions may not necessarily move at the same speed. Using automated vehicle tracking and machine learning, the researchers mapped 36,818 vehicles and nearly nine million vehicle-position data points. Photograph: ( iStock ) To understand these differences, the researchers tested six mathematical traffic models, including established approaches such as Greenshields and Underwood. They also trained two machine learning models: Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Random Forest (RF). But perhaps the most interesting part was their development of stochastic fundamental diagrams. In simple terms, conventional traffic models generally estimate one speed for a given traffic density. Stochastic models go a step further by accounting for the range of speeds that vehicles may actually travel at under those conditions. This allows the models to represent the randomness of Indian traffic more realistically, rather than smoothing over the differences between individual vehicles. From better predictions to smarter road planning The researchers found that the Underwood model performed most consistently among the mathematical models tested, achieving an R² value of 0.86. The two machine learning models achieved approximately 0.83. The research could have practical applications in assessing highway capacity, designing intersections, estimating road speeds, and improving traffic simulations. The data could also help researchers calibrate car-following models, which study how drivers adjust their distance and speed in relation to vehicles ahead. Prof. Maurya explains, "Reliable traffic management begins with models that represent how traffic actually behaves on Indian roads. The high-resolution trajectory data generated through drones allows us to capture interactions among different vehicle types and the large variability that conventional traffic models often overlook." Such India-specific models can support more realistic traffic simulation, better road and intersection design, congestion management, capacity assessment, and the development of intelligent traffic-management systems suited to Indian conditions. Unlike conventional traffic models, the stochastic models developed by the team account for variations in vehicle speeds and distances, even under similar traffic conditions. Photograph: ( Adobe Stock ) For anyone who has spent time on an Indian road, the challenge of predicting traffic is easy to understand. A car slows down, a two-wheeler slips into a narrow gap, an auto-rickshaw changes lanes, and the movement of hundreds of vehicles can shift in seconds. By capturing these interactions in detail, the IIT Guwahati team hopes to make traffic models better reflect what commuters experience every day. The research is a step towards understanding not just how many vehicles use a road, but how they move around one another. And that understanding could eventually help make the daily journey a little more predictable, whether someone is driving to work, taking a bus to school or navigating a crowded intersection.

items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Grist . Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here . Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain. Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer. Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons . Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO2 washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy of Teresus Solutions Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place. Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on. In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps and compressors. Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one-third of what’s inside a full scuba tank . As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp. The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’ chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing. For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry. The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said. As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint. Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance? LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work. LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to remove sugars, salts and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs. Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.” Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously. The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag . CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium. Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend. The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question. Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance. This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/science/carbon-dioxide-is-a-climate-problem-it-might-also-be-a-laundry-solution/ . Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change. items.descriptionOriginal: Garry oak trees, home for bluebirds nested in cavities, were tended by First Nations for millennia. Without their care, 95 percent of the Garry oak ecosystem was lost to agriculture, pesticides, and urban development. Their homes gone, bluebirds left, and were declared extinct on Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands. “Garry oak trees are a great source of insects,” said Jacquie Taylor, coordinator for the Cowichan Bring Back the Bluebirds Project. “They have a real biodiversity of their own, things that live in the bark and on the trees.” Saving them would help save the bluebirds. Canadians and Americans worked together, along with a military base, a slew of permits, thousands of volunteer hours, private property owners, Cowichan Tribes, and lots and lots of tiny, wriggling mealworms to help the bluebirds return. “But most noticeable is the sound: a gentle musical chortling so cheerful and soothing that it immediately banishes all thought of the ills of the world.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Once known as the Garden City for its tree-lined avenues, blooming parks and pleasant weather, Bengaluru is now facing a growing question: How can a rapidly expanding city make room for nature while preparing for heavier rains, water shortages and rising temperatures? Now, a neighbourhood-level climate planning exercise across five wards aims to address some of these concerns through better drainage, rainwater management and urban greening. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has prepared ward-level Climate Action Plans for five pilot wards across the city, identifying environmental challenges and proposing interventions suited to the conditions of each neighbourhood. The initiative is now awaiting budgetary approval from the respective city corporations before implementation can begin. The five wards selected for the pilot are Shantinagar in Central Bengaluru, Jakkur in the North, Begur in the South, Vijinapura in the East and Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar ward in the West. Developed under the GBA's Climate Action Cell, the plans aim to take climate planning beyond city-wide recommendations and identify what individual neighbourhoods need. The assessments cover energy and buildings, transportation, solid waste management, urban planning, greenery and biodiversity, water management, wastewater and stormwater management, and disaster preparedness. According to The New Indian Express, the plans were prepared following sector-wise assessments and consultations with residents, experts and other stakeholders. The exercise recognises that climate-related challenges are not uniform across Bengaluru. While some localities experience recurring flooding, others face water scarcity, declining green cover, rising temperatures or inadequate waste management. Why Bengaluru needs neighbourhood-level climate planning The city's contrasting water challenges illustrate why localised planning matters. Bengaluru experiences heavy surface runoff during the monsoon, even as several neighbourhoods face groundwater depletion and water shortages during summer. A March 18, 2026 report by Mongabay-India, which examined the ward-level planning exercise, highlighted how geography influences flood vulnerability. For instance, Shantinagar, a densely populated urban ward, lies in a downstream valley zone. Hydrological assessments by WELL Labs and Bengaluru's Climate Action Cell found that floodwater can originate beyond the ward's boundaries, making flooding a problem that cannot always be addressed through isolated drainage work within one locality. The five-ward pilot is intended to provide a model for extending climate action planning to other neighbourhoods under the GBA. Photograph: (Bengaluru Climate Action Cell-via Mongabay) Anam Husain, programme associate for Urban Water at WELL Labs, told Mongabay-India that nature-based interventions such as rain gardens, bioswales, permeable surfaces and small retention systems can help slow down rainwater runoff and improve groundwater infiltration. These interventions offer ways to manage excess rainwater closer to where it falls, while also reducing pressure on conventional drainage infrastructure. Rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge are particularly relevant in a city where water scarcity and monsoon runoff exist side by side. Alongside improving stormwater management, wastewater reuse and stormwater reuse can contribute to longer-term water security. Bringing green infrastructure into urban planning Urban greening is another important component of Bengaluru's climate planning exercise. In neighbourhoods experiencing rising temperatures, the GBA is considering measures such as increasing green cover, using heat-reflective cool paints and establishing cool shelters. These interventions can help address the urban heat island effect , in which built-up areas with extensive concrete surfaces and limited vegetation retain more heat than surrounding areas. Bengaluru's existing Climate Action and Resilience Plan also identifies nature-based solutions as an important part of urban development. View this post on Instagram A post shared by ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು ದಕ್ಷಿಣ ನಗರ ಪಾಲಿಕೆ (Bengaluru South City Corporation) (@bscc.gba) Its sectoral recommendations include restoring the city's blue-green networks, increasing tree canopy and expanding green and permeable surfaces to help reduce flood and heat-related risks. The plan sets targets to increase the city's tree canopy by 10% from its baseline by 2030 and 20% by 2040. It also proposes increasing green cover and permeable surfaces to 40% of the city's area by 2040. From climate plans to neighbourhood-level action Public participation has also been part of the planning process. Just recently, The Better India documented how Bengaluru residents are taking small, collective steps to care for their city's shared spaces . From removing 110 kg of plastic waste around Madiwala Lake during a 75-minute plogging drive to watering hundreds of saplings at Vengaiah Lake through the Bhagiratha initiative, the report highlighted how citizen participation can complement urban conservation efforts. Read the report. Other efforts include residents in Balagere, Panathur and Varthur clearing accumulated roadside dust, and volunteers working with civic authorities to restore neglected footpaths and public spaces. The Greater Bengaluru Authority's proposed Climate Action Plans across five wards take this approach further by seeking to integrate local environmental needs into formal urban planning. The five-ward pilot is intended to provide a model for extending climate action planning to other neighbourhoods under the GBA. For Bengaluru, the next step will be translating these local assessments into funded projects that improve drainage, strengthen water management and expand green infrastructure. The effectiveness of the exercise will ultimately depend on how consistently these proposals are implemented and monitored at the neighbourhood level. Sources: 'GBA goes micro local with ward-level climate plans' : By Express News Service, Published on 4 November 2026 'Ward-level plans bring climate action closer to communities' : By Mahima Jain, Published on 18 March 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: When we vote in a national or state election, we often have a document to refer to: the political party's manifesto. It tells us what the party promises to do if elected, from creating jobs and improving healthcare to building infrastructure. And once the government is in power, those promises give voters something to question it about. "But what happens when we vote for our village's Gram Pradhan? What are the promises we can expect them to make? And, more importantly, what can we hold them accountable for once they are elected?" This is the question that IAS officer Dr Heera Lal wants to bring into village elections through a 25-point Village Manifesto. His idea is straightforward: village elections, too, should be fought on issues and written promises, giving people a clearer say in what development should look like in their communities. "Elections are contested in Parliament on manifestos. In MLA seats, on manifestos. But in the village, we do not have any manifesto," he explains. A village's priorities could begin with a blocked drain, an unresolved land dispute or something as basic as sanitation. For him, a manifesto is essentially a written promise . If a candidate commits to addressing specific problems before being elected, villagers have something tangible to refer to afterwards. Without such a commitment, he argues, it becomes difficult for voters to question their elected representative about what they have delivered. Beyond roads, schools and drinking Water The 25-point framework tries to broaden what villages consider development. Conversations around rural progress often centre on a handful of visible needs, such as roads, schools, drinking water and electricity. But several other factors shape a village's quality of life, too. Saurabh Lall, CEO of Model Gaon, which developed the framework , says the idea emerged from recognising that a better life could not be measured through just three or four parameters. "Our first initiative was to make them understand that a better life entails a lot many other things than just having these three, four things being worked upon," he says. The manifesto therefore looks at a wider range of issues, including health, education, sanitation, income generation, employment, access to technology, sustainability, women's empowerment, local talent, dispute resolution and proper documentation of village records. Solar power, better sanitation and access to technology feature among the 25 priorities proposed for village-level development. Some of these priorities may not immediately come to mind when people think about rural development. But they can have a direct bearing on everyday life. A village where small disputes repeatedly escalate into expensive legal cases, for instance, faces a different challenge from one where the most pressing concern is access to irrigation or employment. The framework was deliberately simplified into a one-page document so that villagers could understand and engage with it. It was also designed to be personalised. "All those 25 things could mean different things for different people. And their priorities in life would also differ based on the phase of life that they were in, the context that they were living in," says Saurabh. The idea, then, is not to impose the same development agenda on every village. It is to give communities a framework through which they can identify what matters most to them. What should your village's manifesto actually promise? A list of 25 priorities is only a starting point . The more important exercise is deciding which of those priorities need attention first in a particular village. To do this, the process involves conversations at the ward level, where residents can raise problems they experience in their everyday lives. These meetings typically bring together around 25 to 35 people from a particular part of the village. The concerns can be remarkably specific. Saurabh recalls residents raising issues such as a drain being constructed inconveniently outside someone's home or a neighbour encroaching on a portion of their land. One recurring concern was the number of small local disputes that were escalating into court cases. Residents often had to travel to cities, spend money, and wait for lengthy legal processes to resolve issues that could potentially be addressed locally. Ward-level meetings bring 25 to 35 residents together to discuss everyday problems and decide which issues deserve attention first. "If people stop wasting time in resolving their petty disputes, they would end up either studying or working in their farms or looking for jobs," he says. In such cases, dispute resolution could become one of the village's most important priorities, even if it might not feature prominently in another village's manifesto. The meetings also allow the Gram Pradhan to hear these concerns directly. Rather than treating the manifesto as a document prepared by an outside organisation, the aim is to make it a reflection of what residents themselves want addressed. Saurabh believes this participation is essential to meaningful development. "Unless and until the beneficiary is involved in the designing of the programme itself, it never really gets very comprehensive." From written promises to accountability For a manifesto to mean something beyond election season, its promises must translate into action. That requires villagers to know what their priorities are, and their elected representatives to understand how to work towards them. Saurabh says the process also involves helping Gram Pradhans understand their rights, responsibilities, and the administrative procedures involved in local governance. The aim is to help them identify solutions by bringing together existing government schemes, local resources and relevant expertise. "We said that installing another system is not the solution. Galvanising the existing system is probably going to be more effective," he says. What should a Gram Pradhan promise voters? The manifesto encourages residents to identify their most pressing local needs. This is important because a village's problems do not always require an entirely new project or a fresh allocation of funds. Sometimes, the challenge is knowing which existing resources can be brought together to address a particular need. The larger ambition is to take this framework into upcoming Gram Pradhan elections. Dr Heera Lal describes the campaign with a slogan: "Chunaav mudra se nahi, muddon pe hoga" — elections should be fought on issues, not money. The proposal is to make the village manifesto a part of the election conversation, so candidates can put their priorities in writing and voters can assess them against the needs of their communities. Ultimately, the 25-point framework raises a question that goes beyond any one organisation or development initiative: shouldn't people have a clearer say in what their elected village representatives promise to deliver? A manifesto cannot guarantee that every problem will be solved. But it can give a village something to begin with: a shared list of priorities, written commitments and a way to ask its elected representative what has been done.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals , have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish , levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline to restrictions that removed both compounds from most products, which makes the data one of the clearer measures yet of what a chemical ban does to a river system over time. Two forever chemicals, two bans, one decade of data PFOS and PFOA PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were first developed in the U.S. in the 1930s. Manufacturers adopted them for their resistance to oil, water, and heat, and they ended up in nonstick pans, firefighting foam, and electrical components. The same chemical stability means they take a very long time to break down, which earned them the label forever chemicals. PFOS and PFOA were among the earliest compounds in the family. About 20 years ago, researchers began linking them to tissue damage in animals and to higher rates of certain serious illnesses in people, including testicular cancer . The UK all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. Results from the latest Environment Agency figures The new data, published by the EA this month, covers 10 years of monitoring. Both chemicals declined by nearly a third in river water, while the near-halving in fish points to less of the compounds moving up the food chain. Dr. David Megson, a reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, welcomed the trend. “It’s brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years,” he said. Lower concentrations, same total load Where forever chemicals go after a ban The EA report attaches a significant caveat to its own numbers. Because PFOS and PFOA break down so slowly, the total quantity in the environment has likely not changed much. Concentrations in rivers have dropped because the chemicals have been diluted and carried downstream into the sea. A ban stops new inputs, but it does not remove what is already circulating. Very few methods can destroy PFAS permanently. High-temperature incineration is one of them, and England currently has only two facilities suited to the job. Making polluters pay Megson sees the monitoring record as a starting point for accountability. “There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused,” he said. Regulating PFAS as a group 15,000 compounds, 200 in common use PFOS and PFOA are two of an estimated 15,000 PFAS, of which around 200 are in frequent use. The EA said that “uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS” and that its findings reinforce the case for regulating the chemicals as a class instead of one at a time. The chemicals industry has long resisted a group approach, arguing that evidence of toxicity for most other PFAS is limited or absent and that some have essential applications, including in life-saving medical equipment. Wider monitoring The agency now tests regularly for 60 additional PFAS to map contamination across England, and the government announced earlier this month that it will begin measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies. Taken together with the river data, those programs will show whether the pattern seen with PFOS and PFOA holds for other compounds once restrictions arrive: a slow but steady fall in water and wildlife, with the legacy load still to be dealt with downstream. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It’s 6 p.m. on a Friday, and the dinner you booked two weeks ago is in an hour. Back then it sounded like the perfect plan. But now your couch has never looked softer, your sweatpants feel like a hug, and your thumb is hovering over a message that starts with “So sorry, something came up…” Nothing came up, of course. You just don’t want to go anymore, and you can’t quite explain why. If that sounds familiar, you have plenty of company. According to the Survey Center on American Life , 55 percent of Gen Z adults say they feel relief when plans fall through. In the U.K., research from the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that 68 percent of people under 34 have bailed on plans, and one in 10 do it “very often.” There’s a name for that late-afternoon dread, and once you can name it, it gets a lot easier to put your shoes on anyway. What anticipatory anxiety feels like The doorway as a dividing line Mindy DeSeta , a licensed mental health counselor, calls it anticipatory anxiety. “It’s the stress we feel before something happens,” she says. Part of the pull comes from home itself, which is familiar and predictable in a way a crowded restaurant isn’t. “Walking through the doorway is the visual trigger that separates your safe space from the unknown,” DeSeta said. It’s the same jittery feeling you might have had before a school recital or a big presentation at work, just pointed at something that’s supposed to be fun. Why the dread rarely matches the night Think back to the last time you went out despite wanting to cancel. Chances are, an hour in, you were laughing at something and had forgotten all about the couch. DeSeta has seen that pattern again and again. “In most cases, the anticipation anxiety is often worse than the event itself. Don’t allow the jitters to deter you!” she said. What canceling plans costs your friends When everyone bails, everyone feels it Canceling feels harmless in the moment, and sometimes it’s the right call. But when it becomes a habit for a whole generation, someone is always on the other end of that text. Rachel Schleider, a 23-year-old social strategist said her birthday has become a source of stress for exactly this reason. “I literally dread making plans for my birthday every year because I know people are going to cancel the day before,” she said. She thinks the culture around flaking has swung too far. “We’ve kind of taken it too far and now people are way too comfortable bowing out,” Schleider said. How to manage anticipatory anxiety before a plan Name it, then don’t negotiate with it DeSeta’s first suggestion is to call the feeling what it is. Once you recognize the dread as anticipatory anxiety, you can remind yourself that the feeling isn’t an instruction. Feeling uneasy about going is a different thing from having a reason not to go. Breathe, and look at what the nerves are telling you A few slow, deep breaths can take the edge off the physical side of it, the tight chest and the restless hands. It also helps to flip the meaning of the nerves around. Feeling jittery about seeing someone usually means the plan matters to you, which is a reason to show up instead of a reason to stay home. Set an alarm and let the routine carry you DeSeta’s most practical trick happens before the dread has a chance to build: set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, get in the shower and get dressed without debating it. By the time your hair is dry, you’re most of the way out the door. None of this means you should drag yourself out when you’re sick or running on empty. Rest is a valid reason to cancel. But if the only thing standing between you and your friends is that familiar pre-plan heaviness, it might help to picture the walk home afterward, a little tired and full and glad you went, and let that version of the evening make the decision for you. There’s a name for that feeling first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Although vegans generally have a healthy gut microbiome, they may be at risk of having lower gut bacterial diversity than omnivores, according to the author of a new study. The gut is home to billions of microorganisms. It is a complex ecosystem that regulates many of the body’s functions and helps keep us healthy—when it is in balance. Our diet influences this ecosystem. But what role does it play whether a person is vegan or omnivorous? In a new study, researchers from the University of Copenhagen examined this question by closely investigating the gut microbiome of 75 vegans and 75 omnivorous Danes. The researchers initially expected the vegan group to have the healthiest gut microbiome across all parameters. However, they found one notable weakness: gut bacterial diversity was, on average, lower among vegans than among omnivores. “This came as a major surprise. Because vegans eat only plant-based foods and therefore consume large amounts of dietary fiber and other health-promoting plant compounds that stimulate the gut microbiome, we expected the vegan group to have greater bacterial diversity than the omnivores. But that was not the case,” says Oluf Borbye Pedersen, professor at the Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research. He adds: “The study suggests that the lower average diversity of gut bacteria among vegans may be linked to their lower protein intake. Among vegans, 12% of dietary energy came from protein, compared with 17% among omnivores. However, the vegans who consumed the most protein had biodiversity levels comparable to those of the omnivores. Protein may therefore be an overlooked factor for a diverse gut microbiome among vegans.” The researchers are interested in gut health because it is crucial to overall health. In this context, having a diversity of bacteria is considered beneficial. “Our gut is an enormously complex ecosystem. It can be compared to a rainforest, which functions best when it houses as many different species as possible. The same applies to our internal microbial ecosystem. It should ideally be as diverse as possible,” says Pedersen. “High biodiversity is a sign of a healthy and resilient gut microbiome. And a healthy microbiome is not only essential for digestion and metabolism, it also plays an important role in immune function and brain health.” To understand the differences between vegans and omnivores, the researchers analyzed stool, blood, and urine samples. They then mapped the bacteria and viruses in the gut as well as signaling molecules in the body. “Apart from the reduced diversity of gut bacteria, we found that the vegans had a health-promoting gut microbiome,” says Pedersen. The vegans consumed more carbohydrates and dietary fiber and, on average, less protein and fat than the omnivores. They also had higher levels of several bacterial species capable of breaking down dietary fiber, along with a greater prevalence of the organism Blastocystis, which has been associated with lower blood pressure. The vegans also had lower blood glucose and cholesterol levels. Compared with the omnivores, they also had fewer inflammatory markers in the body. The researchers emphasize that the study is relatively small and observational comparing existing dietary patterns. The results may therefore point to associations, but they cannot establish whether specific dietary habits directly cause changes in the gut microbiome or to gut health, for example whether protein intake directly causes changes in gut biodiversity. As such, Pedersen cannot make dietary recommendations based on the new study. However, he says the findings support the importance of ensuring adequate nutrition, regardless of dietary preference: “Vegans in particular should consider whether they are getting enough protein in their diet, since they do not obtain it from meat, eggs, or dairy products. Good vegan sources of protein include beans, lentils, hemp seeds, chia seeds, quinoa, almonds, and nuts.” The research appears in Microbiome . Source: University of Copenhagen The post Vegan gut bacteria discovery surprises researchers appeared first on Futurity .

Η μελέτη εξήγησε επίσης γιατί: Όταν το…
items.descriptionOriginal: Antibodies that coat the lining of your gut may be playing an important role in preventing colon cancer from developing, scientists have discovered. Mice that lack a specific class of antibodies, called immunoglobulin A (IgA), develop more than twice as many colon tumors as usual, the team reports in Nature . The study also explained why: When the antibodies bind to the cells lining the inside of the gut, it keeps those cells from dividing too quickly—which could lead to cancer. When the researchers gave IgA-deficient mice oral doses of the antibodies, they no longer had a higher risk of developing tumors. “One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer,” says senior author Daniel Mucida, head of Rockefeller University’s Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. “Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?” The discovery illuminates why people with IgA deficiency—who have few or none of these antibodies—are at a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer but also could shed light on other aspects of the complex interplay between the gut microbes, immune system, and cancer—even in otherwise healthy people. Scientists and clinicians have long known that the gut has high levels of IgA. Unlike many antibodies that are highly specific for one pathogen at a time, IgA is a broad-acting first line of defense in the immune system. A single IgA molecule can bind to a wide range of gut bacteria—as well as some healthy human cells—but researchers had long wondered why there were such high levels of IgA in the digestive system. Mucida and his colleagues study how the intestine strikes a balance between protecting the body against invading pathogens and absorbing the nutrients the body needs. In the past, for instance, the lab has discovered the role that gut immune cells play in food intolerances and allergies. In the new work, former Rockefeller postdoctoral fellow Gregory Donaldson—now an assistant professor at UCLA—wanted to tease out exactly how IgA antibodies interact with gut bacteria, and whether that could be relevant to colon cancer. “We know these antibodies bind bacteria and by doing so can shape the microbiome,” he says. “And because IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the US, is linked to colorectal cancer, I wondered whether these interactions might be relevant to the disease.” Donaldson began by studying IgA-deficient mice that were raised alongside normal mice, ensuring that they were exposed to the same germs and food. The mice without IgA developed more colorectal cancers than those who had IgA—echoing what was already known to occur in humans. “We found this was true for several different kinds of models of colon cancer, so that was a really convincing effect,” says Donaldson. Moreover, giving these mice an oral treatment of IgA molecules eliminated the increased risk of cancer. Mucida, Donaldson, and the rest of their group zoomed in to the cells lining the gut, called epithelial cells—where colon cancers first form—to see how they were different in the mice lacking IgA. They discovered that changes in gene expression included ones related to cell division, or proliferation, and that these changes came before any tumors ever emerged. “We assumed there must be some sort of receptor on the epithelial cells that was mediating this,” Donaldson says. Second author Gabriella Lima dos Reis, a graduate student in Gabriel Victora’s lab, homed in on one receptor that is found on the surface of epithelial cells and that IgA can bind to. Called DMBT1, it had already been linked in multiple ways to some cancers, but its exact role in colon cancer was unclear. The team went on to show that DMBT1, in the presence of gut bacteria, acts as a gas pedal for cell proliferation. But IgA, when it binds to DMBT1, acts as a brake. If IgA is completely absent, DMBT1 signaling is unrestrained, letting gut epithelial cells divide more than usual and form tumors. But without gut bacteria, without DMBT1 signaling, or with normal IgA levels, the epithelial cells are kept in check. “If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function—responding to bacteria by producing new cells—can keep dividing, leading to cancer,” Mucida says. “We think this homeostatic effect is IgA’s main function. This was a big surprise.” By establishing DMBT1’s natural function in epithelial cells for the first time, the findings may lay the groundwork for new interventions to reduce colon cancer risk. “Based on the mechanism we discovered, perhaps we could influence epithelial cells to be less likely to develop into a tumor,” Mucida says. “We know, for example, that having polyps increases your chances of getting colon cancer, so we think that there could be an opportunity to target this pathway after polyps are removed. Right now, there are no interventions available at that point.” “What is potentially even more exciting is that there is evidence that individual species of bacteria can have really specific effects on epithelial cells as well,” Donaldson notes. “A lot of research has focused on bacteria that induce tumors or can exacerbate their growth, but we have some evidence that there are bacteria that could do the opposite, just as IgA does. To that end, perhaps we could develop a probiotic supplement that induces a protective IgA response. This is all very speculative, but it’s one direction that we could look toward in the future.” Mucida adds, “Overall, there is a lot more to learn about how the dance between bacteria, antibodies, and epithelial cells in the gut works to maintain health.” Source: Rockefeller University The post Gut antibodies may help protect against colon cancer appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Take a walk through a city park. There are trees lining the paths, lawns stretching between them and plenty of shade. It looks green, perhaps even thriving. But where are the wild grasses that feed grazing animals? The flowering shrubs that attract butterflies? The ponds and stream banks where birds and other creatures find food and shelter? A place can look green while losing what wildlife needs to survive. That is the message emerging from Chandigarh's 2026 wildlife survey. Researchers recorded an impressive range of species, from a leopard and sambar deer to birds and butterflies. Yet they also found that several native trees were struggling to regenerate naturally and recommended greater protection for grasslands, wetlands and other habitats. For Indian cities, where planting drives often signal environmental progress, the findings suggest a better starting point: the habitat and the life it supports. What the survey found in Chandigarh's forests Conducted between 20 and 27 November 2025 by the Chandigarh Department of Forest and Wildlife and the Wildlife Institute of India (WII), the assessment covered Sukhna Wildlife Sanctuary and forest patches beyond its boundaries. Researchers documented 16 mammal species, 132 bird species, 73 butterfly species and 13 species of reptiles and amphibians. They also recorded 43 tree species, 14 shrub species and 22 herb species. The survey detected a leopard and estimated around 603 sambar, a deer species found in the region's forests. The figures show the variety of life these natural areas continue to shelter. But counting species was only one part of the exercise. The report also looked at the condition of their habitats and recommended restoring native vegetation, protecting grasslands, reviving wetlands and streamside habitats, and controlling invasive species. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Photograph: (The Tribune) Knowing which animals live in a forest matters. Knowing whether their habitat can continue to support them tells us what needs attention. A forest can have trees and still need help Imagine a woodland full of mature trees. From a distance, it might seem healthy. Look beneath the canopy, though, and there may be very few young trees coming up to replace the older ones. This is the problem of poor natural regeneration, which the Chandigarh survey flagged in native species including khair ( Senegalia catechu ), siris ( Albizia lebbeck ), Lannea coromandelica and Terminalia anogeissiana . Natural regeneration is simply the process of seeds becoming new plants without people planting them. It allows a forest to renew itself across generations. If young trees are missing, some native species could become less common as older trees die. That is why an increase in tree cover cannot, by itself, tell us whether a forest is doing well. The survey also cautioned against large plantations dominated by one species, known as monocultures. A row of identical trees may offer shade, but a healthy habitat needs different kinds of vegetation, from tall trees to shrubs, grasses and ground cover. Each layer has a purpose. Birds need places to nest, butterflies seek nectar, insects live among leaves and grasses, and herbivores depend on suitable plants for food. The report recommends replacing invasive vegetation with native species. Why does that matter? Why native plants can make a difference Native plants occur naturally in a region. Over time, they develop relationships with the insects, birds and animals around them. Some insects feed on particular plants; birds visit their flowers; other animals carry their seeds to new places. Introduced, or exotic, plants come from elsewhere. Many grow successfully in cities, and some offer flowers, fruit or shelter. But they do not always support the same relationships. Certain species can also spread so aggressively that they push out local vegetation. A 2023 Bengaluru study published in Science of the Total Environment helps explain why the distinction matters. Researchers compared how birds and mammals interacted with native and alien trees. They found that taller native trees with larger floral displays supported more bird species than alien trees with comparable displays. There was another interesting difference. Nectar-feeding birds were more likely to visit native flowers in ways that helped pollination. On alien trees, their visits more often involved 'nectar theft', where a bird takes nectar without transferring pollen in the way the flower needs to reproduce. This does not mean every introduced tree is harmful. The study recognised that alien trees can provide resources for wildlife in cities where natural vegetation has already been lost. The lesson is to understand what different plants actually offer local wildlife, rather than choosing them only because they grow quickly or look attractive. For Chandigarh, that supports the survey's recommendation to prioritise native vegetation that belongs to the landscape. Why an open grassland deserves protection A patch of tall, wild grass might look like an empty plot beside a landscaped park. It is easy to imagine someone deciding to plant trees there to 'improve' it. But a grassland is already a habitat. Its native grasses feed grazing animals, shelter insects and support species that depend on open spaces. Their roots also help hold soil together and influence how rainwater moves through the ground. Planting trees across an existing grassland can change the conditions that make it useful to those species. The result may look greener to us while offering less to the wildlife that lived there. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Photograph: (Chandigarh Help Post) This is why the Chandigarh survey specifically recommended protecting grasslands and restoring native grasses, including Eulaliopsis binata , Arundinella nepalensis and Heteropogon contortus . Across India, open spaces are often treated as land waiting to be developed, tidied up or planted over. Planners first need to ask what habitat is already there. Sometimes, caring for a green space means leaving room for its grasses to grow. Wetlands and riverbanks support different kinds of life The same principle applies to waterbodies and the land around them. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Woodland habitats, meanwhile, recorded the highest bird diversity. These differences matter. A forest, an open grassland and a stream bank may all be part of the same landscape, yet each offers food and shelter to different species. The report therefore called for wetland restoration and better care of streamside habitats , alongside other measures such as controlling invasive species. Research from the East Kolkata Wetlands shows why protecting such spaces requires attention to more than their size or appearance. A 2024 study in Environmental Research examined changes between 1991 and 2023. It found that the number of wetland patches had risen from 2,689 to 4,532, a sign that the landscape had become more fragmented. Over the same period, the study's ecosystem health index fell from 0.67 to 0.55. In simple terms, a wetland can still appear on a city map while its connected habitats are broken into smaller pieces and its ecological condition deteriorates. The Kolkata findings do not describe Chandigarh's wetlands, but they show what cities risk overlooking if they focus only on how much green or blue space remains. The two-day Capacity Building Workshop on Wildlife Survey & Techniques concluded today in Chandigarh! Diverse participants— representatives of civil society organisations, college students, wildlife enthusiasts, media personnel and journalists were sensitized and trained on various wildlife survey and monitoring methods. Thank all the multiple stakeholders for making it impactful. #WildlifeConservation #CitizenScience #WildlifeSurvey #Chandigarh #Sukhna #Chandigarhbirdclub @moefcc @wii_india @GobindsagarBha1 @RuchiBadola2 @gopigv @UDHAYAR230 @Ashik40405287 @Alexjacob11 @NonitaRana04 @RayR5847 — Wildlife Institute of India (@wii_india) November 19, 2025 Chandigarh's survey also recorded the red-eared slider turtle, an exotic aquatic species, and recommended its removal and management in controlled settings. Such species are sometimes released into waterbodies after being kept as pets and can place additional pressure on native wildlife. Wetlands need care as living habitats, not simply as water-filled spaces. What should other Indian cities measure? There is evidence from Delhi, too, that a park's value to wildlife depends on more than its tree count. A 2024 study in Ecological Frontiers examined birds across 64 city parks, recording 90 species and 19,131 individual birds. It found that vegetation characteristics and disturbance affected which birds used the parks. Native trees and lower surrounding urbanisation were also linked with greater bird diversity. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Chandigarh's plantation figures offer another lesson. During 2025–26, the administration planted 6,64,133 saplings against a target of 5,76,221. But third-party monitoring in November 2025 and March 2026 found an overall survival rate of around 79%. For 2026–27, the administration lowered its target to 4,19,854 saplings, including those distributed and sold, and said it would pay greater attention to site selection, quality and care after planting. Survival is important. So is asking whether the right species have been planted in the right place, and whether existing habitats are being protected rather than replaced. The Chandigarh survey was conducted over a short period, so its findings are a snapshot rather than proof that the city's wildlife populations are rising or falling. Longer-term, seasonal monitoring would help show how these habitats and their inhabitants change. But its message is already useful. Before the next plantation drive, city planners can ask a few practical questions: Is this land a forest, grassland or wetland? Which species rely on it? Are young native plants growing back? And what does this place need most? For some spaces, the answer will be trees. For others, it may be restoring a stream bank, protecting a grassland or allowing native shrubs to return. A city's natural wealth lives in more than its canopy. It is in the butterflies visiting riverbanks, the birds sheltering in woodland, the deer grazing on native grasses and the many smaller creatures that depend on them. Making room for all these habitats is how a city makes room for wildlife. Sources: 'Restore native species, wetlands; curb invasives: UT wildlife survey' : By Munieshwer A, Published on 2 October 2026 'Chandigarh's Wildlife Survey Exposes the Cost of Neglecting Native Habitats' : By Urban Acres, Published on 2 October 2026 'Urban park characteristics defining avian community structure in Delhi, India' : By Deepti Kumari, Ashutosh Srivastava, Upamanyu Hore, Published in December 2024 'Native fauna interact differently with native and alien trees in a tropical megacit' : By Purabi Deshpande, Rohan Sharma, Aleksi Lehikoinen, Rose Thorogood, Published on 10 April 2023 'Wildlife Week 2026 inaugurated in Chandigarh with Walkathon; focus on habitat connectivity and wildlife conservation' : By India News Calling, Published on 2 October 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, once the paddy harvest is over, farmers across Haryana face a familiar problem. Their fields are covered with leftover straw, and they need to clear the land before planting the next crop. For many, burning this stubble is the quickest solution. But the smoke that rises from these fields adds to North India's already severe air pollution. Now imagine if that same straw could earn money, create jobs and even help power industries. That's exactly what two women from Haryana and neighbouring Rajasthan set out to do. Sanjana, a graduate from Ghoranwali village in Haryana's Sirsa district, and her friend Sonika, from Bhadra in Rajasthan, saw a business opportunity in something farmers struggled to get rid of. They decided to collect leftover paddy straw , locally called parali , and turn it into biofuel pellets that power plants could use as an alternative fuel. In 2024, they started SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore. Today, the venture reports an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore and employs over 20 people. From a pollution problem to a business idea For Sonika, the idea began with a sight she had witnessed repeatedly after the paddy harvest: thick smoke spreading across the sky as farmers burned crop residue. Concerned about the environmental and public health consequences, she began thinking about how this agricultural waste could be put to better use. Rather than treating stubble burning as a problem with no easy solution, she and Sanjana started exploring ways to convert the residue into a commercially useful product. At their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali, Haryana, machinery processes leftover paddy straw into compact biofuel pellets, giving agricultural waste a productive use. Photograph: ( Peddler media ) The idea was to address two needs together: give farmers a productive use for their leftover crop residue while creating an alternative fuel that industries could use. Government policies and initiatives promoting stubble management also helped create an opportunity for the venture to take shape. Building a factory around farm waste In 2024, Sanjana and Sonika set up their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) scheme. The factory follows a process that begins in the fields. The women source paddy straw through baler operators in Sirsa and surrounding areas. These operators collect and compress the loose residue, making it easier to transport and store. The stubble is then brought to their factory, where machinery processes it into compact biofuel pellets. These pellets can be supplied to power plants as an alternative fuel. By sourcing paddy straw from farmers and baler operators across the region, the founders are creating a market for crop residue. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The scale of the operation is considerable. The unit uses approximately 1 lakh to 1.5 lakh quintals of paddy stubble every year. Since the raw material is available mainly during the harvesting season, the founders also have to plan for the months ahead. They collect and store the residue after harvest, ensuring that the factory has enough raw material to continue production throughout the year. This seasonal sourcing and year-round production model allows them to keep the business running beyond the harvesting window. From discarded straw to a growing rural enterprise The venture's impact extends beyond the pellets it produces. By creating a market for paddy straw, SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited also generates business opportunities for local baler operators and others involved in collecting and transporting the residue. The factory itself provides employment to more than 20 people, bringing work opportunities closer to home for residents in and around the village. From an initial investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore, Sanjana and Sonika have built an enterprise reporting an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore. What began as an effort to address stubble burning has grown into a rural enterprise that employs over 20 people and reports an annual turnover of Rs 8 crore. Photograph: ( Peddler Media ) For the two founders, the next harvest season will bring another opportunity to source more stubble, keep production going and expand their business. Their work has given farmers in the region another possible route for managing crop residue, while creating a market for material that would otherwise have little economic value. In Ghoranwali, the paddy harvest no longer marks just the end of a farming cycle. For Sanjana and Sonika, it also marks the beginning of another season of business, one built around putting farm waste to productive use. Sources: '2 women turn paddy stubble into Rs 8-crore business in Haryana' by Anil Kakkar for The Tribune, Published on 14 October 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Get smart Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans. Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. Will says: As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. Mapping roots In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. “I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” Becca says: On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable tree. On the other hand, I do like the idea of people detouring to see cool trees . What else we’re reading Minnesota announces ‘effective end’ to veteran homelessness, achieving decades-long goal — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from KSTP Free tool helps young men to take responsibility for sexual harm — shared by Contributing Editor Geetanjali Krishna from Positive News ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis? — shared by Michaela Haas from the Guardian In other news… Turns out people love moss! Our Instagram video about how moss is taking over cities has really taken off. To learn more about all the cool things moss can do, read Michaela Haas’s great story. The post What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Αυτό που την έφερε πίσω ήταν μια φράση από έναν μέντορα: μείνετε πιστή σε αυτό που πραγματικά ακούτε από μέσα. Αυτή η γραμμή την ακολουθεί σε κάθε δωμάτιο από τότε. Μεγάλωσε σε ένα…
items.descriptionOriginal: At fourteen, Shakhzoda Saidova slipped away from a conference table with the UN General Assembly and UNICEF in Tajikistan — too nervous, too convinced she didn't belong. What brought her back was a single sentence from a mentor: stay true to what you're actually hearing from inside. That line has followed her into every room since. She grew up in a country where her mother — who finished school with perfect marks and won a law scholarship — was forbidden by her husband's family from ever practicing as a lawyer. Watching that buried ambition became Shakhzoda's compass. Now studying in Romania, she is building SafeVoice: a disarmingly simple website listing real lawyers and crisis shelter numbers for women in Tajikistan facing domestic violence, because she knows what it costs a woman with three children and one free minute to find a page of dead links. She speaks five languages and is already being criticized for living in Europe at nineteen instead of being married. What's striking is the image of her mother, smiling serenely at those who disapprove — "Yes, I allowed that; yes, she's my daughter" — after accepting her daughter's diploma while the teenager boarded a flight towards a future she herself was never allowed to choose.

items.description: Ο φετινός διαγωνισμός Nature Photographer of the Year έλαβε 27.108 συμμετοχές από φωτογράφους σε περισσότερες από 96 χώρες — και ο γενικός νικητής, που ανακοινώθηκε στις 14 Νοεμβρίου, ξεχωρίζει με περισσότερους από έναν τρόπους. Με τίτλο «The One That Left and The One That Stayed», η φωτογραφία του Hannu Ahonen με ένα φύλλο νούφαρου δίπλα σε ένα παγωμένο αντίγραφο με εικόνα καθρέφτη είναι εκπληκτική στο i…
items.descriptionOriginal: This year’s Nature Photographer of the Year competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in more than 96 countries — and the overall winner, announced Nov. 14, stands out in more ways than one. Titled “The One That Left and the One That Stayed,” Hannu Ahonen’s shot of a water lily leaf beside a mirror-image frozen replica is stunning in its own right, but it’s also a “rare” example of a plant photo winning the annual contest, according to the chair of the judging panel, Theo Bosboom. “It is not often that a photograph of a plant is crowned the overall winner of a major photography competition, but the jury could not overlook this fascinating image by Hannu Ahonen,” Bosboom said in a press release shared with Nice News. “First and foremost, the photograph captures a unique situation: a water lily leaf with an almost perfect black-and-white replica of it lying next to it in the water.” He continued, “It takes a moment for the viewer to realize what has happened here: A thin layer of ice that had formed on the leaf has been blown away by the wind. The shapes in the sheet of ice are delicate; even the veins of the water lily leaf are clearly recognizable. Because the water lily and the sheet of ice are still touching, a sense of connection emerges; you realize that they belong together, like yin and yang.” In addition to being named overall winner, the Finnish photographer took the top spot in the Plants and Fungi category. Scroll on to see the other category winners and read commentary from the judging panel on each one. Birds: “Painting From the End of the World” by Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel (France) Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel / NPOTY 2026 “Environmental portraits of wildlife can make us feel closer to the animals despite being farther away from them, when done right. This image of a Magellanic woodpecker in its gorgeous habitat was a perfect example. It stood out from thousands of submissions because of its understated sense of place, beauty, simplicity, and timing. Diagonal lines formed by several trees guide the eyes to discover the bird — expertly framed against the backdrop and placed off-center — while encouraging exploration of the forest and the Patagonian landscape beyond it. Overall, it was a very successful reminder of how the portrayal of nature in its literal state can still be the most powerful of photographic expressions.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Mammals: “Play Misty” by Paul Goldstein (U.K.) Paul Goldstein / NPOTY 2026 “Quiet images can be easy to overlook in the fiercely competitive mammal category, one of the largest in NPOTY. This ethereal image of a giraffe peeking out of the mist revealed its strengths gradually. Initially a little disorienting, it offered just enough of a visual puzzle to keep the viewer engaged until the image resolved. The soft pastel colors create a soothing atmosphere, while the image’s simplicity and quiet emotion ultimately made it stand out among the category’s strongest contenders.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Other Animals: “The Pitcher’s Micro Kingdom” by Marcus Kuan (Singapore) Marcus Kuan / NPOTY 2026 “The lighting, colors, and unexpected gathering of species immediately caught our attention. Kuan beautifully captured a world where crustaceans, amphibians, and carnivorous plants cross paths. As judges, we were drawn to the possibilities unfolding within this single frame. Could the pitchers be digesting invertebrates? Might the frog be exploring a potential egg-laying site, while the crab continues its daily search for food among the plants? The image invites us to imagine the separate lives of these organisms, briefly brought together. The carefully balanced composition, beautifully controlled lighting, and rich greens and reds against the dark nighttime background make this a striking photograph.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Landscape: “In the Circle of Vultures Around the Falls” by J Fritz Rumpf (U.S.) J Fritz Rumpf / NPOTY 2026 “What immediately caught our attention was the incredible light and atmosphere in this photo. The longer we looked, the more fascinating it became. There is so much to discover: the last light of day illuminating the mist rising from Iguazú Falls, the silhouettes of trees and rocks, the birds circling above, the sunlight streaming through an opening in the rock at the center, and the subtle waterfall on the left. The interplay of light and shadow transforms the immense power of the waterfalls into something intimate and almost dreamlike. A beautiful example of how an iconic natural wonder can be captured in a truly extraordinary way.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Underwater: “Beneath Aquatic Constellations” by Matt Pérez (U.S.) Matt Pérez / NPOTY 2026 “Pérez’s photograph immediately drew us in. As a jury, we wanted to linger over it, exploring the details and wondering what we were seeing. Newt egg masses decorate the submerged branches like baubles on a Christmas tree, framing the scene and guiding our eyes towards the pond turtle with its piercing yellow eyes.The scene feels almost otherworldly, busy with intricate details yet still peaceful to look at — an impressive balance to capture in a single photograph. Its beautiful composition, striking lighting, and balance of rich detail and serene feel made this photo stand out to the jury. Matt Pérez also deserves credit for stepping back from the turtles’ courtship behavior to capture this wider view of a male pond turtle within an extraordinary habitat.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Nature Art: “Peach Blossoms in the Snow” by Xuzhong Liu (China) Xuzhong Liu / NPOTY 2026 “This photograph has everything that can make a drone shot interesting and fascinating. First and foremost, there are beautiful shapes and subtle colors, but there is also a sense of alienation. What am I actually looking at, and what is the scale of the landscape in the photograph? The image was taken in September in a wetland area in China, but it reminded the photographer himself of peach blossoms he had previously photographed during a spring trip to Tibet. A good abstract photograph like this also leaves plenty of room for the viewer to decide for themselves what they see in it. This makes it the perfect winner of the nature art category.” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Human and Nature: “Evolution” by Petr Bambousek (Czechia) Petr Bambousek / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its striking depiction of the impact human activity has on local wildlife. The sleeping Malayan sun bear inside a garbage incinerator creates a powerful visual contrast, showing how habitat loss and human waste increasingly force wild animals into close contact with human environments. The image is both unexpected and unsettling, capturing a broader story of how wildlife is forced to adapt as its natural surroundings are altered and destroyed.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Black and White: “Storm on the Sea” by László Tóth (Hungary) László Tóth / NPOTY 2026 “This photo really stood out to us. At first, we were not quite sure what we were looking at. It sparked some wonderful discussions among the jury and made us look even closer. The black-and-white contrast, dark diagonal lines, and striking patterns create a fascinating abstract composition. It looks like a storm at sea, but in reality, it is a thin layer of snow shaped by strong winds on a frozen lake, captured from above.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Animal Portraits: “A Seal’s Worst Nightmare” by Audun Rikardsen (Norway) Audun Rikardsen / NPOTY 2026 “Just when we thought we had seen about every kind of polar bear image there is, along comes this shot taken from inside a hole in the ice looking up at the bear. Once you realize what is happening, you start thinking about how this shot could possibly have been taken. Then it dawns on you that it seems almost impossible, no matter how. Showing something never seen before is a pretty effective method of captivating an audience, and one that carried this image all the way to the top. With oceans warming and ice melting, the ‘What’s going on down there?’ look gives the image a deeper layer of meaning that I appreciate. Right now humanity is looking back up at the bear and shrugging its collective shoulders in pretense. For how much longer?” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Nature of “De Lage Landen”: “Fairies” by Enikő Kálovics (Hungary) Enikő Kálovics / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its ability to transform a familiar landscape into something dreamlike and unexpected. The combination of the tiny lacewings, the autumn forest, and the purplish night sky creates a delicate, atmospheric interpretation of the nature of ‘De Lage Landen.’ The thoughtful use of double exposure adds another layer to the image, capturing not just the insects themselves, but also the sense of wonder and atmosphere of their natural habitat.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Fred Hazelhoff Award, Portfolio: “Eagle Owls in the City” by Simone Baumeister (Germany) Simone Baumeister / NPOTY 2026 “In the portfolio category, the bar is set considerably higher for participating photographers than in the individual categories. Whilst a single fantastic photograph is sufficient there, in the portfolio category you need a whole series of outstanding images that not only complement one another but also fit together well in terms of style and theme. Simone Baumeister has succeeded brilliantly in this with her portfolio on eagle owls in the city. It is clear that she has put a great deal of time into creating the series: She has managed to capture all sorts of special moments with her camera, and the series showcases a wide range of situations, locations, and atmospheres. In doing so, she offers a unique glimpse into the world of a bird that is making a comeback in Germany and which, despite its size, often goes unnoticed by the people around it. Or, as the photographer herself puts it, her images make the invisible visible. And that is one of the great strengths of (nature) photography!” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Youth Photographer of the Year: “Tree of Life” by Parham Pourahmad (U.S.) Parham Pourahmad / NPOTY 2026 “In ‘Tree of Life,’ Pourahmad captured a striking scene that could comfortably hold its own in the adult categories. Black and white was an excellent choice, defining the coyote’s silhouette and revealing the majestic oak’s intricate network of branches. Even within this wider scene, the coyote’s downward gaze is clear. Pourahmad explained that it was searching for rodent prey, a small detail that brings the photograph to life. The image combines a beautiful portrait of the animal’s habitat with an intimate glimpse of its hunting behavior.” – Jury member Louis Guillot
