items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΟΠΤΙΜΙΣΤΩΝ Οι άστεγοι στις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες μειώθηκαν κατά περισσότερο από έξι τοις εκατό το 2025, η πιο απότομη μείωση των αστέγων σε διάστημα ενός έτους σε περισσότερο από μια δεκαετία, η οποία οδηγεί σε περίπου 49.000 λιγότερους ανθρώπους χωρίς στέγη. Ήταν η δεύτερη συνεχόμενη ετήσια πτώση μετά από μια μικρότερη πτώση το 2024 και σπάει μια σειρά αυξήσεων που είχε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Homelessness in the United States fell by more than six percent in 2025, the steepest one-year homelessness decline in more than a decade, which works out to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It was the second straight annual drop after a smaller dip in 2024, and it breaks a run of increases that had pushed the homeless population to record levels. The numbers come from the annual count conducted in communities nationwide. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) announced the results ahead of its detailed report, and a separate analysis of the same count , commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline. However, the two part ways on the question of why. Where the homelessness decline showed up Veterans and the long view The clearest long-term gains are among veterans. Homelessness among U.S. veterans dropped more than seven percent last year and is down nearly 60 percent since 2010. Ann Oliva, CEO of the alliance, ties that record to programs that move people off the street and into housing without preconditions. “Investments in programs like that are much closer to the scale of need for veterans than for any other population experiencing homelessness,” she said. Four big cities and two disaster zones A large share of the drop is concentrated in a handful of places. New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw large numbers of asylum seekers arrive at their shelters during the Biden administration, and according to Devon Kurtz, public safety policy director at the Cicero Institute, a think tank aligned with the administration on homelessness policy, those cities now account for about half of the most recent decline. “That’s also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently,” he said. Kurtz also pointed to San Francisco, which is moving toward more sober-living housing that prohibits drugs and alcohol. Numbers also fell in western North Carolina and Hawaii, both hit by major weather disasters. When HUD and other agencies arrive to help displaced residents, people who were already unhoused often receive assistance they had not been getting before. Rents easing in some markets Oliva described the decline as broad and likely the result of several forces at once, including softer rental markets in parts of the country. Rents remain high, but they have come down from their pandemic peaks, which could slow the number of people losing housing for the first time. Competing explanations for falling homelessness The administration credits enforcement and recovery HUD Secretary Scott Turner attributed the decline to the administration’s broader agenda. HUD also cited stepped-up enforcement against encampments following the 2024 Supreme Court ruling that allowed cities to ban sleeping and camping in public places. The administration argues that the long-standing federal approach of placing people in permanent housing first and offering voluntary treatment afterward has failed, and it blames that approach for the rise in homelessness during the pandemic. Requiring residents to stay drug-free, it says, helps more people reach recovery. HUD wants to redirect several billion dollars in homelessness funding toward short-term housing paired with mandatory addiction and mental health treatment, a plan courts have blocked so far. Advocates credit housing programs The alliance reads the same data differently. “It’s good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working,” Oliva said. She argued that housing-first programs were a major driver of the decline, particularly for veterans , and said the analysis her group commissioned found that cities with camping bans performed worse than the national average. Critics of drug-free housing requirements add that relapse is common, and that such rules can push people back onto the street when it happens. The work still ahead Chronic homelessness moved the other way Both analyses agree that nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. are still living in shelters or on the streets, well above pre-pandemic levels. One group also bucked the trend: people who have been homeless for a long time saw a small increase last year, even as most other groups declined. Oliva said this population, which is more likely to live with mental illness and addiction , needs more permanent housing, while the administration is pushing for treatment-linked short-term options. With HUD’s funding overhaul still tied up in court, the next annual count will show whether the homelessness decline holds, and how far either approach can reach the people who have been without a home the longest. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Η April Surac κατασκεύασε το NeuraSensa ώστε η τέχνη να προσαρμόζεται στους ανθρώπους που το χρησιμοποιούν
items.titleOriginal: April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Αυτό το άρθρο είναι μέρος της σειράς Local Changemakers 2026 του The Optimist Daily, δίνοντας έμφαση στους δημιουργούς αλλαγής 30 ετών και κάτω. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most public spaces are built for an average visitor who doesn’t exist. The lighting, the noise, the textures underfoot, and the pace of a room all assume a certain kind of body and brain, and anyone who takes in the world differently is left to manage on their own. April Surac, a Florida teenager and the founder of NeuraSensa , has spent the past two years making the opposite: art that changes in response to whoever is standing in front of it. How NeuraSensa began in a furniture workshop Textures, materials and a younger sister April grew up in her family’s furniture workshop, where she learned early that materials follow their own logic and that a texture one person finds soothing can be unbearable to someone else. She also grew up with a younger sister who has autism , and that taught her something before she had words for it: the designed world fits some nervous systems far better than others. Paul Moore, who nominated April for this series and has followed the project since the beginning, sees both influences running through everything she makes. “April is one of those students whose work has grown directly out of something deeply personal to her,” he said. April founded NeuraSensa in June 2024, and she has summed up its guiding idea in a single sentence: “I believe design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” NeuraSensa’s responsive textile installations Art that reacts to touch, motion, light and sound The installations layer fabric with embedded sensors, so surfaces shift under a visitor’s hand and the light and sound in the room change as people move through it. For someone whose senses register the world at a different intensity, a space that responds instead of making fixed demands can decide whether they stay or leave. NeuraSensa designs this work for autistic people and others with sensory or cognitive differences, including people living with dementia. The installations have reached more than 15,000 people through gallery exhibitions and community events, with shows at SOBO Windermere Art Gallery and CityArts Orlando. NeuraSensa has also run workshops with organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy of Central Florida and the Brevard Achievement Center , where participants work hands-on with April’s sensory-friendly pieces. Sensory kits for homes, classrooms and hospitals Outside the gallery, NeuraSensa’s Sponsor-a-Kit program has distributed more than 250 therapeutic kits to families, educators, hospitals and disability-serving organizations, putting sensory support tools into places that rarely have them. April also organized a community drive that delivered more than $3,000 worth of tactile toys to Nemours Children’s Hospital in Orlando. Much of this runs on her own resources. She funds NeuraSensa through personal savings, grants, and fundraising, and Moore has watched how much that asks of her. “I have seen firsthand how much of her own time, savings, grant funding and effort she puts into making each project possible,” he said. A young changemaker’s growing recognition The Barron Prize and a TEDx stage In 2025, April was one of 15 top winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes , each of whom receives $10,000 toward their work or education. That same year, she was named a Daily Point of Light honoree by the Points of Light organization, and she has since been nominated for the KidsRights international award and published research through Figshare. According to Moore, she gave a TED-Ed Talk in October titled “ What’s Next: Designing Technology for Every Nervous System ,” which he said she developed with mentorship from a Nobel laureate in neuroscience. “I’ve loved seeing her share each stage of that journey with me, and watching an idea close to her heart grow into work that has now supported thousands of people in our community,” Moore wrote. Sensory-inclusive design beyond compliance From retrofits to spaces built for everyone For a long time, making public space accessible meant meeting minimum requirements after a building or exhibit was already finished. The conversation around neurodivergence in art and public life has moved toward design justice, the principle that spaces should be planned from the start for the full range of human experience instead of patched later for people who fall outside a narrow norm. NeuraSensa sits where art practice and disability advocacy overlap, and April has not waited for museums or city planners to adopt that principle before acting on it. The next phase reaches well past Central Florida. April is developing commissions for galleries in New York City, Los Angeles and London, along with textile-based systems for large installations and wearable sensory tools, designs she is moving toward patent protection. Moore says he is “incredibly proud of how she keeps learning, expanding the project and finding new ways to use her talents in service of others,” and the scale of what she’s attempting suggests the lesson from her family’s workshop has traveled a long way: a room can be built to meet the person who walks into it, wherever that room turns out to be. You can follow her work on NeuraSensa’s Instagram . Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Feel-Good τηλεοπτικά αγαπημένα: 30 σειρές ροής που θα φωτίσουν την ημέρα σας
items.titleOriginal: Feel-Good TV Favorites: 30 Streaming Shows That’ll Brighten Your Day
items.description: Ποια είναι η συνταγή για μια καλή τηλεοπτική εκπομπή; Για κάποιους, είναι ένας συνδυασμός ρομαντισμού και χιούμορ. Για άλλους, είναι μια νοσταλγική ιστορία με συγγενείς χαρακτήρες. Και μερικές φορές συμβαίνει ακριβώς το αντίθετο: ριάλιτι απόδρασης που σε μεταφέρει κάπου μακριά. Ευτυχώς, οι ενθουσιώδεις ιστορίες όλων των ειδών είναι διαθέσιμες για ροή όλες τις ώρες της ημέρας (και της νύχτας).…
items.descriptionOriginal: What’s the recipe for a feel-good TV show? For some, it’s a mix of romance and humor. For others, it’s a nostalgic storyline with relatable characters. And sometimes it’s just the opposite: escapism reality TV that transports you somewhere far away. Luckily, uplifting stories of all kinds are available to stream at all hours of the day (and night). From comedies and coming-of-age-stories to heartwarming reality series, these shows can help you feel a little better about the world. So, make yourself a cup of tea and cozy up on the couch — a heartwarming streaming session awaits! A Man on the Inside | Netflix This is perhaps the most wholesome whodunit you’ll ever watch. In Season One, retired professor Charles (Ted Danson) goes undercover at a retirement community to investigate the theft of a family heirloom. The next season, he takes on a new case at a college campus where he meets Mona, played by Danson’s real-life wife of over 30 years, Mary Steenburgen. We’re excited to see what’s in store for Season Three, which, alas, will be this endearing tale’s final chapter . Abbott Elementary | Hulu This hilarious mockumentary series follows teachers (and an outrageous principal) at a Philadelphia public school who go above and beyond to help their students succeed, despite the hurdles the faculty encounters both in and out of the classroom. Fun fact: Abbott Elementary is named after Joyce Abbott , a real sixth-grade teacher who taught creator and star Quinta Brunson at Andrew Hamilton School in Philadelphia. All Creatures Great and Small | PBS and Prime Video All Creatures Great and Small is based on author and veterinarian James Herriot’s beloved memoirs about his years treating animals in rural Yorkshire beginning in the 1930s. The British series is so peaceful that all six seasons feel like taking a breath of fresh air (the seventh premieres in the U.S. in January 2027). Black-ish | Hulu This Emmy-winning comedy is heartwarming, family-centered, and will keep you laughing. Follow the beloved Johnsons for eight seasons as they navigate highs, lows, and life changes together. Choir | Disney+ Meet the inspiring kids who make up the Detroit Youth Choir (of America’s Got Talent fame ) in this moving Disney+ docuseries. Over six episodes, you’ll find yourself cheering on all of the talented singers as they pursue their dreams and prepare for “the performance of a lifetime”: taking the stage at Carnegie Hall in New York City. Derry Girls | Netflix Witty and wonderful, Derry Girls is a British teen sitcom that follows a tight-knit group of friends during “ The Troubles ” in Ireland. It’s a beautiful example of the power of embracing humor amid hardships, without glossing over truths. English Teacher | Hulu English Teacher is another warmhearted, witty comedy set in the classroom, and often the faculty lounge and principal’s office as well. You’ll follow a group of offbeat high school teachers in Austin, Texas, as they navigate everything from a chaotic camping trip to AI-powered trash cans. The show boasts a rating of 94% on Rotten Tomatoes, and our only complaint is that the episodes, which run just over 20 minutes, aren’t longer — because the characters are endlessly fun to be around. Extraordinary Attorney Woo | Netflix South Korean series Extraordinary Attorney Woo follows a young lawyer who is on the autism spectrum as she navigates everyday interactions in her unique and authentic way. The show, which is dubbed in English, has a 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes and was the most-viewed title on Netflix for a week . Gilmore Girls | Hulu For a dose of mother-daughter love, Gilmore Girls offers seven seasons (and a four-part reunion series) of feel-good content. The young mom and her teenage daughter — played by Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel, respectively — talk fast, drink a lot of coffee, and lean on each other through family drama, job changes, and romantic ups and downs. Hart of Dixie | HBO Max If you’re a fan of Gilmore Girls , this wholesome show will be right up your alley. Rachel Bilson stars as Zoe Hart, a doctor from New York City who inherits half of a family practice in the small, fictional town of Bluebell, Alabama: a perfectly cozy community where neighbors support each other, get tangled up in romance, and attend many a quirky festival. Home for Christmas | Netflix The first season of this Norwegian show follows Johanne, a 30-year-old single nurse, as she gives herself 24 days to find a boyfriend to bring home for Christmas. Three seasons later, the show (always set during the holidays) remains full of tender moments about navigating romance, independence, and family expectations. Is It Cake? | Netflix The premise is super simple and super silly: Contestants bake elaborate cakes that look like everyday items, including purses, paintings, and rubber ducks. The desserts are then placed next to the real objects they resemble, and guest judges have to guess which one is the cake. It’s fun to play along, though it’s delightfully tricky! Love on the Spectrum U.S. | Netflix There are plenty of reality shows about finding love, but Love on the Spectrum stands out — not only because its stars are neurodivergent but also because it possesses a warmth and hopefulness that make you truly root for the cast as they seek meaningful relationships. The U.S. version is a spinoff of the Australian series , and both are available to stream on Netflix. North of North | Netflix If you need a reminder that good things can come during uncertain times, this show fits the bill. Set in the tiny, fictional Arctic community of Ice Cove, North of North follows a young Inuk mother as she embarks on a new chapter after leaving her marriage. Viewers follow along with her highs and lows as she tries to get a handle on dating and building a career, while breaking down traditional gender expectations. Psych | Prime Video and Peacock Watch a quick-witted and perceptive police consultant (played by James Roday Rodriguez) solve cases using the power of observation — and the help of his reluctant BFF (played by Dulé Hill). The eight-season show combines comedy, drama, and detective work, all the while highlighting the infectious friendship between the two main characters. Tip: Keep an eye out for pineapples ! Queer Eye | Netflix The “Fab Five” gives emotional makeovers to ordinary folks across the country. But they don’t focus on appearance alone: The team explores the powerful connection between how we look, how we treat ourselves, and how we interact with the world — a reminder we can all use. Schitt’s Creek | Hulu Riches-to-rags is the premise of Schitt’s Creek : a series about a wealthy family who loses all their money and moves into a motel in a (very) small town. Laugh-out-loud moments, endearing friendships, and perfectly quotable one-liners earned this rewatchable, lighthearted show an Emmy for outstanding comedy in 2020. Shrinking | Apple TV On paper, Shrinking doesn’t sound particularly feel-good — it follows a father (played by Jason Segel) navigating parenthood and his career as a therapist following his wife’s sudden death. However, the show portrays grief through a lens that’s undeniably uplifting. It’s impossible not to fall in love with the nosy neighbors and hilarious coworkers, especially Paul, the lovably gruff mentor played by Harrison Ford (who earned his first Emmy nomination for the role at age 83). Sister, Sister | Paramount Plus A ’90s classic, Sister, Sister — starring twins Tia and Tamera Mowry — is still a joy to watch decades after it originally aired. Equally heart-filling and funny, the six-season series captures the magic of sisterhood and the positive impact of supportive family units. Somebody Feed Phil | Netflix There are many foodie travel shows out there, but this one has Phil Rosenthal. The creator of Everybody Loves Raymond supplies just the right amount of wholesome dad jokes as he tries local cuisine in Kyoto, Copenhagen, and Cape Town, among dozens of other cities around the world. All eight seasons are packed with enticing eats and conversations, but we’re partial to the first two, which include scenes of Rosenthal video chatting with his mom and dad before they passed away in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Somebody Somewhere | Prime Video Described as “a totally platonic love story” by HBO, Somebody Somewhere is about two coworkers (played by Bridget Everett and Jeff Hiller) who become dear friends. Audiences watch as they develop the sweetest bond that’s filled with lots of laughs and good vibes. “I hope that people come away with ‘never give up on yourself,’ because a lot of people do,” said Everett. St. Denis Medical | Peacock and Netflix Think of this as a hospital-centered version of The Office (another comfort TV favorite). This sitcom chronicles the day-to-day lives of nurses and surgeons as they navigate wacky medical scenarios and even wackier workplace dynamics. But we’d be remiss not to mention that there’s plenty of heart among the staff, who lean on each other as they care for patients. Stick | Apple TV A love letter to golf, Stick follows a former pro golfer seeking redemption by mentoring a teen prodigy who has his own complicated relationship with the game. The soun d track is stacked with hits, and you’ll never listen to “Cecilia” by Simon & Garfunkel the same way again. Survivor | Netflix (Select Seasons) and Paramount Plus (All Seasons) A show that just keeps on giving, Survivor has delivered over 50 seasons of real-life drama about “castaways” competing for a prize of $1 million. While the concept has remained mostly the same for more than two decades, every season delivers new personalities and social dynamics. Ted Lasso | Apple TV The epitome of comfort TV, Ted Lasso centers on an American football coach (Jason Sudeikis) who is hired to manage a British soccer team. Even if you’re not a sports fan, this four-season series is so charming and rich with wholesome humor that makes it a feel-good favorite for everyone. Tex Mex Motors | Netflix Watch old junkyard cars from Mexico get radically restored in Texas, thanks to a talented team of experts on Tex Mex Motors . While the car transformations are fun to watch (and very impressive), the restoration pros are the real stars of the show. The Dog House | HBO Max and Hulu ​If you haven’t watched The Dog House yet, you’re in for a treat. The unscripted show follows staff at a British animal rescue charity as they match pups with new pet parents. It’s a joy watching people light up when they fall in love with their new best friend — and of course, seeing the pups fall in love with their new best friends, too. The Durrells in Corfu | PBS and Prime Video The Durrells in Corfu is a British series based on memoirs about a family who left England for Greece in the 1930s. Not only is the story full of wit and heart, but it’s also set in the dreamiest of settings. And after you watch the show’s four seasons, we recommend checking out this documentary about the real Durrells . The Great British Baking Show | Netflix Of all the comfort shows streaming lately, The Great British Baking Show (titled The Great British Bake Off in the U.K.) takes the cake — pun intended. Each week, contestants bake all kinds of mouthwatering treats in hopes of making it to the finale, where one talented baker earns the coveted cake stand and is crowned winner. But unlike so many other competition shows that can feel cutthroat, the judges offer kind, constructive feedback, and the contestants often help one another finish their creations. You can stream most seasons on Netflix, including the most recent with new judge Nigella Lawson, a star addition as far as the Nice News team is concerned. Younger | Netflix In Younger , Liza, a 40-year-old mom (played by Sutton Foster), pretends to be in her 20s to land an entry-level assistant job at a publishing house in New York alongside Kelsey (played by Hilary Duff). A love triangle, book deals, and many stories of female friendship ensue over seven seasons of lighthearted TV. Highly recommend for fans of Lizzie McGuire . A version of this article was originally published in July 2023.

items.descriptionOriginal: W hat might it be like to be a bird? Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles. “Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough grassland in which to hunt voles and mice, and space undisturbed by people and dogs. Suddenly the landscape around Lawy looked more like a series of obstacles and threats a wild animal needed to conquer: “Once I really began to delve into what it might be like to be a kestrel, I realized actually my options were very limited because it’s so difficult to find areas where I can find food.” Clatworthy dam impounds the headwaters of the River Tone. © River Tone Lawy’s experience is part of a pioneering experiment by Accelerator for Systemic Risk Assessment (ASRA), an independent nonprofit initiative hosted by the United Nations Foundation in collaboration with the University of the West of England (UWE) and funded by the Ecological Citizen(s) Network . The project, Risks Beyond Human Eyes, asks people around the River Tone catchment to explore risks not from the conventional perspective of human visitors, landowners, planners or conservationists, but through the sensory worlds and needs of other species: fierce otter, threatened salmon, quiet red deer, sharp-sighted kestrel or blind earthworm. Over a period of several months, 18 participants swam like salmon, surfed the river to mimic how an otter might glide through the water, or hid in hollows like earthworms. The setup sounds fanciful until its practical implications emerge: If conventional risk assessments systematically overlook what matters to other species, could temporarily shifting the human viewpoint reveal problems — and solutions — that would otherwise remain invisible? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] For Lawy, it has already changed how she manages land. She came to the project as a local resident, concerned about the water quality of the River Tone. People want to bathe in it, yet the water is too polluted with runoff from the nearby fields, herbicides, pesticides and other toxins. “But animals haven’t got that choice,” she says. “They are constantly living in this very poor-quality water.” These insights are part of the logic of the ASRA project, challenging the human-centeredness of conventional risk assessment. “Of course we’re not pretending that a person literally becomes an otter or kestrel,” project co-director Phil Tovey explains, “but this kind of disciplined attention exposes aspects of an animal’s environment that humans routinely fail to notice.” The resulting testimonies are not intended simply to produce moving stories about wildlife, but are treated as input to a wider systemic-risk assessment, alongside scientific and other evidence such as water quality. Participants in the project working on a course of action. Credit: Darren Honeywell According to the 2026 Living Planet Index , freshwater species populations declined by 85 percent between 1970 and 2022 , the steepest decline of any of the major ecosystems assessed. It’s one thing to read this number as an intellectual piece of information and another to attempt the perspective of a salmon, like some of the study participants, and arrive at the life-threatening realization that they couldn’t overcome a river barrier to get to their food source. Lawy experienced firsthand that a landscape designed to look accessible and attractive to humans appears radically different to a species trying to feed and reproduce. While repeatedly sitting outside over several weeks, Lawy never actually saw a kestrel. There were too many people, too many dogs, too much disturbance. “Kestrels actually need some space from us,” she realized. Lawy also saw the hay meadows in a different light. Once the hay is cut, Lawy suddenly noticed, the landscape can become a stark, hostile expanse. “There is no cover,” she says. During a hot, dry summer, that lack of shelter can mean the difference between life and death. At the next meeting of Friends of Longrun Meadow, Lawy proposed a “mosaic of habitats,” retaining more long grass and larger riparian margins alongside the river instead of the more manicured grounds. The River Tone under the M5. © River Tone Lawy says she now asks people to adopt a new perspective. “I want you to think more from an animal perspective,” she tells them. “Rather than us thinking we need to trim that hedge, are we leaving places for birds and insects and all these other species who live here? Are we providing feeding corridors for bats?” Much to her surprise, the group “straightforwardly accepted these insights,” Lawy reports. The larger ambition of ASRA’s experiment is to translate these observations into protective action. Phil Tovey, who co-leads the project with Miguel Prado Casanova of UWE, describes the River Tone as a system in which risks compound. For instance, research has found that kestrels living within 30 meters of a major road show elevated cortisol from stress, and they shift from reproduction towards survival. “So when we then look at overall coverage of roads in the region, you can just see the scale of harm, disruption, physical and mental injury that is really widespread,” Tovey concludes. “One of the things that we do in ASRA for a systemic risk response is we look at the underlying structures, the historical conditions and what are the barriers to transformation.” A former Royal Marines Commando, Tovey served on operations across the world, from peacekeeping in Northern Ireland to working with indigenous forces in Afghanistan and deployments across Africa and the Middle East. Before joining ASRA, he worked as the Head of Futures in the U.K.’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Rain patters downstream of French Weir. © River Tone He likens the emotional testimonies of the study participants to the shocked reports of civilians caught in war zones. He also conducted roughly two dozen of his own field experiments, switching between species and testing the instructions given to participants. “I’d be going out at four in the morning, roughly knowing where the red deer hang out.” For Tovey, connecting the participants’ testimonies to scientific evidence and a structured framework for mapping risk means “setting the conditions for deeper structural change.” For example, the river and its tributaries contain more than 337 weirs and other obstacles over about 33 kilometers, creating problems for migrating salmon and other creatures. “No one has really considered the density and volume of these pressures on the animals,” Tovey says. “But when I sit as an otter, I see these barriers because as an otter I’m only about six centimeters off the ground.” Conventional assessments tend to divide problems into categories: transport, agriculture, water quality, habitat, biodiversity. Tovey’s digital mapping of the River Tone risks is effectively “bright orange” as different risks overlap. The problem is not merely the number of individual hazards, but their density and interaction. Changing the perspective does not mean abandoning scientific evidence, but it can show which actions will have the most impact. “As a research team, asking a bunch of humans to try and inevitably fail to engage in living as a chosen animal, the absurdity of trying to actually do that was taken really seriously,” says Tovey, addressing the obvious criticism of anthropomorphism. “We never once claimed that Helen was a kestrel, but using the structured process we set out, we need to make an imaginary leap to calibrate what that environment would be like for the animal. Then we start to see barriers in a different way.” The research team briefing the Systemic Risk Assessment. Credit: Darren Honeywell For Lawy, the exercise in changing perspective led to changes in land management, and then to a recognition that she wants to press for changes beyond her local group. “It’s amazing how quickly that local action on a relatively small area can lead you to realize that actually we need some policy changes within the landscape to really make that difference,” she says. The project inspired an even more ambitious question: What does the river need? One of the study participants works in the city council. According to Tovey, “she became instrumental in stitching together the work and applying it to River Tone as a subjective person.” A working group quickly formed, resulting in the adaptation of Somerset’s very first River Rights Charter, which recognizes the river’s rights to regenerate, flow and be protected from harm. Lawy’s stint as a kestrel is part of a growing global movement to shift from an anthropocentric view, inspired by programs such as NYU Law School’s More than Human Life as well as bestselling authors like Charles Foster , whose book Being A Beast portrayed him living as badger, deer, fox and swift. It also marks a return to Indigenous values. In 2008, Indigenous peoples led Ecuador to become the world’s first country to formally recognize the “Rights of Mother Earth,” a ruling that the Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature (GARN) and others subsequently used successfully against a road construction company that dumped rubble into the Vilcabamba River. As a result, the government was forced to clean up the river. Tovey agrees that rivers and other elements of nature should have the right to be represented. “I have never met my MP,” he says. “Yet we accept political representation for humans. What’s problematic is making sure it’s done with integrity.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The approach remains experimental. There are obvious limits to humans attempting to understand other species, and the researchers themselves acknowledge the need for more time. But Tovey hopes to expand ASRA’s work to larger areas. “We have started to forge connections with our sister rivers, reaching out to those groups and thinking about a wider solidarity movement,” Tovey says, intending to integrate the lessons from the River Tone project. Lawy’s experience suggests another potential benefit: changing what people care about. “One of the really important things that’s come out of this for me,” she says, “is the emotional connection that you get back with nature.” That emotional connection is not taken as a substitute for evidence. Rather, it can make evidence harder to ignore. The post The People Who Became Wildlife appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Suzanne Peck , a lecturer of art at the Rochester Institute of Technology, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Glass as a material is full of contradictions. Depending on the form and use, glass can be fragile or strong, opaque or transparent, rough or smooth. The studios my colleagues and I teach and learn in, as glass instructors, echo this abundance of physical opposites. These environments are simultaneously immersive, complex, seductive, and demanding. When the studio is in action, you might hear glass breaking, hot metal being quenched in water, glassblowing pipes rolling on the workbench rails, and some good tunes on the stereo. You might smell hot beeswax and burning newspaper. You might feel a bit of waste glass under your shoe or the intense heat from the furnaces and a breeze from a well-placed fan. Glassblowers learn to listen, to feel, and to find some focus within and among the kinetic. The constant stimuli of the glass studio may not seem anything like a sterile science lab, and yet glass artists need to accrue knowledge of physics and chemistry to achieve any kind of control with this dynamic material. They must choose a material with the desired properties and during the process judge factors such as heat and malleability. Glass as a Material At Rochester Institute of Technology, where I help run the glass program, we primarily use two types of glasses. In our hot glass studio we melt “soft” glass . This glass is specifically formulated to be melted in a furnace and used by the glassblower. It’s a combination of fine mesh silica sand, soda ash, and lime, with small amounts of a few additional ingredients that keep the glass beautiful when it’s at its top temperature of 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit (1,204 degrees Celsius). In our flameworking studio, we use a borosilicate glass . You might recognize this glass as the brand Pyrex made in Corning, New York. This is a super heat-resistant glass. It melts at a higher temperature than soft glass and arrives to our students in preformed rods that they can melt and shape by torch in our flameworking studio. The differences in chemistry really change how these glasses look and behave. Picofluidicist/Wikimedia Commons Pyrex cookware is made out of a specially formulated, heat-resistant type of glass called borosilicate. Glass, from a material science perspective, is categorized as an amorphous solid , meaning that glass’s molecules are arranged in a near-random pattern and there is no sharp melting point . Rather, glass gradually softens over a wide temperature range. Gathering Glass Once you’ve adjusted to the chaos of the studio, it’s time to start working. We have two furnaces in our hot glass studio, where we work with soft glass, so anytime during the school year there is between 700 to 1,200 pounds of glass. It’s kept in the furnace at its molten state (2,200 degrees F or 1,204 degrees C), ready to be gathered and transformed. AP Photo/Keith Srakocic Glass artists heat up their glass in a furnace so that it’s molten and easy to mold. When we work with the material, transforming it with tools and breath and heat, it needs to be kept in a workable heat zone — probably between 1,100 and 2,000 F (593 and 1,094 C). When the glass dips below that range, we perceive it as solid, though at the molecular level it is still dynamic and acting more like a liquid. To make anything — a sculpture, a tumbler, a celestial magical orb, or a pumpkin — you start by gathering glass out of the furnace on a metal rod. Once you’ve gathered your glass, you start making decisions. Elizabeth Lamark/RIT An artist works in the Glass Hot Shop at RIT. When glass is in its molten state, the artist can shape it and blow into it. You might ask yourself: What tools do I need to begin to shape and transform this glass into the object I have in mind? If you wait too long and the glass begins cooling down, you’ll need to reheat it to reintroduce malleability , allowing you to continue working it without breaking it. A big part of glasswork is moving between the reheating chamber and the bench, where the artist uses tools to move and stretch the molten glass into the desired shape. You’ll need to alternate between these two stations many times. Glassblowing is a team activity. I have physical and intellectual support from my colleagues: breath from their lungs, protection from the heat, additional bits of glass brought from the furnace to add to my object. We almost never work alone. So, say I want to make a very basic clear tumbler. This is a simple conceptual object — utilitarian, domestic, and intimate. It is also a tricky one to make well: too heavy and it feels bad in the hand, too thick at the lip and it dribbles when you drink, too thin at the bottom and it will break before it is complete. Maybe I want to design it so it is slightly conical: wider at the bottom than the top, so it’s less likely to tip over. Maybe I want it to have a little indent for the user’s thumb as a gentle invitation to her hand. First I make my design: I draw it. I share it with my team so they can predict the process and the object’s needs. Then we begin. Working With Physics I gather glass out of the furnace, let it cool a bit, then introduce a bubble in the glass by blowing into the pipe, the hollow rod that attaches to the object I’m making. I reheat, sit at the bench, and begin to shape the glass using both gravity and the Jills, a cooling and shaping tool. The Jills is kind of like a large pair of tongs. It hasn’t changed much in design for 2,000 years. AP Photo/Gerry Broome Glass artists use a variety of tools to shape their work. I ask for some air from my teammate, and she blows into the pipe while I’m shaping the glass. The bubble transforms into a pill shape, slightly wider at the bottom. I constrict the area right in front of the pipe. I’m focusing on shape and heat, taking care to not let the glass get too cold. If the glass drops to about 1,000 F (538 C), it enters a danger zone. If it’s not yet finished, it needs to be warmed up in the reheating chamber; or if it is done, put away in a kiln to cool slowly. If glass cools too quickly, the molecules freeze into a chaotic pattern, which causes stresses that result in fracture. To combat this volatility, when the glass object is done and ready to be cooled, we place the object in an annealer : a kiln set to a resting temperature of 930 F (500 C). This temperature is like a Goldilocks zone for our glass: It’s not so hot that the glass will deform, but not so cool that the glass will stress and break. Once the kilns are full, a computer guide takes them down to room temperature over about 10 hours. As I continue to work on my cup, I get more heat, focusing on the very end of the bubble — the part that will be the base of the cup. I then sit down and have another member of my team flatten the bottom with a wooden paddle while I tool the glass with the Jills to keep its shape. The cycle continues on and on. The process is quick, but also there are so many little steps that it would take nearly a full-length book to describe them all. When asked how long it takes to make a tumbler, I’ll often answer, “About 10 years or 10 minutes, depending on how you think about time and material knowledge.” This is both glib and true. Glass demands attention, dedication, and a willingness to make connections between physics and chemistry and your observable experiences. It is a highly challenging and equally rewarding material to work with and alongside. I count myself very lucky. Κανένας κολυμβητής δεν το άφησε εκεί. Όπως τα περισσότερα από αυτά που συλλέγονται στις πιο δυσπρόσιτες ακτές της Ελλάδας, οδήγησε i…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM At some point in the past three decades, a beer can printed with a Spanish-language ad for a 1990s World Cup washed up on Patroklos, a small islet in the Saronic Gulf about 65 nautical miles (75 miles) from Athens. No swimmer left it there. Like most of what collects on Greece’s harder-to-reach shores, it rode in on the currents, and it stayed until a crew working on a Greek coastline cleanup picked it up, sorted it, and wrote it down. That last step, the writing down, is what makes this project more interesting than a beach sweep. Every bottle, net, and wrapper the crew logs becomes a clue about where the Mediterranean’s waste starts its trip. A Greek coastline cleanup run from the sea The Typhoon and its 20-person crew Greece has the longest coastline of any Mediterranean country, and much of it has no road leading to it. Since July 2019, the Typhoon Project has reached those stretches by water, using a 72-meter (236-foot) ship as its base. Each day, a crew of 20 heads ashore in five inflatable boats and gathers, sorts, and records between 500 and 1,000 kilograms (roughly 1,100 to 2,200 pounds) of waste, which then goes to the appropriate facilities for recycling. The project belongs to the Public Benefit Foundation Athanassios C. Laskaridis , a Greek foundation whose work centers on protecting the environment and the sea in particular. By February 2023, the crew had completed its first full circuit of the islands and most of the mainland coast. Seven years, 1,140 tonnes Across more than 10,000 cleanup operations, the Typhoon has removed 1,140 tonnes (about 1,257 US tons) of trash. Peggy Xirotagarou, the foundation’s executive director, has learned that the number means more to people as an image than as a weight. “To help people picture it in their minds, we are talking about 22 Olympic-size swimming pools or around 1160 large containers,” she said. Marine litter as a research record Counting every item on every beach The cleanup is half the job. The other half happens after the bags are on board, when the crew records what was found, item by item and beach by beach. Thanasis Besios, who manages the Typhoon Project, considers that record as valuable as the cleared sand. “One part of the project is collecting the waste, but the second is collecting the data. We carry out detailed recording of all the waste. We know exactly what quantity there is, how many kilos, how many items from each beach. At the moment we have the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean, and we are developing it every day,” he told Euronews. Researchers are putting that record to use. The project works with the Laboratory of Marine Geology and Physical Oceanography at the University of Patras to study waste on the seabed of the Saronic and Thermaic Gulfs, and with the Marine Remote Sensing Research Group at the University of the Aegean, which uses remote sensing technology to locate and map plastics. Tracing coastal pollution back inland The Cyclone program Seven years of sorting led the foundation to an uncomfortable conclusion about its own beaches. Plenty of what lands on the coast was never thrown into the sea in the first place, and illegal, unmanaged landfills are still running in many parts of Greece. “By observing the waste we were finding on the shores, we realised that a large proportion came from inland,” Xirotagarou said. The foundation’s response, launched in 2024, is a land-based counterpart called Cyclone . “It involves large-scale clean-ups in lakes, rivers and archaeological sites. We have created three large teams in different parts of Greece, where every day we collect more than 1,000 kilos of waste,” she said. Schools on every stop Wherever the Typhoon drops anchor, the team also visits local schools, then brings students out to the shoreline. Xirotagarou sees the classroom work as the long game behind the whole operation. “Because that is the ultimate goal. For them to become responsible citizens and for this reckless use of single-use plastics to stop,” she said. A project that began by picking up after the sea has ended up asking where the trash started. A crew can clear an islet in an afternoon, but slowing what reaches it depends on the steadier work the foundation has added since 2024, from the river and lake crews to the classroom visits. The Greek coastline cleanup will keep finding cans like the one on Patroklos, though its logbook now gives Greece a much clearer sense of which ones drifted in from abroad and which started a few miles inland. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Very few Americans have ever eaten foie gras. It’s a niche luxury, served mostly in high-end restaurants, and yet on November 3 it produced some of the most lopsided results of the night in two American cities. In Washington, DC, 73 percent of voters backed a ban on selling the force-fed duck liver, and in Denver, 66 percent did. They weren’t alone. Across this year’s midterms , animal welfare ballot measures had a strong showing, and the pattern in what passed and what didn’t says something about how voters approach animals when the question in front of them is narrow and specific. Foie gras bans win by wide margins How foie gras is produced Foie gras comes from ducks that are force-fed through a metal pipe about 60 times in the final weeks before slaughter, until their livers swell to six to 10 times their natural size. Producers and many fine-dining chefs maintain that the practice is harmless, or at least no worse than other factory farming methods, while veterinary research has concluded it can be quite painful for the birds. DC and Denver join a growing list “Tonight DC decided that force-feeding a bird has no place here,” said Cady Witt of Pro-Animal DC, the group that put the measure on the ballot. The District’s ban on sales takes effect in July 2027 . California, New York City, Pittsburgh, and Portland, Oregon, already restrict foie gras sales, though the earlier city bans came from officials rather than voters, according to Ballotpedia . Outside the U.S., more than 20 European countries prohibit foie gras production; Brazil banned both its sale and production this year, and India has barred imports since 2014. Producers and chefs plan to fight back The votes may not be the last word. A representative from Hudson Valley Farms, the country’s largest foie gras producer, told Axios the company is considering legal challenges. In DC, Bart Hutchins, chef and owner of the restaurant Butterworth’s, wrote in a Washington Post op-ed that he was “incredibly disappointed” the measure reached the ballot, The Hill reported , and he has since hosted four-course foie gras dinners to raise money for a possible lawsuit. Colorado rejects a constitutional hunting amendment What Amendment 83 asked voters Colorado’s Amendment 83 would have written “the right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods” into the state constitution and named hunting and fishing as the preferred way to manage wildlife populations. About 55 percent of voters opposed it, according to unofficial results . Supporters argued that hunting and fishing rights shouldn’t depend on statutes or on whoever sits on the state wildlife commission, and 24 states already have some version of the protection in their constitutions. The amendment also exempted nongame and endangered species. Why “traditional methods” mattered Hunting and fishing are already protected by Colorado statute, so critics focused on the phrase “traditional methods.” “Read plainly, traditional methods could be interpreted to include practices like poisoning, leg hold traps, gill nets, or baiting and hounding,” Rebecca Niemiec, co-director of Colorado State University’s Animal-Human Policy Center and a Colorado Parks and Wildlife commissioner, told Vox in October. Colorado currently bans those practices. Vox reporter Neel Dhanesha described the stakes for animals that were never the intended target: “Steel-jawed traps and poisons don’t discriminate between, say, a deer, a wolf , and a lynx.” Opponents also worried that naming hunting the preferred management tool could sideline alternatives such as wildlife birth control and relocation. Where voters drew the line on animal welfare Conservation funding passes in several states Wildlife habitat did well this year too. Massachusetts voters approved a measure to fund nature conservation, and voters in Brevard County, Florida, renewed a tax that pays for manatee and dolphin habitat restoration. Conservation measures in Arkansas and Rhode Island also passed. Broader bans have a harder time Not every animal measure finds a majority. In 2024, Denver voters turned down a ban on fur sales, which drew 42.4 percent support, and a ban on slaughterhouses within city limits, which drew 36.3 percent, according to Ballotpedia. Set beside this year’s foie gras results, the two votes suggest that measures targeting one specific practice tend to fare better than ones that would reshape a whole industry. Farm animal laws and the candidates who opposed them Several candidate races also touched on animal welfare policy. In 2016, Massachusetts voters banned the sale of eggs and pork from hens and pregnant pigs kept in small cages, and California voters passed a nearly identical law two years later. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas and Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa, both Republicans, have sponsored bills to override those state laws, most recently the Save Our Bacon Act, and both lost their races this year. In Colorado’s Eighth Congressional District, Democrat Manny Rutinel, a state lawmaker and former Earthjustice attorney who sued meat companies over pollution, defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Gabe Evans. In Iowa, Chris Jones, a water quality expert who campaigned on cleaning up livestock and farm pollution, narrowly lost his bid for agriculture secretary. Neither major party has made animal welfare a central campaign issue, but the results will shape how these debates play out in Congress and statehouses over the next two years. For the campaigners in DC, the win came down to thousands of individual signatures and votes, a slow, ground-level way of changing what a city allows on its menus. Witt closed her statement on election night by thanking the people who did that work: “Thank you to everyone who signed the petition and voted to make DC a kinder place for animals.” Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: The bots roll along blood vessels to stir up stagnant blood and push drugs toward clots. Drugs that break up blood clots are vital for treating strokes, heart attacks, and clogged blood vessels in the lungs, but sometimes blockages are so large that medication struggles to get through. Now, researchers are building tiny magnetic robots to help medicines reach their targets. Severe blockages in blood vessels pose a tricky problem. The bloodstream is the only way to deliver clot-busting drugs, but if a clot stops the flow, there is no other way to carry them there. A team at ETH Zurich in Switzerland has a workaround. Magnetically driven microbots that roll along vessel walls can stir up stagnant blood so the drug gets pushed towards the clot. In lab tests, the approach dissolved clots six times faster than with the drug alone, and in experiments on pigs, it restored blood flow to an area twice as large after 30 minutes. “To our knowledge, we are the first to show in a clinically relevant large-animal model that the use of microrobots in this way does indeed enhance thrombolysis [the process of dissolving blood clots],” Schürle said in a press release . The bots are a far cry from your traditional robot. Just eight micrometers long, each is shaped like a grain of rice and made of a sugar-based polymer laced with magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles. During fabrication, the researchers expose the devices to a rotating magnetic field that pushes the nanoparticles into a straight line, essentially creating a bar magnet running the length of each bot. When a magnetic control system outside the body applies a rotating field, the internal magnet spins and causes each bot to tumble head over tail. The bots themselves don’t carry drugs. Rather, they’re released near a blockage along with clot-busting medicine. As the bots roll along the vessel walls towards the restriction, they create currents that carry the drug into the clot. To test the approach, the team built an artificial network of vessel-like channels and plugged it with clots made of pig blood. They compared what happened when they added the clot-dissolving drug alone to what happened when they added the drug and the bots together. Adding the bots cleared the clots six times faster than when they tried just the drug. To see if the strategy would work in real biological systems, the team blocked arteries in live pigs and treated them with just drugs and drugs plus microbots. After 30 minutes, the area with restored blood flow was twice as large in animals that received the bots. The work adds to a growing body of research into clot-busting magnetic microrobots. Last year, a separate ETH Zurich team led by Bradley Nelson published a paper in Science describing a dissolvable gel capsule that could be steered through blood vessels and release a clot-dissolving drug when heated by a high-frequency magnetic field. Others have taken a more mechanical approach. Researchers at the University of Twente and Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands used 3D-printed, screw-shaped robots containing tiny magnets to drill into clots, removing enough material from a blocked artery taken from a sheep to get blood flowing again. While the ETH team have filed a patent application for their bots, it’s still early. The paper describing the results has yet to clear peer review, and human trials are a long way off. Nonetheless, the results are another indication that microrobots could one day become a valuable new tool in a doctor’s arsenal. The post Tiny Magnetic Robots Help Dissolve Blood Clots Six Times Faster Than With Drugs Alone appeared first on SingularityHub .

Ο ιδιοκτήτης Σον Γουάιτ ολοκληρώνει την περικοπή για έναν μεσήλικα μαύρο ενώ ένας άλλος πελάτης περιμένει εκεί κοντά. items.descriptionOriginal: I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says. The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives. Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how comfortable they were discussing intimate concerns — and how closely they listened to their barber. “It’s been said to me many times that many Black men trust their barber more than they trust their doctor,” he says. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] CLIP sought to build on that familiarity as a way to reach people with undiagnosed hypertension. The condition is both common and easy to miss. About six in 10 non-Hispanic Black men in the United States have hypertension, according to federal data. Yet high blood pressure often produces no symptoms. Among men ages 18 to 39 who have hypertension, the federal data found, fewer than one in four know they have it . Routine access to health care can make early detection more likely, but access is only part of the problem. A 2019 study linked medical mistrust and perceived racism in health care with delayed checkups and blood-pressure screening among Black men. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” says Sean White. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Led by NYU Langone in partnership with Community Health Action of Staten Island (CHASI), CLIP brought blood-pressure screening and health support into 22 Black-owned barbershops from Staten Island zip codes with high hypertension prevalence . Against Da Grain was one of them. W hite’s appointments that Tuesday often stretched beyond 30 minutes. “The barber chair is perfectly set up for measuring blood pressure,” Ravenell says. Some patients experience what’s known as “white coat syndrome,” meaning the stress of a clinical setting causes their blood pressure to rise temporarily. By contrast, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened, so with proper technique, a reading taken at the barber shop may better reflect their usual levels. The challenge, Ravenell adds, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Unlike in a clinical setting, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened. Credit: Tolu Olasoji During CLIP, local Black male community health workers measured patrons’ blood pressure, counseled them, and connected them with medical and social services. Barbers encouraged customers to participate, but screenings were offered without pressure. “I allowed the men to decide whether they wanted to engage with me,” says a community health worker. Importantly, the community health workers were often themselves customers at the participating barbershops and knew the barbers and customers. Ravenell says that familiarity meant “their presence is not an intrusion, as it might be for someone with a white coat.” Across the program, 636 men were screened. Four hundred sixty-one were found to have elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension, 430 of whom enrolled in the study. Participants were 38 years old on average; only 24 percent reported having a primary care provider, and about half had health insurance. The study followed up with enrolled men at six-month intervals through 18 months, even after recruitment at individual shops had ended. At 18 months, community health workers obtained a repeat blood-pressure reading from 96 percent of participants. That level of follow-up, Ravenell says, is unusual and difficult to achieve in a long-running study. Dr. Chidinma Ibe, a community health workers researcher at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Equity, calls the figures “extremely, extremely impressive,” adding that they reinforce the value of meeting people where they are. D espite these successes, however, CLIP did not produce the primary result researchers had hoped for . At 12 months, participants’ systolic blood pressure had changed little. Fewer men met the study’s definition of incident stage two hypertension at 12 months, but the difference was no longer statistically significant at 18 months. Dr. Ibe says that given that the intervention was among men with elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension rather than severely uncontrolled disease, the limited movement in its main blood-pressure outcome was “not terribly surprising.” The challenge for CLIP, notes Dr. Joseph Ravenell, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji For Derek Griffith, a University of Pennsylvania professor who studies Black men’s health, success in simply reaching men is separate from controlling their blood pressure. He says the major determinants of blood-pressure control remain in what men experience outside both barbershops and clinical care. Dr. Idris Robinson, research project manager for Penn’s Program for Research on Men’s Health, likewise cautions against treating the barbershop itself as the intervention. “The blood pressure outcomes weren’t rooted in some magical equation where barbers plus Black men equals guaranteed improvements in Black men’s health,” he says. Sustained engagement, he argues, also depends on collaboration among academic and community partners, barbers’ relationships with clients, and a wider support network. “That infrastructure is critical.” That becomes crucial after an elevated reading. When this occurred with CLIP participants, community health workers explained what the number could mean and encouraged medical follow-up. When it came to a referral, notes Joseph Ebron, CHASI’s director of health equity, “We would let them know what we offer, but it was up to them to take it.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji Even when people wanted help, navigating existing services could complicate the handoff. Workers sometimes met people who thought they lacked coverage, only to discover they were already enrolled elsewhere but were not getting the help they needed. And because they were already attached to another provider or organization, CHASI could not always simply move them into a different service. “We can’t just, like, snatch them,” says Ebron. Ibe points to a structural problem behind that handoff: the fragmented American health care system. Insurance issues, the absence of an established primary care relationship, and weak connections between community organizations and clinical teams can all interrupt the route to care. “If the [community health worker] isn’t employed by that clinic, there’s only so much they can do,” she says. Sustaining even the community side required labor. Active recruitment through Against Da Grain lasted about two months. “We did it for some time without receiving any type of payments,” says White, adding that the program brought “a lot of extra work.” CHASI adapted around the business in real-time: For instance, Ebron says to work around Against Da Grain’s preferences, they screened outside, where workers could pull up a small mobile health unit and barbers could direct interested customers to it. Workers learned to take up less space, getting rid of tables and flyers in favor of a simpler setup: a blood-pressure monitor and materials carried in a bag. Though CLIP is now over, there are larger screening events every two to three months and health workers can return to shops when requested. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Ravenell sees funding — and therefore sustainability — as the broader limitation. When CLIP ended in September 2025, he says Staten Island screening partners continued some services “essentially pro bono” during a funding gap. His team has since received two new NIH grants to build on CLIP’s infrastructure and train community health workers to screen in barbershops for diabetes and diabetic eye disease. For now, CLIP itself is over, though Ebron says CHASI conducts larger screening events every two to three months and can return to shops when requested. Whether the model can travel is another question. Ravenell says Staten Island had an advantage before CLIP began: CHASI had already spent more than 30 years working in the borough through community health workers. “Replicated, yes, easily, no,” Ebron says, because success depends on what already exists locally. CLIP reinforced White’s sense of responsibility to the community he has served for more than 35 years, while sharpening his awareness of the health concerns moving through it. “It helped me realize how many people have elevated levels,” he says. Join Cancel anytime Around noon at Against Da Grain, White’s final appointment brings in a young couple and their son, there for the boy’s first haircut. His mother livestreams the occasion to relatives. When the boy climbs down, his father takes his place in the chair. One generation giving way to another, if only for a haircut. Όταν η Lilly Pettus έφερε μια καρέκλα τραπεζαρίας -- μετακόμισε σε έξι πολιτείες για τριάντα χρόνια, κρατώντας στο ξύλο της το βάρος του οικογενειακού γέλιου και της σκληρής συνέλευσης…
items.descriptionOriginal: Across church basements and community halls, Americans are gathering not just to fix broken lamps and cracked chairs, but to push back against an economy that profits from loneliness and waste. When Lilly Pettus brought a dining room chair -- moved across six states over thirty years, holding in its wood the weight of family laughter and hard conversations -- to a repair caf in Decatur, Georgia, she left with something more than a mended joint: strangers' hands had pressed her family's history back together. "When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it's very lonely," says Martine Postma, who founded Repair Caf International in 2010, and the repair caf s she helped seed around the world are a quiet argument against that loneliness. In neighborhoods where the need is economic as much as environmental, and in ones where it is sentimental, the impulse turns out to be the same: a refusal to let things, and the connections they carry, be so easily discarded. What these gatherings reveal, almost incidentally, is that the skills of care have never really disappeared; they've just been waiting for a place to gather.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In a 2023 clinical trial of 121 people in the UK, wearing a prototype wrist device reduced tic frequency by an average of 25 percent. The Tourette’s wrist device, called Neupulse , came out of research at the University of Nottingham, and three years on, the people using it describe its effect in far stronger terms than a one-in-four reduction would suggest. How a Tourette’s wrist device targets tics Rhythmic pulses to the median nerve Neupulse sends rhythmic electrical pulses into the median nerve, which runs through the wrist and into the hand. Trials have shown that this stimulation changes activity in the brain regions responsible for movement control, and that the rhythm of the pulses can lower both the frequency and the intensity of tics. The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company, Neurotherapeutics Ltd, which secured £1 million (about $1.3 million) in additional funding to bring it to market. Stephen Jackson, the Nottingham professor who has led the research, described the response from users as “a dream come true.” Some of the feedback he has received is very concrete. “We’ve had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking,” he said. Others told the team they could move through an airport and board a flight without tics. Tourette’s syndrome in the UK Tourette’s syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition, usually beginning in childhood, that causes involuntary sounds and movements known as tics. More than 300,000 people in the UK have it, according to the charity Tourettes Action , and there is no cure. The condition reached a wider audience in 2023 when singer Lewis Capaldi, who has Tourette’s, tried the device before a concert in Nottingham, and again through the film I Swear , a drama based on the life of Tourette’s campaigner John Davidson. Three users, three measurable changes Katie, 15: years of constant vocal tics Katie, from Hertfordshire, started having tics at age seven. Her snorting tic ran almost nonstop, to the point of leaving her with a sore throat that kept her in bed for two weeks, and it disrupted her sleep, her eating, and her school attendance. “It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, ‘why are you doing that?'” she said. Her mom, Julia, called it “heartbreaking” to watch. “You feel helpless. You feel you don’t know where to turn really,” she said. After reading about the Nottingham research, Julia brought Katie to try the device in December, before it went on sale. The effect was immediate, Katie said, and she became “really calm.” “It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life,” she said. On the drive back to Hertfordshire, she “just cried the whole way home.” Ollie, 15: a different diagnosis, a similar response Ollie’s case extends the picture, because he does not have Tourette’s. Nearly two years ago he cracked his neck, and about 48 hours later the movement had become involuntary and constant. “It was incredibly sudden,” he said. He was later diagnosed with functional neurological disorder (FND), a condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals. His father, Alex, said sleeping, eating and drinking all became “incredibly difficult.” Ollie stayed inside for about a month at one stage and missed six to seven months of school ahead of his GCSEs, the exams British students sit around age 16. He came close to telling his parents not to bother with the device. A few months ago, when he switched it on for the first time, he phoned home. “You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped,” Alex said. Ollie put it this way: “It’s like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it’s like getting part of your life back.” Mylo, 17: from trial participant to owner Mylo, from Buckinghamshire, was 13 when he joined the 2023 trial. He recently received his own device as a gift and said the urge to suppress his facial tics went away “instantaneously.” “As soon as it comes on, I can feel it,” he said. “I feel different… I feel new almost, which is strange.” Why Neupulse is not yet an NHS treatment Wellness product versus medical device The device comes in two versions. Neupulse-C is sold as a consumer wellness product, and the university says “thousands” have been purchased. Neupulse-M is the version intended for marketing as a medical treatment for tics and Tourette’s syndrome, and it is still working through regulatory approval. That distinction determines whether the National Health Service can offer it. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has identified the technology as “promising” but asked for more evidence of long-term benefit. In 2025, it said its committee would meet again to assess the device’s clinical and cost-effectiveness. “They were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval,” Jackson said. “That’s something we’re working towards.” He hopes to see the Tourette’s wrist device available through the NHS “in the next year or so.” Early reports from the Tourette’s community Emma McNally, CEO of Tourettes Action , said the users she has spoken with have given the device “nothing but praise.” “Some people have said it’s helped them to go to places that they’ve not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library,” she said. Others told her it helped them come out of a tic attack and feel more relaxed. Wrist stimulation beyond Tourette’s syndrome The Nottingham team is now testing the same approach on other conditions. Early trials have examined whether the pulses can reduce tremors in people with Parkinson’s , and Jackson said the university plans a UK-wide clinical trial covering anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The next milestone is regulatory, since medical approval for Neupulse-M would open the door to NICE guidance and NHS prescriptions, and the trials that follow will show whether a signal sent through the wrist can shape movement and mood in conditions well beyond tics.
