items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You know that feeling when it’s two in the afternoon, and you can’t quite account for where the morning went? Not because you weren’t doing things, but because the busyness didn’t add up to anything you can point to. It’s demoralizing in a specific way, and it has surprisingly little to do with how early your alarm went off. Time management experts Melinda Rathkopf, M.D., M.B.A. , and Julie Morgenstern , the author of multiple bestselling books on productivity, say most of what shapes your morning was set in motion the night before, and the solution is usually far simpler than the elaborate routines you’ve seen floating around online. Start the night before Where do both experts begin? The evening before. When you make decisions about tomorrow before you go to sleep, you take some of the friction out of the morning itself. “Preplanning the day ahead and making decisions ahead of time makes the rest of your day potentially calmer and less stressful,” says Rathkopf. “Set yourself up by knowing what’s coming.” Transition time is one of the things that tends to get left out when people plan their days. It’s easy to schedule back-to-back tasks and forget that moving between them really does take time. Build that in the night before and the morning feels a lot less like you’re already behind before you’ve started. This extends to sleep, too. Rathkopf recommends starting with how much sleep you genuinely need to feel refreshed, then working backward from your wake time to set a consistent bedtime. “ Sleep is so vital to daily functioning and brain health,” she says. Most people schedule everything else first and try to fit sleep in around it. She suggests reversing that. Put the phone away before bed and after waking up If there’s one habit both experts come back to, it’s keeping your phone out of your first and last hour of each day. Morgenstern is direct about it. “The number one thing that can boost morning productivity has to do with screen time ,” she says. “We should not be on our devices an hour before bed, and we should not be on our devices for our first hour of the morning.” Checking your phone first thing does more than eat up time. It pulls you into a reactive state before you’ve had a chance to figure out your own priorities for the day. “The phone can be a useful tool, but it’s designed to keep us on there,” Morgenstern says. “Think of it like sugar — you have to really manage your consumption, and take charge. It’s the key to morning productivity, engagement, your relationships, everything.” She recommends replacing that screen time with something restorative: reading, getting outside, or having a conversation with someone. The goal isn’t deprivation; it’s starting the day on your own terms instead of somebody else’s notifications. Keep your routine simple One persistent myth about productive mornings is that they require an elaborate ritual. If you’ve ever felt vaguely inadequate watching someone describe their two-hour routine involving cold plunges , journaling, and a complicated smoothie, you’re not alone. Those routines often backfire. “It can make you stressed out — ‘Oh god, I didn’t meditate long enough!'” Morgenstern says. “Add three to four elements maximum for a morning routine. Otherwise, you’re habituating to something that’s unsustainable.” Find the small handful of things that reliably start your morning feeling calm and grounded, and stick with those. If you’re getting ready alongside young children, Morgenstern suggests completing your own routine before they’re up, then putting some thought into making their mornings smoother too. Laying out clothes or choosing breakfast the night before can take a surprising amount of stress out of a weekday morning. Train your brain with predictability Your brain is a creature of habit in the most useful sense. “Our brains love predictability,” says Rathkopf. “When you have a predictable routine, you’re reducing your stress and cognitive load.” When your morning follows a consistent pattern, you spend less mental energy on logistics and more on the work itself, which sounds obvious until you notice how rarely most mornings feel that way in practice. Morgenstern describes building a regular block for deep thinking as a kind of training for your brain: “If you have a predictable head-down time, your brain gets acclimated to it — it’s 10:30, that’s when we do our deep thinking. I’ve never seen anyone build proactive work with an erratic schedule.” For creative work especially, consistency turns out to matter more than inspiration. Start with the work that matters most A lot of mornings get swallowed by emails, messages, and reactive tasks before you ever reach work that needs your purest attention. “The number one difficulty people have is that the day starts off all reactive, and they can’t get to proactive work,” Morgenstern says. Her suggestion is to start with the most important thing on your list, the one that needs your freshest thinking. Even if everything else gets away from you after that, you’ve done something that mattered. “Even if you only get that one thing done, you’ll feel the greatest sense of relief that you’ve done your job,” she says. If your workplace opens with a morning meeting, Morgenstern recommends blocking off a half hour to an hour right after it for focused work, to address anything that came out of the meeting before settling into your main task. Better yet, see if you can get your whole team to protect the first hour of the day. Build in small moments of recovery Self-care doesn’t need to be a whole thing. What Morgenstern recommends is more modest: short pauses woven throughout the day, especially during your busiest stretches. “Add microbursts of self-care in your day — five to 20-minute activities that recharge you,” she says. A short walk, some music on your commute, ten minutes with a book. Small enough to fit into almost any day, and consistent enough to keep you from burning out by three in the afternoon. “The harder you’re working, the harder you have to recover,” she says. Stopping feels like the last thing you can afford when you’re slammed, but that’s usually when it matters most. Give yourself room to change, and to have off days Both experts caution against treating your morning routine as something fixed. Life changes, seasons change, your circumstances shift, and what works at one stage may not work at another. “You may need to change it based on other obligations, at different stages of your life, or even in different seasons,” says Rathkopf. And when a morning doesn’t come together the way you hoped, she has one more piece of advice: don’t be hard on yourself about it. “Everybody’s different, and what you’re seeing in posts is someone else’s best versions and best days,” Rathkopf says. “They have those not-so-perfect days, too.” A morning routine isn’t something you get right once. It’s something you keep adjusting until it fits. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.description: Οι προτάσεις επιλέγονται ανεξάρτητα από την ομάδα μας, αλλά ενδέχεται να προκύψει προμήθεια στο Nice News, κάτι που βοηθά να διατηρείται το περιεχόμενό μας ελεύθερο. items.descriptionOriginal: Recommendations are independently selected by our team but may result in a commission to Nice News which helps keep our content free. We likely all have a person in our lives who’s impossibly hard to shop for. Maybe they’re the family member who says they “don’t want anything” or the friend who seems to already have it all. You can go two routes for recipients like these: Get them something practical (items that make life a little easier) or not so practical (gifts intended simply to delight). To help with your search this holiday season, we rounded up a mix of both. And if you’re still on the hunt for the right present after perusing this guide, check out the Nice News team’s favorite products of the year for more ideas. Aura Digital Picture Frame For the sentimentalist who always asks for more photos Courtesy of Aura A sweet gift for loved ones near and far, Aura’s digital frames let people share photos from multiple phones and then display them like a slideshow. My sister and I each have one, and it’s a thrill to see new pics of my niece and nephew pop up on mine. For those who prefer tangible photos, consider pairing a fun frame with this compact printer that makes 4-by-6-inch prints directly from a smartphone. Shop Aura Shop Amazon Soligt Wooden Cookbook and Tablet Stand For the one who uses their iPad to pull up recipes in the kitchen Courtesy of Amazon This nifty stand is ideal for holding medium-sized cookbooks as well as iPads, Kindles, and other tablets. It features a kickstand you can position at multiple angles, and its elegant cutting board-esque design helps it blend in with other kitchen accoutrements. Your recipient can use it to watch tutorials or read recipes — or to FaceTime you while they’re cooking. Shop AMAZON La Lune Upcycled Leather Crossbody Bag For the stylish friend who’s always on the go Courtesy of La Lune Everyone needs a purse — and this one from La Lune couldn’t be more practical. The vivid Electric Blue Crossbody fits a phone, wallet, keys, sunglasses, and lip balm, making it an easy pick for errands, sightseeing, or a dinner out. Handcrafted by Los Angeles artisans from upcycled Italian leather, each vintage-inspired bag from La Lune comes from a limited supply of leftover leather with its own color and grain that softens with wear. It’s a gift as distinctive as the person who will carry it, and it will last for years to come.* Shop La Lune *Indicates a Nice News brand partnership or affiliate Bee Cups Watering Stations For the gardener who wants to attract more wildlife to their yard Courtesy of Bee Cups Bee Cups are patented watering stations, and they happen to be both practical and whimsical. Each cup holds about a teaspoon of water — just enough to hydrate a visiting bee or butterfly while preventing them from getting submerged. They’re handmade from 100% porcelain, so they’ll hold up in changing weather conditions, and painted with a special UV-reactive glaze to mimic flowers, so they’re extra enticing to pollinators. Shop Bee Cups SHOP AMAZON Fitbit Air For the person who wants to track their steps without getting distracted by notifications Courtesy of Google Think of this as a yoga-class-friendly fitness tracker. It delivers the benefits of typical trackers — like monitoring steps, sleep, and heart rate — but it’s screen-free, with no buttons or notifications (the data is accessible via a companion app). It’s also water-resistant, and a single five-minute charge can last up to a week. Tip: Include a few replacement straps with the gift so your recipient can select the best color for their outfit on any given day. Shop GOogle SHOP AMAZON Ban.do Quilted Blanket For the one who loves a cozy night in Courtesy of Ban.do This quilt is as cozy as it is cheerful. It’s soft, machine washable, and a sweet way to help someone stay snug. Check out the brand’s other four designs, which are equally as delightful to look at. Shop Ban.do Terrain Forget-Me-Not Flower Press For the crafty soul Courtesy of Terrain Hobby gifts can be hit-or-miss, but this one’s sure to go over well with gardeners and flower lovers. It comes with everything needed to start preserving blooms (sans the blooms themselves) in one very pretty package. They can then use the pressed flowers to make things like coasters, jewelry, and boho decor . If you think your loved one would rather skip over the DIY component, consider this lovely preserved flowers keepsake box or picture frame . Shop Terrain Loop Earplugs For the concertgoer who’s concerned about their hearing Courtesy of Loop Know someone with misophonia — or a pal who simply wants to protect their hearing? Loop earplugs lower the decibel level of noise (to varying degrees based on the different models), and work wonders for focusing, calming an overstimulated nervous system, enjoying concerts without damaging your eardrums, and sleeping. Each pair comes with a handy case and four sets of washable, silicone ear tips. Shop Loop Shop AMAZon Cabin Nine 20-Minute Candles For the analog enthusiast Courtesy of Cabin Nine Who knew a timer could be so lovely? This set includes 12 small beeswax candles that each burn for approximately 20 minutes, as well as a reusable candle holder, matches, and a charming blue tin to keep everything in. It’s ideal for anyone who wants to carve out more time for journaling, reading, meditating, or yoga without relying on a digital timer. Shop Cabin nine Algae Cooking Club Nara’s Roasted Garlic Oil For the home chef who doesn’t like the smell of garlic on their fingers Courtesy of Algae Cooking Club For the foodies, this oil gives dishes all the flavor of garlic without them having to actually chop any garlic. It’s made primarily from algae, which has an extremely high smoke-point (higher than avocado oil) and is infused with garlic, yuzu, miso, and scallions. In other words, it’s delicious and can be used for sautéing, roasting, drizzling, you name it. Shop algae cooking club Shop AMAZON Audible Membership For the bookworm who loves to listen to their literature Courtesy of Audible Got a friend with a never-ending TBR list? An Audible gift membership lets them download an audiobook each month from a catalog of over 1 million titles. If they already have a login, that’s no problem — they’ll just receive more credits to use. You can give three months for $45, six months for $90, or a full year of reading for $150 (with no automatic auto-renew). It comes quite in handy when they’re 135th in line for a library book in the Libby app. Optional: Pair the membership with this silly mug . shop Audible SHOP AMAZON America the Beautiful Parks Pass For the nature lover Courtesy of Recreation.Gov Another blend of practical and delightful, the America the Beautiful Pass covers entrance fees and standard amenity fees (aka day-use fees) at more than 2,000 national parks and federal recreational sites for one year. The digital version is convenient, but you can add in a physical card at checkout for people who might prefer to keep the pass in their car’s glove compartment. Shop Recreation.gov Baggu Packing Cubes For the frequent traveler Courtesy of Baggu A packing cube goes a long way, particularly for overpackers who could use a little help squeezing just one more thing into their bag. Baggu’s cubes are a favorite of Staff Editor Ally Mauch, who says “you’d be amazed at how much you can fit in these.” The cherry on top? They come in such fun, punchy patterns and colors. Shop Baggu Shop Amazon Board For the avid game night host Courtesy of Board Where to start with this snazzy gift? It’s a “face-to-face game console” that’s designed to be a happy medium between digital games and board games. The touchscreen device lays flat on a table and comes with physical pieces that interact with the screen, so players can gather around for a classic yet modern game night experience. It includes a built-in starter pack of seven games, and tons more can be purchased with no subscription required. Oh, and it made Time magazine’s Best Inventions of 2026 list. Shop Board Q uokka Hotel Wildeluxe 1,000-Piece Puzzle For the one who loves a good challenge Courtesy of Amazon This is no ordinary puzzle. It doubles as a mystery game with 321 “secrets” that are unlocked by putting together the 1,000 pieces, opening the riddle envelopes, and listening to an accompanying audio story. It’s gotten rave reviews, and it’s under $25. Shop AMAZON Related: 19 Gifts for Readers Who Always Have Their Nose in a Book

items.title: Ένα σημείωμα 22χρονου για το ανάρμοστο
items.titleOriginal: A 22-Year-Old's Note on Unbecoming
items.description: Στα είκοσι δύο, ο Haile Thomas καθόταν με μια ερώτηση που οι περισσότεροι από εμάς κουβαλάμε ήσυχα για δεκαετίες: τι κάνω με όλη αυτή την ύπαρξη; Αντί να απαντήσει, έκανε κάτι πιο γενναίο -- έγραψε το δρόμο της στην ίδια την αβεβαιότητα. Ο προβληματισμός της δεν φτάνει ως συμβουλή αλλά ως άδεια: να νιώθει ημιτελής και ολοκληρωμένη ταυτόχρονα, να σταματήσει να περιμένει…
items.descriptionOriginal: At twenty-two, Haile Thomas sat with a question most of us quietly carry for decades: what do I do with all of this existence? Rather than answer it, she did something braver -- she wrote her way into the uncertainty itself. Her reflection arrives not as advice but as permission: to feel incomplete and whole at the same time, to stop waiting for the map that will never come. She offers a quietly radical image of identity -- that growing up is less about finding yourself than noticing "the entity that gets dressed," the spaciousness beneath every costume we try on and discard. There is no finish line in her telling, only transformations meeting us in the moments we least expect. "Growing up is a never ending journey," she writes -- and somehow that lands not as defeat but as relief. What she offers, finally, is not wisdom so much as weather: a loosening, a liquefying of the hard certainties we grip when life refuses to hold still.

Αλλά τα παιδιά είναι παραγωγικοί δημιουργοί, οπότε τι πρέπει να γίνει με όλους αυτούς τους χάρτινους καμβάδες κατασκευών καθώς κατακλύζονται συνεχώς; Καλλιτέχνης Σ…
items.descriptionOriginal: A stick figure family, a googly-eyed monster, a happy rainbow. Children’s artwork represents how they see the world at any given age — a sweet, fleeting perspective that the adults in their lives yearn to preserve. But kids are prolific creators, so what’s to be done with all these construction paper canvases as more continuously flood in? Artist Shana Blakley came up with a creative way to save her kids’ drawings while breaking out of a rut she’d been in with her own work: She turned them into a big, colorful collage to hang in her family’s home. When she shared the result on Instagram, her comment section exploded. The idea clearly resonated with other moms, dads, and grandparents. Heirloom Collage Shana Blakley’s first kids’ artwork collage “We want to honor what our kids make,” Blakley told Nice News, adding: “Nearly every parent around the world has a growing pile of kid art, and it’s in our nature to save it. We feel guilty throwing it away, but storing it also begins to feel unsettling. There comes a time when you realize how much of it you have and you ask yourself: ‘What am I keeping this for?’” Heirloom Collage Molly Revers with her grandkids and the collages made from their artwork Shortly after posting the piece last year, she launched Heirloom Collage and started taking commissions. Now, she offers an online course that guides participants in producing their own artist-quality collages out of kiddos’ creations. The course consists of six video modules totaling one hour, and Blakley provides feedback in a private Facebook group where students can post their in-progress and completed work. Molly Revers enjoys dabbling in different artistic endeavors, so she signed up for the $99 e-course. “The most meaningful aspect was the joy it brought me when creating the collages and the joy it brought my little grandsons when they saw their work displayed in such a cool way,” she shared. “They love picking their favorite creations and memories associated with them.” Heirloom Collage Another parent’s completed collage For Blakley, who lives in Richmond, Virginia, and began her career as a fine artist over a decade ago, the project reconnected her to a sense of spontaneity after a period of creative stagnation. “Halfway through it, I recall thinking, ‘[My kids] didn’t second-guess their creativity in these pieces, so I shouldn’t either,’” she said. “That was a big breakthrough for me.” It’s something many adults, artists or not, can relate to. “A lot of my students haven’t made art since they were kids, and this brings them back to it,” Blakley added. Overall, though, the memorable shared experience of making that first collage with her two children — the youngsters helped select the included drawings and “were buzzing with pride” — is what she wishes for her clients. “That connection is what lasts, and they end up with something their family really treasures,” she said. Heirloom Collage Jeanine Long-Tuohy with her granddaughter Ava and the collage they made Jeanine Long-Tuohy, who loves her granddaughter Ava’s artwork, created her first piece with Ava’s help and has since started a new one with another grandchild. “Working on this made me feel like there’s a lot more we can do together,” Long-Tuohy said. “It’s a memory they will always have of me.”

items.descriptionOriginal: In South Sudan in 2024, just out of high school, Nyakangba Nelson Luka Poyo asked himself what kind of life a kid born in 2021 in Tambura would have apart from killing, hatred, bloodshed, and living in a camp. Amid tears, that question gave him his life’s purpose. He thought if young people had opportunities to learn and communicate, and the space in which to express themselves, they could realize alternatives to violence. He called it a “Peace Voice.” Young people make up an estimated 70% of South Sudan’s population, yet they have no voice. They are swept up into conflict at a shockingly young age. In a Peace Journey program, Nyakangba learned about Laddership, and how to become a “ladder” for others lifting them up through support and opportunities. Now, through Peace Voices to Vision, he helps young people “develop a common understanding of how to live together peacefully. Everyone deserves peace.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Lafora disease is a rare genetic condition that typically affects kids and adolescents, causing frequent seizures and the gradual loss of cognitive function. There is no cure, so the focus for many parents inevitably turns to quality of life. That’s something Detroit mom Azeza Kasham was struggling to maintain for her 17-year-old son, Gigi Breadiy, earlier this year. He was diagnosed in 2019, just days after his older brother died of the disease. Kasham’s husband has his own health problems and isn’t able to work, and the couple has two younger boys as well, so she took on multiple jobs to pay off medical debt. Breadiy uses a wheelchair, and the family home wasn’t fully accessible, so caring for him was becoming increasingly difficult. She’d tried fundraising on social media, but still felt like she was drowning. A stranger she connected with online would be her rescue buoy. Josh Liljenquist is a Minnesota content creator with over 23 million followers. Many of his videos fall into the somewhat controversial random-acts-of-kindness genre, but the 28-year-old’s main focus is rallying tangible support for people in need. After learning about Breadiy, he posted footage of himself meeting mother and son in February. Less than two months later, a GoFundMe he launched for them had raised nearly $600,000. “It’s just completely changed my life, you know?” Kasham shared during a recent phone call with Nice News. “It’s enabled me to give Gigi everything he needs, but that’s not all [Josh] did. And that isn’t even the most important thing. He restored my faith in humanity.” In the nearly seven months since meeting, Liljenquist and Kasham have become extremely close. “She’s literally like my second mom,” he said, adding: “She keeps saying that I changed her life, but I think she changed my life more than I changed hers.” His own mother also speaks to her often, and even flew out to Michigan to spend time with the family. The women connected so strongly because they both know what it’s like to care for a sick child, and the financial toll it can take. For the first six years of Liljenquist’s life, he was in and out of the hospital. He has a genetic disorder called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as well as eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the esophagus. That background has led him to direct more energy into helping families experiencing similar situations. “I want other parents to not have to deal with the same thing that my parents dealt with,” he said. But his fundraising has benefited people in all sorts of circumstances: a man in need of a new roof, a couple facing homelessness, a woman hoping to open a permanent pay-what-you-can cafe. For Kasham, the support from Liljenquist’s felt like God had answered her prayers. He, too, felt a divine hand in their meeting. The fact that they belong to different religions was a moot point. “She kept asking me, ‘Well, you know, you’re a Christian person. I’m Muslim. Does that matter?’ And I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, no, not at all,’” he recounted. “That’s the first thing she would ask me. And I said, ‘Why would that matter?’” Before the GoFundMe, Kasham had to bathe Breadiy in the garage because the shower wasn’t accessible. Now, the family has paid down debt and made upgrades to their home, including a roll-in shower, that allow him dignity and privacy. “He has his good days. He has his bad days,” she said, noting that his seizures have worsened in recent months. “But one thing he has that puts the biggest smile on his face is he has his own space.” You can donate to Lafora disease research through Chelsea’s Hope .

Η πόλη Lahaina, η οποία κατέχει μια βαθιά θέση στην ιστορία της Χαβάης και κάποτε χρησίμευε ως πρωτεύουσα του Βασιλείου της Χαβάης, υπέστη τη μεγαλύτερη καταστροφή: τα περισσότερα από τα κτίριά της καταστράφηκαν και χιλιάδες κάτοικοι εκτοπίστηκαν. Η καταστροφή εξέθεσε τα τρωτά…
items.descriptionOriginal: O n August 8, 2023, fast-moving wildfires swept through several parts of West Maui. The town of Lahaina, which holds a deep place in Hawaiian history and once served as the capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom, suffered the greatest devastation: Most of its buildings were destroyed, and thousands of residents were displaced. The disaster exposed vulnerabilities that had been building long before the flames, from a shortage of affordable housing and dependence on tourism to questions around land use, water access and food security. The post Maui Is Becoming a Living Laboratory for Regenerative Tourism appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Ένα πακέτο χαρτομάντιλων στο Ikea
items.titleOriginal: A Pack of Tissues at Ikea
items.description: Η θλίψη έχει τον τρόπο να μας κάνει ενέδρα σε συνηθισμένα μέρη. Ήταν στη μέση ενός καταστήματος της Ikea, περιτριγυρισμένο από καναπέδες και ζευγάρια που χτίζουν μαζί ζωές, που μια πρόσφατα χήρα γυναίκα κάθισε και έκλαψε. Ένας περαστικός άγνωστος σταμάτησε, πίεσε ένα πακέτο με χαρτομάντιλα στα χέρια της, ακούμπησε μια παλάμη στον ώμο της και περίμενε σιωπηλή μέχρι ένα νεύμα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Grief has a way of ambushing us in ordinary places. It was in the middle of an Ikea store, surrounded by display of sofas and couples building lives together, that a recently widowed woman sat down and wept. A passing stranger stopped, pressed a packet of tissues into her hands, rested a palm on her shoulder, and waited in silence until a nod signaled she was steadier. Then, she simply walked on. That wordless exchange, offered without expectation or introduction, cracked something open: "I knew then that a relationship was possible, because there are good people in the world." What followed, over the next decade, was a new love, a rebuilt life, and a quiet personal ritual -- the widow now carries tissues wherever she goes and has pressed them into the hands of four strangers crying in restaurants and bars. Kindness, it turns out, doesn't just comfort; it teaches, and those who receive it often become its most faithful carriers.

items.title: Ο καλλιτέχνης έχει αποστολή να σχεδιάσει ορόσημα σε κάθε σταθμό του μετρό του Λονδίνου — Δείτε τι έχει κάνει μέχρι στιγμής
items.titleOriginal: Artist Is on a Mission to Sketch Landmarks at Every London Tube Station — See What He’s Done So Far
items.description: Ο Ντάνιελ Τε, ένας Αμερικανός καλλιτέχνης που ζει στο Λονδίνο, έχει βάλει στο στόχαστρο του να σκιτσάρει διακριτικά ορόσημα στους 272 ενεργούς σταθμούς του μετρό της πόλης. Η 27χρονη πρόσφατα ολοκλήρωσε και τις 16 στάσεις στη γραμμή Victoria Line σε έναν μαραθώνιο σκίτσο 10 ωρών, ξεκινώντας με το Brixton και ολοκληρώνοντας με το Walthamstow Central. Πέρασε περίπου μισή ώρα σε κάθε στάση δ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.title: Φανταζόμαστε τις ποώδεις πόλεις του μέλλοντος
items.titleOriginal: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία έχει εκδοθεί από κοινού από το Reasons to be Cheerful και το Outrider Foundation . Το 2012, ο Philip Wallisfurth ήθελε να σώσει ένα δέντρο. Πολίτες στο Άαχεν της Γερμανίας διαμαρτυρήθηκαν για τα σχέδια για ένα εμπορικό κέντρο που απειλούσε ένα δέντρο 150 ετών. Ο Wallisfurth, τότε ένας επίδοξος καλλιτέχνης του δρόμου, αναρωτήθηκε αν μπορούσε να χρησιμοποιήσει βρύα - αντί για τα συνηθισμένα του…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story has been co-published by Reasons to be Cheerful and the Outrider Foundation . I n 2012, Philip Wallisfurth wanted to save a tree. Citizens in Aachen, Germany, were protesting plans for a shopping center that threatened a 150-year-old tree. Wallisfurth , then an aspiring street artist, wondered if he could use moss — instead of his usual spray can — to support the campaign. He harvested moss from a local park, used yogurt as an adhesive and stuck two-meter-high letters onto the construction fence, spelling out “greener living.” The reactions surprised him. “People loved it,” he recalls. “Many took pictures and some spontaneously hung flowers in small vases onto the fence.” He had stumbled upon a medium that was soft, tactile and alive — and a natural way of occupying public space. YouTube tutorials suggested mixing moss with buttermilk in a blender, but the results disappointed him. Through trial and error with different mosses and yogurts, he developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti.” Artist Philip Wallisfurth developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti with moss.” Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth Two years later, whiskey maker Jack Daniel’s hired him for a campaign. In Cologne, Wallisfurth covered an eight-by-eight-meter wall with moss lettering, spelling out a motto he lives by: never give up trying to do what you really want to be happy Now an artist with international projects and a studio in Berlin, Wallisfurth, 42, mostly paints large, colorful murals and designs anamorphic installations, room-filling works that seem to change shape depending on the viewer’s perspective. But moss continues to appeal to him for several reasons. He feels it’s uniquely suited to transform uninspiring urban spaces into places that feel more welcoming — and it has environmental benefits, too. He learned from speaking with scientists that moss can convert carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide into oxygen. “It also acts as a natural air filter and absorbs noise,” he notes. Moss continues to appeal to Wallisfurth for its ability to make spaces more welcoming and its environmental benefits. Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth There are more than 13,000 recognized species of moss. The unassuming plant that most homeowners would like to scrape off their driveways offers more than unusual shades of green. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. Wallisfurth dreams of turning entire structures — for instance, train stations — into buildings where moss improves the air and atmosphere. As cities grapple with increasingly dangerous heat, Wallisfurth’s artistic experiments intersect with a serious question for architects and climate researchers: While concrete, asphalt and masonry store the sun’s energy, cities are searching for ways to keep buildings and public spaces cooler. Could this small, overlooked plant become part of the answer? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. A 2026 field study in Seoul showed moss-based green roofs reduced peak roof-surface temperatures by about 19° Celsius and maximum indoor temperatures by 2 to 3.5° Celsius during heat waves, while a 2026 peer-reviewed study from TU Delft in the Netherlands found that hydrated moss can produce evaporative cooling and insulate underlying surfaces. Credit: Lukas Gojda / Shutterstock Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. As promising as these findings are, the reality is more complex than a green coating that simply cools whatever it covers. According to the Dutch researchers, the cooling effect only lasts as long as the moss is hydrated. Crucially, they found that dry moss exposed to direct sun can actually become warmer than bare mortar. So the question changes: Can cities engineer walls and roofs with moss that stays moist when cities most need cooling? Several startups are betting that the solution lies in redesigning the surfaces themselves. In London, Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Founder and architect Nicky Naidu wants to change how the construction industry thinks about moss, which is often treated as a sign of neglect. “Moss gets a bad rep. But moss has intrinsic beauty, and we want to bring that beauty to cities,” Naidu told Reuters . “It’s carbon negative, bioreceptive, cost-effective and fire-safe. Everything that the industry needs and requires.” The company’s panels are made of a base material Naidu describes as bioreceptive concrete designed to support the growth of moss. The living wall systems incorporate controlled irrigation, delivering moisture directly rather than relying on rainfall or conventional surface spraying. Naidu argues that the moss walls are easier to maintain than conventional green walls because moss needs no soil to flourish. Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Courtesy of Alive Labs In the Netherlands, Respyre has developed a similar concept with “Mosscrete,” a bioreceptive concrete that can be seeded with moss and also features an “ integrated, automated irrigation system that keeps the moss sufficiently hydrated, particularly during warmer and drier periods .” Both companies have moved from the prototype stage to making their panels commercially available. In Berlin, Green City Solutions built the world’s first vertical moss farm on 1,200 square meters to grow moss for sustainable air filters. The next step for the industry is to measure results in real life under varying temperatures and conditions, to determine where moss performs well enough to justify the investment. Not every experiment requires new materials or elaborate infrastructure. In Santiago de Compostela, Spain, a chance observation during the pandemic led city officials and university researchers to reconsider the vegetation growing between the city’s paving stones, including moss. After thermal cameras showed that stone surfaces with these small patches of greenery measured up to 25° Celsius cooler than bare paving, the city opted to leave the “urban microgreen” in place as a low-cost way to mitigate heat. A Respyre test panel after irrigation. Courtesy of Respyre Philip Wallisfurth keeps experimenting with the greenery, too. For a temporary installation, he transformed an entire living room in Berlin into an otherworldly moss-covered landscape. Again, he noticed people’s positive reaction. “The smell simply calmed people down,” he observed. “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” Wallisfurth learned that most conventional moss art one finds in rooms is made from moss that has been dried and preserved with chemicals, eliminating the need to water it but also killing most of its environmental benefits. “It’s dead,” he says. His own bio-art has limits. Without preservation, the moss typically dries and dies within three to six months, depending on the surrounding dryness and acidity. “Like street art,” Wallisfurth notes, “it’s impermanent, too.” The walls of a bank building in Utrecht before and after renovation with Respyre’s bioreceptive concrete. Courtesy of Respyre But learning more about moss also made him reconsider where his material comes from. His sister, a nature guide, calls moss the “lungs of the forest” and told him it was wrong to take moss from forests and public spaces. He now sources his moss from an abandoned army training ground that is likely to soon be a construction site. His desire to create sustainable moss installations sometimes clashes with his clients’ expectations. Several big corporations approached him about creating moss pieces, he says, only to dismiss his concerns about sustainable sourcing. “They told me: ‘We don’t care. It just needs to look green in the pictures.’” He shakes his head. “That was a downer. It showed that most people only look at it as a means to an end.” The exchange captures a broader risk in the rush to make cities greener: The living material can become a visual shorthand for sustainability, even when its environmental value has not been proven. It might look green but actually be greenwashing. Credit: CinemaPhoto / Shutterstock “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” –Philip Wallisfurth In addition to making his own moss art, Wallisfurth enjoys running moss workshops for kids at schools. Children love to experiment with the soft, tactile material, he says. Growing up in a rural part of the Eifel in Germany, he remembers walking barefoot across moss, and nature was his refuge when his own childhood was marked by loss. His parents died of cancer when he was young, and his brother was killed when Wallisfurth was only 14. He trained as a foreign-language correspondent and hotel manager before moving to Berlin and pursuing art. He turned to art explicitly as a means to brighten places up and turn rooms into positive spaces. “That’s what drives me,” he says. “Positivity is simply a much better way to deal with things. Of course, not everything is positive, but I have to try to stay positive.” His favorite projects begin with dark, inhospitable places and turn them into areas where people like to spend time. “That’s my goal as an artist.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime He believes he wouldn’t be an artist without his biography. And he sees a similar resilience in the plants: “A specialist once told me I could put moss in the oven at 270° Celsius, and if I water it afterward, it will come back to life.” In that way, he says, “Maybe I’m a little like moss. You can destroy it, but it simply grows again. It’s a fighter.” The post Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: 'Ελα μαζί μου. Σε πήρα».
items.titleOriginal: 'Come With Me. I Got You.'
items.description: Τριάντα χρόνια αφότου η μητέρα της πέθανε ξαφνικά ενώ υπηρετούσε στο Ειρηνευτικό Σώμα, η Κέιτ Ρόγκαν εξακολουθεί να κουβαλά τη μνήμη ενός ξένου που συνάντησε τη θλίψη της με τέσσερις ήσυχες λέξεις: «Έλα μαζί μου. Σε πήρα». Η γυναίκα καθοδήγησε τον Ρόγκαν από ένα προσγειωμένο αεροπλάνο, μέσω μιας πτήσης που ακυρώθηκε, σε μια νύχτα ξενοδοχείου και μέχρι την αγκαλιά της αδερφής της στο baggage cla…
items.descriptionOriginal: Thirty years after her mother died suddenly while she was serving in the Peace Corps, Kate Rogan still carries the memory of a stranger who met her grief with four quiet words: "Come with me. I got you." The woman guided Rogan off a grounded plane, through a canceled flight, through a hotel night, and all the way to her sister's arms at baggage claim - then disappeared, nameless, into ordinary life. What stays is not just the kindness, but what Rogan came to understand about herself in that moment: "I was this strong, independent young woman, but in that moment, I could not handle life without somebody helping me." Some losses crack us open in ways that expose how much we need each other, and some strangers seem to know this before we do.

items.description: Το να κάνετε τα καθημερινά σας βήματα μπορεί να είναι λίγο πιο εύκολο αν ζείτε στο Hoboken του New Jersey. Νωρίτερα αυτό το μήνα, το Architectural Digest δημοσίευσε μια λίστα με τις εννέα πιο βατές πόλεις στις ΗΠΑ με βάση πρόσφατες μελέτες, το εργαλείο Walk Score του Redfin και διαβουλεύσεις με μεσίτες, κατοίκους και ειδικούς στον τουρισμό. Η πόλη του 1 τετραγωνικού μιλίου, που βρίσκεται ακριβώς απέναντι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Getting your daily steps in may be a little easier if you live in Hoboken, New Jersey. Earlier this month, Architectural Digest released a list of the nine most walkable cities in the U.S. based on recent studies, Redfin’s Walk Score tool, and consultations with realtors, residents, and tourism experts. The 1-square-mile city, which sits just across the Hudson River from downtown Manhattan, earned the top spot due to its ample public transportation and dense street grid. It received a 97 out of 100 on Walk Score, which measures the ability for residents to run errands and access amenities without a car — factors that can go a long way for physical health, mental health, and the health of the planet. View this post on Instagram “[Walkability] can benefit everything from household finances and health to the environment and overall quality of life,” Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, told the outlet. She added: “Walkable neighborhoods also create more opportunities for people to interact with local businesses, use public spaces and resources, and connect with their neighbors.” Science backs up those benefits. A 2021 paper showed higher walkability was associated with lower mortality rates in a cohort of 13,832 women. And a 2020 study of over 31,000 adults found that those living in high-walkability areas were 150% more likely to engage in adequate levels of physical activity and 76% less likely to be obese. Additionally, research from 2013 suggested that participants who walked more in their neighborhood experienced improved social interactions and felt more social cohesion within the community. RELATED: How 11,000 Twins Helped Illustrate the Importance of Making Cities Walkable In terms of the planet, Elizabeth Sawin, director of the Multisolving Institute, a research organization focused on climate change, equity, health, well-being, and biodiversity, summed up the power of walkability in a 2024 interview with Grist: “Every trip taken on foot instead of by a fossil fuel-powered car reduces greenhouse gas emissions.” Here’s the full list of America’s most walkable cities from Architectural Digest : 1. Hoboken, New Jersey 2. West Hollywood, California 3. Boston, Massachusetts 4. San Francisco, California 5. New York, New York 6. Washington, D.C. 7. Chicago, Illinois 8. Miami, Florida 9. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

items.titleOriginal: What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives
items.description: Καλώς ήρθατε πίσω στην εβδομαδιαία μας ματιά στα παρασκήνια για το τι κάνει να μιλάει η ομάδα μας. Πείτε μας τι έχετε διαβάσει στο info@reasonstobecheerful.world και ίσως το παρουσιάσουμε εδώ. Στην τσάντα Μια παρέμβαση χαμηλού κόστους και χαμηλής τεχνολογίας σώζει ζωές σε μαιευτήρια σε όλη την Αφρική. Όπως αναφέρουν οι New York Times σε μια ιστορία που μοιράστηκε το Contributing…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. In the bag A low-cost, low-tech intervention is saving lives in maternity wards across Africa. As the New York Times reports in a story shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas, the maternal drape is a plastic pouch that can be used to easily measure blood loss. This allows health workers to act quickly in the case of postpartum hemorrhage, which is extremely dangerous. When combined with the necessary treatments, this intervention cut deaths by postpartum hemorrhage by about two-thirds. “The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite,” Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, told the Times . “It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems.” Michaela says: I had no idea a simple, low-cost plastic bag is saving so many mothers’ lives. Bird’s-eye view In a lighter (but just as surprising) story of lives being saved, googly-eyed buoys are helping prevent seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. According to a Mongabay story that caught the attention of Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, these devices scare the birds away from the fishing gear. A study off Cornwall, England, found that nets fitted with kites shaped like birds of prey had 71 percent lower odds of catching seabirds, and nets with spinning “looming-eye” buoys had 59 percent lower odds. Becca says: I kinda love these “googly-eyed buoys,” despite their uncanny resemblance to Clippy the paperclip . What else we’re reading The fix for America’s terrible internet is hiding in Tennessee — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Vox What If a Crisis Pregnancy Center Was Pro-Choice? — shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby from The Cut The planet’s vital signs are getting worse. One of the easiest fixes is your diet. — shared by Michaela Haas from Grist In other news… Just after last week’s historic midterm elections, we wrapped up The Depolarization Series , an exploration of the many ways people are defying division and really listening to those who disagree with them. You can check out the full series here — and don’t miss the many fantastic videos we shared on Instagram. The post What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Επιπλέον καρέκλες στο Driveway
items.titleOriginal: Extra Chairs in the Driveway
items.description: Στο Fargo της Βόρειας Ντακότα, ο Prakash Mathew και η σύζυγός του Jane είχαν έναν όμορφο κήπο που οι άνθρωποι συχνά σταματούσαν να θαυμάσουν. Σκέφτηκαν να γράψουν τα ονόματα των επισκεπτών τους και χαιρετούσαν τον καθένα ονομαστικά την επόμενη φορά. Με την πάροδο του χρόνου, παρείχαν επιπλέον καρέκλες και κάλεσαν τους ανθρώπους να καθίσουν και να συνομιλήσουν, και ένα διαφορετικό είδος κήπου εμφανίστηκε. «Όταν πήγαμε για το δικό μας…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Fargo, North Dakota, Prakash Mathew and his wife Jane had a beautiful garden people would often stop to admire. They made a point of writing down their visitors' names and would greet each by name the next time. Over time, they provided extra chairs and invited people to sit and chat, and a different kind of garden emerged. "When we went for our walks, we could hardly walk two blocks without stopping and talking to someone." Jane died suddenly in December of last year. When summer came, Prakash continued to go to the driveway, and people still joined him. He asked, "What if we did this — sat in my driveway, but intentionally, every other week, with a topic?" Everybody loved it. Driveway Dialogues was born. A neighborhood spirit had been planted, "with a garden, a few extra chairs in front of the house, and a curiosity to care for others."

items.title: Τα παραβλεφθέντα οφέλη των μικρών χώρων και συμβουλές για να αξιοποιήσετε στο έπακρο το δικό σας
items.titleOriginal: The Overlooked Benefits of Small Spaces, and Tips for Making the Most of Yours
items.description: Το έτος που έκλεισα τα 30, μετακόμισα σε μια ήσυχη γειτονιά στο Westside του Λος Άντζελες. Ήμουν 10 λεπτά από την παραλία της Βενετίας και είχα ένα διαμέρισμα αποκλειστικά για μένα. Το μόνο αλίευμα (εκτός από το πάρκινγκ στο δρόμο); Ήταν 450 τετραγωνικά πόδια. Κάποιοι φίλοι με βοήθησαν να βελτιστοποιήσω το μέρος: Συναρμολογήσαμε ένα προσαρμοσμένο κρεβάτι Murphy, εγκαταστήσαμε ένα πτυσσόμενο τραπέζι στον τοίχο και cho…
items.descriptionOriginal: The year I turned 30, I moved to a peaceful neighborhood on Los Angeles’ Westside. I was 10 minutes from Venice Beach and had an apartment all to myself. The only catch (besides street parking)? It was 450 square feet. A couple of friends helped me optimize the place: We assembled a custom Murphy bed, installed a wall-mounted folding table, and chose decor that made it feel joyful and airy. Though I lamented not having more space at times, I discovered that my scaled-down quarters came with some perks. Styling the studio so intentionally felt empowering, and because it was so small, I often enjoyed my meals out in the courtyard under the sun. Years later, despite having married and moved into a comfortable condo, I still occasionally yearn for more square footage, particularly during dinner parties or when family visits for the holidays. To refresh my perspective, I spoke to interior design experts and therapists who helped illuminate some of the unexpected benefits of having a smaller home — and offered tips for making the most of yours. Benefits domin_domin—iStock/Getty Images Plus Cost and Cleaning We’ll start with perhaps the most obvious but still occasionally overlooked perks: “Less square footage means less time cleaning and organizing. Owning less means spending less time managing and maintaining your belongings,” Phoenix-based interior designer Mackenzie Collier explained in an email to Nice News. “That frees up more time for hobbies, socializing, and anything else you’d rather be doing!” She added that smaller spaces force us to be more thoughtful about what we buy and why (a welcome mindset shift for many), and that the money we save on quantity can be used to invest in quality — e.g., well-built furniture, bespoke decor, art. And it’s not just our shopping carts that feel the difference, Sierra Troitsky , an interior designer in Indianapolis, pointed out. “Smaller spaces are often more economical and environmentally friendly as they cost less to heat and cool,” she said. Mental Well-Being Less square footage can contribute to a greater sense of well-being because it can encourage us to be neat and organized, “which is calming for the brain,” said Sipora Weissman , a licensed therapist in Ventura, California. In a tiny room, a pile of unfolded laundry is a lot more noticeable than in a large one, for example, so we may be more inclined to actually, you know, put it away . “As a therapist who works with adults who get overstimulated easily, living in a small space can be overwhelming or it can actually be very supportive to someone’s nervous system,” Weissman explained. “If you fill that small space with tchotchkes and clutter, that will be a recipe for an unsettled brain. There are many scientific studies that show the negative impacts of clutter on the brain. But if you take this small space living situation as an opportunity, it can be very conducive to your mental health.” More Intentional Decor Just as I experienced when decorating my tiny quarters, less to work with can have a focusing effect. “A small living room lends itself to intentional decorating because you’re forced to narrow in on fewer, impactful pieces that set the tone for the space — say, a beautiful sofa, a well-sized rug, task and accent lighting, and some meaningful artwork,” said Elena Navarro, an interior designer and professional organizer at Sparkly Maid Austin . View this post on Instagram She added: “I love that limited square footage forces you to really think through everything that you bring in the door, from new dishes to cozy throw blankets to holiday decor. Where is the item going to live? Do you use it enough to warrant giving it a permanent home?” Better for Gathering and Bonding The reason celebrity chef Ina Garten considers six people the ideal number for a dinner party is the same reason your modest home might lend itself to more meaningful gatherings: intimacy. “Small group events tend to produce an environment that allows for more personalized conversation,” explained Whitney Willborn , a Texas-based licensed clinical social worker, adding that it’s easier to not only include everyone in the conversation but also to spot when others appear to be excluded. If guests are spread out in different rooms or fragmented into groups, it’s trickier to notice when a new friend is standing awkwardly by themself, for example. Your own family might benefit from a smaller floor plan, too. Collier recently moved out of a 900-square-foot home, and her household has experienced some nostalgia for the cozier living situation. “There was nowhere to escape to, so we’d sit together, watch a movie, or play games,” she said. “Those shared moments became some of our favorite memories.” Spend More Time in Community My al fresco dining habit of yore highlights how the wide world can beckon when your indoors isn’t vast. Collier had the same experience. “I’ve found that living in a small space encourages me to spend more time outdoors and in my community,” she shared. “Whether it was tending to my garden, or heading to a local coffee shop to work, living small naturally pushed me to get out into the community more.” Tips Double Duty Interior designer Preeti Shah made her name in New York, where minuscule apartments are no big deal (one of the tiniest is an infinitesimal 55 square feet !). When she moved to an area of Houston filled with massive homes, she was bemused. At around 3,000 square feet, her house is among the smallest — yet she said it’s where her neighborhood pals prefer to hang out. Courtesy of Preeti Shah Shah’s lounge area with convertible coffee-to-dining room table A design principle Shah prioritizes, in any sized space, is double duty. “Anything I purchase, I would like for my client to be able to use it in more than just one way,” she shared. Ottomans are great for seating and storage, twin beds can become kings when guests stay over, and dining chairs should be comfy enough to be used as additional living room seating. In her own house, rather than a dining room table that sits unused, she opted for a convertible coffee table that lifts and extends to seat 10. Size and Amount Matter Troitsky explained that getting furniture that’s sized correctly can help a lot with how large your home feels (e.g., an enormous couch in a tiny bedroom might make the space seem small). But that doesn’t mean you should automatically purchase miniature versions of everything you’d buy for a bigger area. “It’s best to take inventory of what you actually use, need, and love, and start there,” Navarro said. She added: “For holiday decor, instead of trying to deck out every inch of your small living space, pick one or two areas to really lean into — the Christmas tree, the mantel, the coffee table, etc.” Get Comfortable With Borrowing Why use up valuable storage space on extra glassware and guest seating for your one annual holiday get-together when you can call a friend and ask to borrow theirs? As a bonus, it gives you both an excuse for a visit. Another option is to rent what you need when you need it. Ultimately, do your best to remember that, as Navarro put it, “the goal is always to make your guests feel at home — not to impress them with how big your place is!” RELATED: Make Your Home Happier With These Dopamine-Inducing Decorating Tips

items.description: Στο Botton Village στο βόρειο Γιορκσάιρ, ένας ερευνητής φιλοσοφίας επισκέπτεται έναν παλιό του φίλο και βρίσκει κάτι που δεν περίμενε: έναν άντρα που μεταμορφώθηκε. Ο Μαξ, ο οποίος δυσκολευόταν να βρει τη βάση του σε συμβατικές ρυθμίσεις περίθαλψης, μετακινείται στην κοινότητα Camphill Esk Valley με αυτό που ο φίλος του περιγράφει ως «μια σταθερή ευκολία που δεν είχα δει πριν…
items.descriptionOriginal: At Botton Village in North Yorkshire's moors, a philosophy researcher visits an old friend and finds something he didn't expect: a man transformed. Max, who had struggled to find his footing in conventional care arrangements, moves through the Esk Valley Camphill Community with what his friend describes as "a settled ease I hadn't seen in him before." His explanation is simple and quietly devastating: "It's been the best two years of my life. Much better than anything before." What the researcher gradually comes to understand - through months of shared meals, garden work, and community forums - is that Max hadn't just found better support. He had found a place where his presence mattered, where contribution and belonging were woven into the daily fabric of life rather than delivered on a schedule. The article raises a question that conventional social care policy rarely pauses long enough to ask: if what people most need is genuine community, what does it mean that we have built a system structurally designed to provide everything but that?

items.titleOriginal: Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το Open Campus. Περνώντας από το συμβουλευτικό γραφείο του New River μια μέρα, η Stephanie Addikis παρατήρησε ότι τα βιβλία ζωγραφικής και τα Lego που είχε βοηθήσει να αποθηκεύσουν σε ένα κοντινό κουτί ήταν… «πολύ αγαπημένα». Αυτό ακριβώς ήλπιζε ότι θα συμβεί. Το «απασχολημένο κουτί» με παιχνίδια είναι μέρος μιας νέας προσπάθειας στο New River για προμήθεια…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Open Campus . W alking by New River’s advising office one day, Stephanie Addikis noticed that the coloring books and Legos that she had helped stock in a nearby box were … “well-loved.” This was just what she was hoping would happen. The “busy box” stuffed with toys is part of a new effort at New River to support parenting students. When students are filling out the FAFSA or visiting with their adviser, they can bring their children and know they will have toys nearby to entertain them. “I don’t think we realized how many kids were coming on campus until we put these out, and now they’re really being utilized,” said Addikis, who is the adult career coach and community outreach specialist at New River. New River Community College is working to integrate more support for parenting students throughout campus. Courtesy of New River Community College A report released a couple weeks ago from The Institute for College Access & Success, or TICAS, showed that about a quarter of students attending rural-serving institutions are parents. But those colleges are also less likely to have childcare on campus than their non-rural counterparts. A lack of data on the number of parenting students is one of the biggest challenges for colleges trying to support them, according to one of the authors of that report, Erika Roberson. There’s a reason that Addikis was so excited to see used toys on campus: She does not know exactly how many parent students go to New River. While at least five states have now required public colleges to ask students if they have children, and Virginia just passed similar legislation this spring , the lack of standardized data collection makes serving these students even more difficult. And supporting them matters because student parents are more likely to be students of color, low-income and the first in their families to go to college. Those challenges combined make them less likely to graduate than their non-parenting peers. But, like rural places do, these colleges are getting creative in expanding support even with limited data and funding. To collect more thorough data, Roane State Community College in eastern Tennessee is partnering with Achieving the Dream . Others are collaborating with local churches, women shelters, groups like United Way and other nonprofits to connect student parents with resources. Our reporter at partner newsroom The Fort Worth Report, Dang Le, recently reported on new childcare centers that opened at Tarrant County College with the support of the college, county and a childcare nonprofit. “Not all these schools are receiving robust grants to do this work,” Roberson said. “Maybe there are existing partnerships that schools have that they might be able to tap into to more explicitly support their student parents, or maybe there are ways in which they can modify syllabi to include family-friendly policies that don’t have dollar signs on it.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Rather than one new program, it’s a cultural shift that student parents are looking for, according to another recent report focused on six public rural-serving colleges and universities in California . In other words, student parents want to feel seen — by their counselors, advisers, professors and other staff members or peers. While parents make up a large portion of students at rural-serving schools, it’s common for these students to still feel isolated . That’s why several colleges featured in the TICAS report are starting peer parenting groups and hosting events. New River, for example, has a dedicated family study room with child-sized furniture in their library (which also serves as a public library) and consistently hosts events or dinners for students and faculty with children. New River provides care packages for new and expecting parents, including diapers, wipes, a Walmart gift card and t-shirts. Courtesy of New River Community College Addikis said she felt this cultural shift even more prominently at New River when funding to parent-support programs decreased. New River was one of the first five colleges to receive the College Attainment for Parent Students grants from the Virginia Foundation for Community College Education. In those first couple of years, the college created cohorts of 20 student parents, and each parent was eligible for $2,000 stipends per semester, including summer semesters. Now, the foundation associated with the community college system gives each of the 23 schools some funding, so the grant amounts have decreased. New River adjusted by starting an application process, and they granted 17 students $500 each this year. Addikis said more than half of the students who applied said they rely on friends and family for childcare, so this stipend will likely help reimburse things like gas or food. But with fewer financial resources, Addikis started to look at what she could do to grow relationships with these student parents and remind them that they are not on their own. For example, she has a work-study student who is also a parent this semester, and that student is planning to start a student parent club on campus. The challenge, she said, still remains in increasing awareness about the resources on campus. One thing that she said helped was creating a section of their first-year orientation course specifically for adult learners and highlighting resources available for parents. “I see it now as a warm hug, and a lot of love and support and just a building of awareness,” she said, talking about how the parent support has changed with less funding. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Still, researchers like those at TICAS still advocate for increased data and funding for student parent support, especially on rural campuses. Two federal grant programs in particular focus on this area: Childcare Access Means Parents in Schools and Basic Needs for Postsecondary Students. “I don’t want policymakers to forget rural parenting students,” Roberson said. “And if policymakers are really interested in strengthening rural economies, I think it’s important that they also invest in rural parenting students.” The post Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.title: Ο γάμος της ακυρώθηκε, έτσι προσκάλεσε 11 ξένους στην Ιρλανδία
items.titleOriginal: Her Wedding Was Canceled, So She Invited 11 Strangers to Ireland
items.description: Όταν ο αρραβώνας της Bridget Devaney τελείωσε μετά την επείγουσα ιατρική περίθαλψη του αρραβωνιαστικού της, έμεινε να κρατά σχέδια για ένα ταξίδι στη Βόρεια Ιρλανδία και μια ημέρα γάμου που δεν θα ερχόταν ποτέ. Αντί να τα εγκαταλείψει όλα, δημοσίευσε μια ανώνυμη πρόσκληση στα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης και 11 γυναίκες από τις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες, τον Καναδά και την Ουαλία είπαν ναι - σε έναν ξένο, μια χώρα, μια…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Bridget Devaney's engagement ended after her fianc 's medical emergency, she was left holding plans for a trip to Northern Ireland and a wedding day that would never come. Rather than abandon it all, she posted an anonymous invitation on social media, and 11 women from the United States, Canada, and Wales said yes - to a stranger, a country, and an uncertain week. "When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," Bridget told BBC News NI. On the day originally reserved for her wedding, the women dressed up and stood together against Northern Ireland's coastline for photographs that captured something the original plans never could have. What the trip quietly reveals is how much people are willing to show up for one another -- and how belonging can find us even in the ruins of what we thought our lives would look like.
